cards.method: Unit-root suite (ADF/KPSS/PP/ERS-DFGLS/Zivot-Andrews)
cards.when: heavy unit-root work with an explicit choice of deterministic model, DF-GLS (greater power), or Zivot-Andrews (ONE endogenous break)
cards.when_not: a fast yes/no with a p-value (-> #1); seasonal (-> #89); MULTIPLE breaks (-> #3); panel (-> #6)

alternatives.criterion: a fast ready-made p-value without the test regression
power is critical, series close to unity
ONE break at an unknown date (bpoint = the estimate)
multiple breaks

output_key_fields: teststat: numeric; cval: matrix of critical values 1/5/10% (-> nested rows+dim+axis labels)
model/type/lag: deterministic spec & lags (documents the decision)
bpoint (unitroot_zivot_andrews): estimated break position; tstats: rolling t-stat profile; yd (unitroot_dfgls): GLS-detrended
testreg/model/res: heavy lm/text -> stubbed by to_mcp
interpretation_traps: NO p-value: compare teststat with cval by hand
tail polarity: ADF/PP/ERS/ZA reject when teststat < cval (left tail); KPSS when teststat > cval (right tail)
the result carries the test regression alongside the statistic, not just a verdict; unitroot_zivot_andrews handles ONE break ONLY
sources: Elliott Rothenberg Stock 1996 (Econometrica 64(4):813, DF-GLS; cval MacKinnon 1991)

cards.method: Structural change (Bai-Perron multiple breaks / Chow-F / CUSUM)
cards.when: testing & estimating the structural stability of a relationship; CUSUM (dating-free), sup-F (one break), Bai-Perron (multiple breaks + dates)

cards.when: seasonally adjusting a monthly/quarterly series + isolating trend/seasonal/irregular via regARIMA+SEATS/X-11
cards.when_not: TESTING a seasonal unit root (not adjustment -> #89); non-seasonal; no X-13 binaries (STL/10); structural breaks (-> #3)

cards.method: Panel unit-root (LLC/IPS/Fisher/Hadri + Pesaran CIPS)
cards.when: stationarity in a macro panel (i×t, large T); LLC/IPS/Fisher/Hadri (purtest) or CIPS (2nd generation, robust to cross-section dependence)
cards.when_not: univariate (-> #1/#2); ESTIMATING a panel equation FE/RE/GMM (-> category 08); panel cointegration; short-T micro panel

alternatives.criterion: CIPS under cross-sectional dependence; LLC/IPS when the units are independent
IPS heterogeneous root per unit; LLC a common root (more powerful if it holds)
confirmatory (H0 stationarity), as KPSS is against ADF

output_key_fields: run_panel_unit_root: a flat record {statistic, p_value, parameter, method, data_name, alternative}
args/idres: arguments + per-individual ADF regressions (records); adjval/sigma2 only for levinlin/ips
ips_tbar_crit: critical values only for ips_stat=tbar (lags=0)
run_cipstest: the whole test record
interpretation_traps: polarity: LLC/IPS/Fisher/CIPS have H0=unit root; BUT hadri has H0=stationarity (the opposite, like KPSS)
IPS non-rejection != all units I(1); it rejects if SOME units are stationary (heterogeneous alternative)
gate: ips_stat='tbar' does not apply when lags>0 (stop); tbar/hadri/levinlin not available for unbalanced panels
1st-generation purtest is size-distorted under cross-section dependence -> CIPS
sources: Levin Lin Chu 2002 (J.Econometrics 108:1); Im Pesaran Shin 2003 (115:53)
precondition_tools: make_panel_frame (panel structure before cipstest: pseries gate)
run_cipstest (model=cmg if cross-sectional dependence is present)

cards.method: Classical univariate forecasting: ARIMA, ETS, Theta and TBATS
cards.when: univariate forecasting of one ts with automatic ARIMA/ETS, a robust Theta baseline, or TBATS for multiple/non-integer seasonalities
cards.when_not: multivariate structure (VAR/VECM), calendar holidays (prophet), intermittent/non-gaussian (smooth/ADAM)

alternatives.criterion: you want a keyed indexed-table workflow, distribution-valued forecasts, or several models fitted at once
you need ETS+ARIMA+regression unified or a non-gaussian error
holidays/calendar effects dominate

output_key_fields: mean: point forecasts (ts -> {values,start,frequency})
lower/upper: prediction interval bounds per level (matrix)
level: confidence levels (80,95)
fitted/residuals: in-sample one-step values for diagnostics
accuracy: training-set measures (RMSE,MAE,MAPE,MASE,ACF1)
model: fitted object (compact stub in to_mcp)
interpretation_traps: accuracy(fc) is in-sample (training-set), NOT out-of-sample generalisation — for OOS use 15-model-evaluation (tsCV/DM) or a holdout
MAPE is unstable/infinite when y≈0 (growth rates) — prefer MASE (<1 = better than naive)
ETS/ARIMA prediction intervals assume gaussian innovations — they understate under heavy tails
run_auto_arima gate: exog_handle not a data frame + NROW(exog_handle)==length(y); run_tbats gate: NCOL(y)==1
y must be a series with the correct frequency, otherwise a non-seasonal fit results
sources: Hyndman & Khandakar 2008 JSS 27(3) (automatic ARIMA order selection)
precondition_tools: c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test

cards.method: Tidy ARIMA and ETS forecasting over grouped series
cards.when: ARIMA/ETS over many keyed series at once (an indexed table + a model formula) with distribution-valued forecasts, manual pdq/PDQ orders, or the ETS state components
cards.when_not: a single plain series without the keyed-table overhead (-> #7); Theta/TBATS/multiple seasonality (-> #7); non-gaussian (-> #10); intermittent demand (-> #135)

alternatives.criterion: non-long-format quick use or Theta/TBATS
ETS+ARIMA+exog_handle together or a different error distribution

output_key_fields: forecast: a table carrying a distribution column -> quantile grid (probs+mean+sd); median≈point
glance: 1-row sigma2/log_lik/AIC/AICc/BIC + ar_roots/ma_roots (complex -> {re,im})
long-format: coefficients (term,estimate,std_error,statistic,p_value)
components: ETS-only dable with states (level,slope,season)
fitted/residuals: in-sample (type innovation vs regression)
interpretation_traps: <distribution> is NOT a number — take median or mean, not the raw cell
ar_roots/ma_roots are complex; stationarity/invertibility ⇒ modulus>1 (sqrt(re^2+im^2))
glance does NOT compute accuracy — for OOS you need new_data + accuracy (15-model-evaluation)
missing values: ETS is a hard error (the gate rejects any gap), ARIMA reverts with a warning — do not confuse the two
sources: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd ed.
Hyndman, Koehler, Ord & Snyder 2008, Forecasting with Exponential Smoothing: the State Space Approach
precondition_tools: c00_data_utilities/replacement_missing_values.impute_kalman (for ETS, if anyNA)

cards.method: Additive/logistic-trend forecasting with holidays and multiple seasonalities (Prophet)
cards.when: decomposable additive trend+seasonality(Fourier)+holidays+regressors with automatic changepoints; calendar effects, gaps/irregular index, an interpretable decomposition
cards.when_not: clean monthly/quarterly macro series without a calendar (ARIMA/ETS are more accurate); autoregressive dynamics; a very short series

alternatives.criterion: clean low-frequency macro series without calendar structure
explanatory regressors with state-space rigour
the objective is causal impact, not a forecast

output_key_fields: forecast: df records; ds,yhat(point),yhat_lower/upper(interval),trend,*_terms(components)
future: the future df (ds + regressors)
regressor_coefficients: center/coef per regressor (only with regressors)
cv: per cutoff yhat,y(actual),cutoff,ds,horizon (run_prophet_cv)
metrics: horizon + mse/rmse/mae/mape/mdape/smape/coverage
interpretation_traps: the default interval_width=0.8 ⇒ 80% intervals, NOT 95%
without mcmc_samples>0 the intervals capture trend uncertainty only (MAP) — they understate
run_prophet_cv is expensive (many re-fits)
horizon/units in cross_validation are time units (180 days ≠ 180 monthly periods)
coverage in metrics must be ≈ interval_width for calibrated intervals
gates: seasonality_mode∈{additive,multiplicative}; logistic->cap; regressors->an explicit future with the columns; macro spacing>=28d auto-disables weekly/daily
sources: Taylor & Letham 2018 Forecasting at scale (The American Statistician)
prophet reference manual + Facebook Prophet docs

[#19] SVAR / IRF / FEVD / Blanchard-Quah (theory-based identification)
Category: 04-structural-shocks
Nodes: vr_svar · vr_bq · vr_irf · vr_fevd
WHEN: a reduced-form varest exists + credible theoretical restrictions (A/B contemporaneous or Blanchard-Quah long-run) for a full IRF/FEVD system.
NOT when: no credible restriction (-> #20/#21); you want robustness to misspecification or non-linearity (-> #22).
Alternatives: #20 data-driven SVAR identification (there is no theory for A/B -> statistical/data-driven identification.) · #21 sign-restriction SVAR (only qualitative sign priors -> set-identification.) · #22 local projections (robustness to non-linearity/misspecification or an externally identified shock (LP-IV).)
Output: irf: 3D array {values,dim,axis labels} — the response to an impulse per horizon · Lower/Upper: bootstrap CI bands at ci (0 inside => not significant) · fevd: named list per variable — shares of forecast variance per shock · A/B/Ase/Bse: structural matrices + SE; Sigma.U: residual covariance · LRIM: long-run impact matrix (BQ/SVAR) · LR: LR test of overidentifying restrictions (small p => the restrictions are rejected)
Pitfalls: Cholesky is ordering-dependent: the variable order is a theoretical assumption, not a given. · bootstrap bands measure only sampling uncertainty given the ID — they do not correct a wrong identification. · an unstable VAR (roots>=1) => explosive IRF, invalid CI; a stability post-check is required (roots). · Blanchard-Quah: the long-run restriction holds in first differences — the wrong order of integration invalidates the LRIM. · the IRF sign/normalization is a convention (a unit positive shock).
Sources: Blanchard-Quah 1989 AER · Sims 1980 · Lütkepohl 2005 New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis · Enders 2015 Applied Econometric Time Series ch.5 · Pfaff 2008 JSS 27(4) (VAR, SVAR and SVEC models)

cards.method: Data-driven SVAR identification (Cholesky / changes-in-vol / distance-cov / non-Gaussian ML) + HD + counterfactual + wild/mb bootstrap
cards.when: a reduced-form VAR fit without credible theory -> statistical identification through heteroskedasticity (svar_id_volatility_change), independence (svar_id_distance_covariance) or non-Gaussianity (svar_id_non_gaussian_ml); plus historical decomposition & counterfactual.
cards.when_not: exact theoretical restrictions -> #19; only sign priors -> #21; Gaussian and homoskedastic shocks -> statistical identification fails.

alternatives.criterion: exact contemporaneous/long-run restrictions exist.
only qualitative sign priors -> set-identification.

alternatives.alt: #22 local projections with an external instrument
alternatives.criterion: an external instrument/proxy for one shock (full-system ID is not needed).

output_key_fields: B: structural impact matrix (column j = the immediate response to the j-th shock)
model: the identified model handle (feeds svar_irf/svar_fevd/svar_hd/svar_cf and the bootstraps)
svar_id_volatility_change: Lambda (post-break heteroskedasticity), Lambda_SE, wald_statistic (test of equal eigenvalues)
svar_id_non_gaussian_ml: df (the t degrees of freedom of the shocks), sigma, B_stand
svar_hd: hd — the contribution of each shock to the historical path; svar_cf: actual vs counter
wild/mb boot: point/mean/lower/upper bands (default 0.16/0.84), SE, nboot, design, distr
interpretation_traps: svar_id_volatility_change wald_statistic: the identification is valid ONLY if the test REJECTS equal eigenvalues of Lambda — otherwise the shocks are not identified (a spurious B).
statistical ID identifies the columns of B only up to sign & permutation — you must label which column = which economic shock.
svar_id_distance_covariance and svar_id_non_gaussian_ml break down if the shocks are Gaussian (at most one Gaussian shock is allowed).
the stochastic routines (svar_id_distance_covariance, svar_id_non_gaussian_ml, the bootstraps) take an explicit seed (default 2025) for reproducibility.
svar_wild_boot: fixed vs recursive design; svar_mb_boot for dependent residuals.
sources: Lange, Dalheimer, Herwartz & Maxand 2021 JSS (data-driven SVAR identification)
precondition_tools: c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test

cards.method: Sign-restriction SVAR (Uhlig rejection & penalty, Rubio-Ramirez/Waggoner/Zha)
cards.when: only qualitative expectations about the direction of the responses (sign restrictions) -> Bayesian set-identification (sampling rotations).
cards.when_not: exact restrictions -> #19; point-identified statistical identification -> #20; the rejection sampler can accept very few draws when the sign set is tight.

alternatives.criterion: exact contemporaneous/long-run restrictions.
statistical/data-driven point identification (without subjective sign priors).

alternatives.alt: #22 local projections with an external shock
alternatives.criterion: you already have an identified shock/proxy.

output_key_fields: irf_median/irf_lower/irf_upper: posterior summary bands (steps x nvar) at lower_q/upper_q
fevd_median/_lower/_upper: FEVD bands
n_keep: accepted draws; steps; nvar; type (median/mean); constrained; variables
interpretation_traps: set-identification, not point: the bands are the range of many admissible models (identification uncertainty), not the sampling uncertainty of a single model.
the pointwise median IRF does NOT correspond to a single structural model (Fry-Pagan 2011 critique).
constrained polarity/sign convention: the 1st element = the shock of interest, the sign = the direction; the wrong sign -> the inverted shock.
too few accepted rotations -> cryptic errors (ldraw/SDraws) which the wrapper translates into a gate (increase draws, relax the restrictions).
the sampler takes an explicit seed (default 12345); the plotting target is deliberately omitted — this node returns data, not charts.

cards.method: Local projections (Jordà) + LP-IV / non-linear state-dependent / panel
cards.when: IRF without a full VAR (one regression per horizon), robust to misspecification; state dependence (two regimes), external instrument/proxy (LP-IV + 2SLS), panel FE/IV/GMM; fiscal multipliers (cumul_mult).
cards.when_not: you want full-system FEVD/HD and efficiency -> #19/#20; very long horizons with little data (the local-projection variance explodes).

alternatives.criterion: full-system FEVD/HD, efficiency, lower variance at long horizons.
identification exclusively through sign priors (LP needs an already-identified shock).
a static/dynamic panel without an IRF horizon.

output_key_fields: irf_lin_mean/low/up: matrices — row = response variable, column = horizon (transposed relative to the IRF array of #19)
irf_s1_*/irf_s2_*: regime 1/2 responses (non-linear); fz: logistic switching function values
variables, hor, lags, shock_type (0=sd,1=unit), trend, confint, cumul_mult, use_twosls
interpretation_traps: confint is a MULTIPLIER, not a probability: 1=68%, 1.65=90%, 1.96=95% (Newey-West band width).
orientation: in irf_lin_mean rows are variables and columns are horizons — do not confuse it with the 3-D IRF array of #19.
the LP variance grows with the horizon -> wide bands at large h; do not over-interpret long-horizon significance.
cumul_mult=True gives cumulative multipliers, and only when lags_criterion is unset; shock_type 0 = one standard deviation, 1 = unit.
LP-IV: validity depends entirely on the instrument (relevance+exogeneity); there is no built-in weak-IV test; endog_data MUST be a data_frame, not a series.
precondition_tools: c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test
c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_kpss_test

cards.method: Johansen procedure + restricted VECM + Phillips-Ouliaris/Engle-Granger residual tests
cards.when: A system of >=2 I(1) series; testing the cointegration rank + extracting beta/alpha, or a residual-based test (coint_phillips_ouliaris, Pu/Pz).
cards.when_not: You need p-values for the rank (go to #24); mixed order I(0)/I(1) (go to #25, ARDL bounds).

alternatives.criterion: You want p-values for the rank + 5 deterministic specs.
Single equation with a mixed order of integration I(0)/I(1).
The rank is known (=1) and you want an unbiased estimate of beta.

output_key_fields: teststat: statistics per rank hypothesis (compare with cval)
cval: critical values 10/5/1% (NOT a p-value)
lambda: eigenvalues
V: normalised cointegrating vectors (beta)
W: loading weights (alpha, speed of adjustment)
PI: Pi = alpha beta'
coint_phillips_ouliaris teststat/cval: Pu or Pz; res = the residuals of the cointegrating regression
cajorls beta/rlm_coef: restricted VECM at rank r
interpretation_traps: coint_johansen gives ONLY critical values, NOT a p-value — compare teststat > cval (#24 documents the same convention).

coint_johansen(type=..) returns ONLY the selected test type per call: teststat/cval hold trace OR max-eigen, not both — to compare trace vs eigen call it TWICE (type='trace' & type='eigen'); by contrast rank_test gives trace AND eigen p-values together in one call.
The K of coint_johansen (lags in levels) = lag+1 of vecm_rank_test (an off-by-one).
KPSS has the opposite polarity among the preconditions: reject H0 ⇒ non-stationary.
Pz is invariant to the normalisation; prefer it when there is no natural dependent variable.
the result serialises to a compact stub → rely on the atomic fields.

Category: 05-cointegration

WHEN: A system of >=2 I(1) series; testing the cointegration rank + extracting beta/alpha, or a residual-based test (coint_phillips_ouliaris, Pu/Pz).
NOT when: You need p-values for the rank (go to #24); mixed order I(0)/I(1) (go to #25, ARDL bounds).
Alternatives: #24 rank_test (You want p-values for the rank + 5 deterministic specs.) · #25 ARDL / #26 dynamic ARDL-ECM (Single equation with a mixed order of integration I(0)/I(1).) · #27 modified-OLS cointegrating regressions (The rank is known (=1) and you want an unbiased estimate of beta.)
Output: teststat: statistics per rank hypothesis (compare with cval) · cval: critical values 10/5/1% (NOT a p-value) · lambda: eigenvalues · V: normalised cointegrating vectors (beta) · W: loading weights (alpha, speed of adjustment) · PI: Pi = alpha beta' · coint_phillips_ouliaris teststat/cval: Pu or Pz; res = the residuals of the cointegrating regression · cajorls beta/rlm_coef: restricted VECM at rank r
Pitfalls: coint_johansen gives ONLY critical values, NOT a p-value — compare teststat > cval (#24 documents the same convention). · coint_johansen(type=..) returns ONLY the selected test type per call: teststat/cval hold trace OR max-eigen, not both — to compare trace vs eigen call it TWICE (type='trace' & type='eigen'); by contrast rank_test gives trace AND eigen p-values together in one call. · The K of coint_johansen (lags in levels) = lag+1 of vecm_rank_test (an off-by-one). · KPSS has the opposite polarity among the preconditions: reject H0 ⇒ non-stationary. · Pz is invariant to the normalisation; prefer it when there is no natural dependent variable. · the result serialises to a compact stub → rely on the atomic fields.

Single equation, mixed order of integration.
Known rank=1, you want an unbiased beta with t-tests.

output_key_fields: beta: cointegrating vectors

cards.when: Single-equation cointegration with regressors of mixed order I(0)/I(1); a bounds test without pre-classification; multipliers/ECM/cointegrating equation.
cards.when_not: Any I(2) series (the bounds test breaks down); multiple cointegrating relations (go to the system Johansen).

cards.method: Dynamic ARDL/ECM + stochastic simulation + PSS bounds + residual diagnostics
cards.when: A single-equation ARDL/ECM when you want counterfactual shock simulation (response path chart-data) + native PSS bounds + BG/SW residual diagnostics.
cards.when_not: You do not need simulation/diagnostics (go to ARDL); system/multiple relations; I(2) series.

alternatives.criterion: The same PSS bounds, richer multipliers/auto-order, without simulation.
System VECM.
Unbiased estimation of beta.

output_key_fields: coefficients/AIC/BIC/log_lik/nobs/residuals
simulation: a frame with the central path + ll95/ul95 (chart data, only when simulate=True)
fstat/tstat: PSS statistics (NOT a p-value)
f_bounds/t_bounds: named vectors of critical I(0)/I(1) × 10/5/1%
bg_statistic/bg_pvalue: Breusch-Godfrey autocorrelation
sw_statistic/sw_pvalue: Shapiro-Wilk normality
interpretation_traps: dyn_pss_bounds does NOT give a p-value — compare fstat/tstat with the I(0)/I(1) bounds (as in #2).
An inconclusive region between the bounds ⇒ NO conclusion.
data MUST be a plain data_frame, NOT a series (hard gate).
dyn_pss_bounds REQUIRES ec=True (the error-correction form).
simulate=True is Monte Carlo (stochastic) → wrapper seed=2025; a different seed ⇒ different interval bands.
A Breusch-Godfrey rejection ⇒ autocorrelation undermines the validity of the bounds test.
sources: Jordan & Philips 2018 (cointegration testing and dynamic simulation of ARDL models)

cards.method: Global VAR (GVAR)
cards.when: a panel of many countries (the same variables) + bilateral trade weights: country-specific VAR with weighted foreign variables — cross-border spillovers
cards.when_not: one country -> a VAR (#11, category 03); cointegration -> a global VECM (not exposed); IRF (not implemented on this card)

alternatives.criterion: one country, or the weighting structure does not matter to you
you want spillover matrices instead of structural coefficients; no external weight matrix
cointegration dominates (out of scope)

output_key_fields: country_var_models: a list of varest objects (one per country, via country_names)
coef_white/coef_nw: coefficients with White/Newey-West HAC SE; gv_coef*(sheet=k) the coefficient table of country k
foreign_variables: weighted foreign variables per country (the heart of the GVAR)
gv_residual_correlation: mean cross-sectional residual cor, VAR vs GVAR (a reduction is good)
gv_structural: G0/G1/G2/F1/F2 structural matrices (for downstream IRF/forecast)
interpretation_traps: weight_matrix is accessed POSITIONALLY -> the wrong column order = silently wrong (gated where the mis-order is detectable)
the 'ID' column is EXACTLY upper case (the documentation says 'id' — stale); Time must be a character-parseable date (not an integer)
weight_matrix is mandatory (omitting it fails obscurely); a real N x N matrix, not a frame; a zero diagonal
p is restricted to {1,2} (documented); >=2 variables; a strictly balanced panel
GVAR_GF returns only G0/G1/F1 when the minimum lag=1 (data-driven shape)
sources: Dees, di Mauro, Pesaran & Smith 2007 (J. Applied Econometrics 22:1)
di Mauro & Pesaran 2013 The GVAR Handbook
precondition_tools: c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test (+ KPSS confirmatory) — stationarity per variable

cards.method: Connectedness (Diebold-Yılmaz, full)
cards.when: a multivariate series (markets/returns/macro): a spillover matrix from the VAR FEVD (Diebold-Yılmaz) — static/rolling/TVP-VAR; TCI/TO/FROM/NET
cards.when_not: you want a decomposition per frequency band -> #52; a structural GVAR of countries -> #50; univariate (meaningless)

alternatives.criterion: the distribution of spillovers per frequency band (short/long run)
generalized (Pesaran-Shin, order-invariant) with no Cholesky ordering; orthogonalized with a structural ordering
TVP = smooth variation over time; rolling = discrete windows

output_key_fields: TCI: Total Connectedness Index (%) — systemic interconnection
TO/FROM: transmits to / receives from; NET=TO-FROM (positive=net transmitter)
NPT/NPDC: net pairwise directional connectedness
TABLE/CT: the full spillover matrix (row=origin, column=recipient)
interpretation_traps: Diebold-Yılmaz = predictive/forecast-error connectedness, NOT structural causality
minimum sample n>=nlag*(k+1)+2 (VAR); otherwise silent NaN se/a wrong dimension (gated)
x MUST carry a date index and have >=2 columns
connectedness is fixed to 'Time' (frequency = #52); model is restricted to VAR/TVP-VAR
the progress message ('Estimating model') goes to stderr — not a violation of the no-print rule
precondition_tools: c01_preparation_prechecks/unit_root_normality.run_adf_test (+ KPSS) — stationarity (the VAR requires it)

alternatives.criterion: the total spillover suffices, or you want TVP/QVAR built in
BK12 is order-invariant (the dominant choice); BK09 uses a Cholesky ordering
within=True is the share inside the band; False the absolute contribution to the total

cards.method: Spatial regression (lag/error)
cards.when: cross-sectional data with spatial dependence: ML estimation of spatial lag (SAR, rho)/error (SEM, lambda)/SAC-SARAR + impacts (direct/indirect/total)
cards.when_not: only building weights / testing autocorrelation -> #54; GMM/2SLS/Bayesian/SLX (not exposed); no spatial structure -> lm

alternatives.criterion: the neighbouring dependent variable has a substantive effect (spillover)
the spatial dependence is a nuisance in the errors
both, or + spatial lags of the regressors

output_key_fields: coefficients/coef_table: Estimate/SE/z/p; rho (SAR)/lambda (SEM) spatial parameters + SE
spr_impacts: direct/indirect/total effects — REQUIRED to interpret lag/Durbin (the raw coefficients are misleading)
lr_test_vs_ols/wald_test_rho/lm_test: spatial-dependence diagnostics, as atomic records
hausman_test: error models ONLY; bp_test: Breusch-Pagan heteroskedasticity
interpretation_traps: spr_impacts is MANDATORY for lag/Durbin/SAC: the raw coefficients are misleading because of the feedback through W
method='moments' was excluded (it fails on ML fits); Hausman is for error models ONLY (gated)
the weights argument MUST be a spatial weights object built by spw_weights; a plain matrix gives 'No neighbourhood list'
an invalid Durbin value (a string that is not a formula) is silently ignored (the fallback is False, gated)
quiet=True is always hardcoded (otherwise the optimiser prints)
sources: LeSage & Pace 2009 Introduction to Spatial Econometrics (direct/indirect/total impacts)
Bivand & Piras 2015 JSS 63(18) (comparing implementations of estimation methods for spatial econometrics)

c09_cross_section_networks/spatial_weights_diagnostics.spw_moran_test (is there any spatial autocorrelation at all? otherwise this is pointless)

cards.method: Spatial weights / diagnostics
cards.when: preliminary work: building spatial weights from coordinates (kNN/distance/grid) + testing spatial autocorrelation (Moran/Geary/join-count/local Moran)
cards.when_not: estimating a spatial model -> #53; polygon GIS/shapefiles (poly2nb/sf not exposed); EB smoothing/MC tests (out of scope)

alternatives.criterion: a fixed number of neighbours per unit
adjacency by distance (a variable number)
a regular grid of cells (rook/queen)

alternatives.alt: Moran vs Geary vs join-count vs local Moran
alternatives.criterion: Moran is general; Geary captures local differences; join-count is for factors; local/LISA answers WHERE

output_key_fields: neighbours (nb) and the weights list: spatial weights (style='W' row-standardized is the classic choice)
spw_neighbour_diagnostics: cardinalities, no_neighbour_count, n_components (islands)
moran_test/geary_test/joincount_test: atomic records {statistic, p_value, estimate, alternative}
local_moran: data_frame Ii/E.Ii/Var.Ii/Z.Ii/Pr + quadrant (HH/LL clusters, HL/LH outliers)
interpretation_traps: Moran I: +1=positive autocorrelation (clusters), rejecting H0=structure is present
Geary C has the INVERSE scale: C<1=positive autocorrelation, C=1 random, C>1 negative (do not read it like Moran)
dnearneigh with d1>=d2 does NOT error -> silently an nb with zero neighbours everywhere (gated)
the missing-value policy is not forwarded as a value: it is resolved by a literal switch
spw_geary_test does NOT allow a 'pass' missing-value policy (structurally excluded)

cards.method: HP / Baxter-King / Christiano-Fitzgerald filters
cards.when: a fast trend/cycle decomposition (output gap) without estimating a model; CF-asymmetric fills the end (end-of-sample gap, no missing tail) but is internally full-sample time-varying/revisable — real-time only at the endpoint; a non-revisable real-time gap -> #92 one-sided HP
cards.when_not: you want standard errors or credible bands (-> #58/#59/#60), a common trend across several series (-> #61), or a non-revisable Basel gap (-> #92)

alternatives.criterion: real-time / Basel III credit gap (non-revisable)
avoiding the spurious cycles of the HP filter
you want SE bands + a model-based forecast

output_key_fields: trend: potential output (ts)
cycle: output gap in % of 100*log(GDP) (ts)
lambda: the effective smoothing parameter
na_each_end: how many observations stay blank at each edge (the BK / symmetric-CF endpoint problem)
interpretation_traps: an interior gap silently blanks the WHOLE cycle (silently wrong, so a hard gate)
BK and the symmetric/fixed CF leave nfix observations blank at EACH edge -> the most recent gap is missing
the two-sided HP is revised at the edge (endpoint bias) -> NOT for real-time policy
the choice of lambda (1600 quarterly / Ravn-Uhlig) changes the gap dramatically

CF-asymmetric fills the end BUT the values are revised just as with the two-sided HP: interior points use future data (time-varying weights, Christiano-Fitzgerald 2003) — only the last observation is genuinely one-sided

cards.method: oaxaca (Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition)
cards.when: cross-section; decomposing the MEAN gap of a continuous outcome between TWO groups (0/1) into explained/endowments vs unexplained/coefficients (+interaction, three-fold)
cards.when_not: >2 groups; a causal claim (unexplained ≠ discrimination); a non-linear/binary outcome; a time-series/panel gap

alternatives.criterion: you want an explicit interaction term + a complete accounting split with no reference choice (Jann 2008)
you want 'how much of the gap closes if we equalised X'; choose group_weight (pooled or A/B)
the gap varies across the DISTRIBUTION (glass ceiling/sticky floor), not only at the mean
a binary or count outcome; outside this wrapper (the regression function is locked to least squares)

output_key_fields: twofold: overall per reference weight (group_weight); coef_explained/se_explained (endowments), coef_unexplained/se_unexplained (+_A/_B)
twofold_variables: the decomposition per regressor (column variable)
threefold: coef_endowments, coef_coefficients, coef_interaction (+SEs)
threefold_variables: three-fold per regressor
x_means: mean_A/mean_B/mean_diff per regressor (the raw material of the endowments effect)
y: y_A/y_B/y_diff — mean outcomes & the total gap (= the sum of the components)
n: n_A/n_B/n_pooled; n_dropped: the rows silently dropped for missing values
interpretation_traps: an invalid group, input or formula makes the decomposition emit a message and return nothing at all rather than raising — hence a pre-gate and a post-gate that the result is non-empty
a degenerate fit: a per-group least-squares fit that is rank-deficient or has df_residual<=0 comes back with misleading coefficients and NO error; hence a post-gate on each group regression
'unexplained' ≠ discrimination: it absorbs omitted variables & functional-form error (Jann 2008); NOT causal
sign: y_diff=y_A−y_B (group=0 → A); check which group is 0/1 before interpreting; the components sum to y_diff
the two-fold split depends on the reference group_weight; a different weight → a different explained/unexplained split
the bootstrap standard errors are stochastic → the generator is seeded before the call (the same seed → an identical split)
rows with missing values are dropped silently → n_dropped reports them
sources: Blinder 1973 J. Human Resources; Oaxaca 1973 Int. Economic Review (the original decompositions)
Jann 2008 Stata Journal 8(4):453-479 (two-fold reference schemes, three-fold, unexplained≠discrimination)

cards.when: residual diagnostics for a regression (lm/glm): serial correlation (BG), heteroskedasticity (BP), wrong functional form (RESET)
cards.when_not: ARCH in a time series (→ #77); unit root or stationarity (→ category 01); models beyond least squares/GLM (→ the VAR serial-correlation test, #11)

cards.method: Descriptive statistics as data (ACF/PACF/CCF/rolling/correlation matrix + per-pair correlation inference)
cards.when: pre-model exploration/diagnostics; ARMA order id (ACF/PACF), lead/lag (CCF), rolling stats, correlation matrix — all numeric data; desc_cor_test when you need INFERENCE (p-values/CI) per pair with multiplicity control
cards.when_not: formal stationarity (ACF is indicative -> ADF/KPSS cat.01); causality (CCF != Granger); partial/conditional correlation (conditioning on third variables -> regression cat.06/07); autocorrelated series without prewhitening (the i.i.d. null of cor_test is violated -> inflated Type I)

alternatives.alt: ACF cut-off -> MA(q), PACF cut-off -> AR(p)
alternatives.criterion: Box-Jenkins order identification — use them together
rank-based, robust to non-linearity/outliers vs pearson (linear)
smoothing (non-causal) vs align=right (causal, default)

desc_correlations = POINT estimates (p×p matrix, no hypothesis, no p-value) -> exploration/heatmap. desc_cor_test = per-pair INFERENCE (statistic, df, p-value, conf_int) + MANDATORY multiplicity correction. The point estimates are IDENTICAL (test-covered) — the difference is ONLY the inference

BH controls the FDR (more powerful, for screening many pairs); holm/hochberg/hommel/bonferroni control the FWER (when EVERY false positive is costly). Bonferroni is dominated by holm — use holm. The alias 'fdr' is NOT exposed (identical to BH)

pairwise = the maximum n per pair but a DIFFERENT sample per pair (the p-values are not strictly comparable); complete = a listwise drop giving a COMMON sample across all pairs (comparable, smaller n); 'raise' = a hard stop on any missing value

output_key_fields: acf/pacf/ccf: numeric + lag + n_used; ci_upper/ci_lower = ±1.96/sqrt(n) white-noise band
desc_rolling: the rolled series (index-aligned, blank at the edges) + the index
desc_correlations: correlation (matrix->nested+axis labels), n=rows supplied, n_pairwise=per-pair complete

desc_cor_test: pairs = long-format records PER PAIR (var1, var2, n, estimate, statistic, statistic_name, parameter, p_value, p_adjusted, conf_low, conf_high, ties, exact_used); ALWAYS read p_adjusted, NOT p_value
desc_cor_test: pair_order = an EXPLICIT deterministic order (upper triangle by COLUMN INDEX (1,2),(1,3),..,(p-1,p) — NOT alphabetical), so that stored workflows reproduce (§5)
desc_cor_test: n_rows_input / n_rows_used / n_missing_cells (n_missing_cells is measured BEFORE the listwise drop); any_ties / any_exact_fallback / warnings = degradation flags
interpretation_traps: non-stationary series: the ACF decays slowly and linearly (an artefact, not structure) — test stationarity first

CCF: with ccf(x, y) (as the wrapper calls it) lag k estimates cor(x[t+k], y[t]) -> NEGATIVE lags = x leads y (x leads, peak at lag<0), POSITIVE lags = x lags behind (y leads); confirm the lag sign in the raw object before concluding lead/lag
desc_correlations: with pairwise completion and gaps the scalar n OVERSTATES — read n_pairwise (a strong correlation on a small n_pairwise is fragile)

desc_cor_test: Kendall and Spearman define NEITHER a confidence interval NOR degrees of freedom — the wrapper returns an explicit blank in conf_low/conf_high/parameter, NEVER a silently omitted field. The interval is defined only for Pearson, and only on at least 4 complete pairs (live-verified)

desc_cor_test: with ties cor_test silently DOWNGRADES the exact p-value to an asymptotic approximation and ONLY warns ('cannot compute exact p-value with ties'). The wrapper exposes this as DATA: ties / exact_used / any_exact_fallback / warnings (each warning carries its pair). Check exact_used before trusting small p-values

desc_cor_test: for spearman with n>1290 AS 89 is abandoned silently (WITHOUT a warning) in favour of the t-approximation. the cor_test routine states 'n < 1290' while the stats code checks 'n <= 1290' — the wrapper encodes the CODE (live-verified), which is why exact_used is reliable

desc_cor_test: on a constant (zero-variance) column the correlation test does NOT error — it ONLY warns ('the standard deviation is zero') and returns a blank estimate and p-value (live-verified for all 3 methods). The wrapper makes this a HARD GATE, per column AND per pair: a column can have variance overall yet be constant on the rows a given pair shares

desc_cor_test: for pearson cor_test SILENTLY ignores exact/continuity (live-verified: identical p-value, no warning) -> the wrapper makes them a hard gate so the user does not think they had an effect

desc_cor_test: the i.i.d. null of cor_test is violated for autocorrelated macro series -> inflated Type I error. For lead/lag in time series use desc_ccf (with prewhitening) or Granger (cat.06), NOT desc_cor_test on raw levels

desc_cor_test: the single n>=4 gate is DELIBERATELY stricter than the per-method minimum (pearson n>=3, kendall/spearman n>=2 — live-verified) so that the output schema does not change silently with the method; at n=2/3 kendall/spearman return a degenerate |r|=1 with p=1
sources: Box, Jenkins & Reinsel, Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control (ACF/PACF order id)
Enders 2015 Applied Econometric Time Series 4th ed. §2 (correlogram)
the cor_test routine (the engine) — the exact rules: Kendall for n<50, the Spearman AS 89 algorithm, an interval only for Pearson on >=4 complete pairs, and the tie definition with its n<=1290 cutoff
Benjamini & Hochberg (1995), JRSS-B 57(1):289-300, doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x (FDR — default BH)
Holm (1979), Scand. J. Statist. 6:65-70 (step-down FWER; dominates Bonferroni)
Benjamini & Yekutieli (2001), Ann. Statist. 29(4), doi:10.1214/aos/1013699998 (FDR under dependence — BY)

c00_data_utilities/replacement_missing_values.impute_kalman (fill the gaps first — the input gate rejects gaps and infinities)

The alias 'fdr' is NOT exposed (identical to BH)) · use='pairwise' (default) vs 'complete' (pairwise = the maximum n per pair but a DIFFERENT sample per pair (the p-values are not strictly comparable); complete = a listwise drop giving a COMMON sample across all pairs (comparable, smaller n); 'raise' = a hard stop on any missing value)
Output: acf/pacf/ccf: numeric + lag + n_used; ci_upper/ci_lower = ±1.96/sqrt(n) white-noise band · desc_rolling: the rolled series (index-aligned, blank at the edges) + the index · desc_correlations: correlation (matrix->nested+axis labels), n=rows supplied, n_pairwise=per-pair complete · desc_cor_test: pairs = long-format records PER PAIR (var1, var2, n, estimate, statistic, statistic_name, parameter, p_value, p_adjusted, conf_low, conf_high, ties, exact_used); ALWAYS read p_adjusted, NOT p_value · desc_cor_test: pair_order = an EXPLICIT deterministic order (upper triangle by COLUMN INDEX (1,2),(1,3),..,(p-1,p) — NOT alphabetical), so that stored workflows reproduce (§5) · desc_cor_test: n_rows_input / n_rows_used / n_missing_cells (n_missing_cells is measured BEFORE the listwise drop); any_ties / any_exact_fallback / warnings = degradation flags
Pitfalls: non-stationary series: the ACF decays slowly and linearly (an artefact, not structure) — test stationarity first · CCF: with ccf(x, y) (as the wrapper calls it) lag k estimates cor(x[t+k], y[t]) -> NEGATIVE lags = x leads y (x leads, peak at lag<0), POSITIVE lags = x lags behind (y leads); confirm the lag sign in the raw object before concluding lead/lag · desc_correlations: with pairwise completion and gaps the scalar n OVERSTATES — read n_pairwise (a strong correlation on a small n_pairwise is fragile) · desc_cor_test: Kendall and Spearman define NEITHER a confidence interval NOR degrees of freedom — the wrapper returns an explicit blank in conf_low/conf_high/parameter, NEVER a silently omitted field. The interval is defined only for Pearson, and only on at least 4 complete pairs (live-verified) · desc_cor_test: with ties cor_test silently DOWNGRADES the exact p-value to an asymptotic approximation and ONLY warns ('cannot compute exact p-value with ties'). The wrapper exposes this as DATA: ties / exact_used / any_exact_fallback / warnings (each warning carries its pair). Check exact_used before trusting small p-values · desc_cor_test: for spearman with n>1290 AS 89 is abandoned silently (WITHOUT a warning) in favour of the t-approximation. the cor_test routine states 'n < 1290' while the stats code checks 'n <= 1290' — the wrapper encodes the CODE (live-verified), which is why exact_used is reliable · desc_cor_test: on a constant (zero-variance) column the correlation test does NOT error — it ONLY warns ('the standard deviation is zero') and returns a blank estimate and p-value (live-verified for all 3 methods). The wrapper makes this a HARD GATE, per column AND per pair: a column can have variance overall yet be constant on the rows a given pair shares · desc_cor_test: for pearson cor_test SILENTLY ignores exact/continuity (live-verified: identical p-value, no warning) -> the wrapper makes them a hard gate so the user does not think they had an effect · desc_cor_test: the i.i.d. null of cor_test is violated for autocorrelated macro series -> inflated Type I error. For lead/lag in time series use desc_ccf (with prewhitening) or Granger (cat.06), NOT desc_cor_test on raw levels · desc_cor_test: the single n>=4 gate is DELIBERATELY stricter than the per-method minimum (pearson n>=3, kendall/spearman n>=2 — live-verified) so that the output schema does not change silently with the method; at n=2/3 kendall/spearman return a degenerate |r|=1 with p=1
Sources: Box, Jenkins & Reinsel, Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control (ACF/PACF order id) · Enders 2015 Applied Econometric Time Series 4th ed. §2 (correlogram) · the cor_test routine (the engine) — the exact rules: Kendall for n<50, the Spearman AS 89 algorithm, an interval only for Pearson on >=4 complete pairs, and the tie definition with its n<=1290 cutoff · the p_adjust routine (the engine) — BH/BY/holm/hochberg/hommel/bonferroni; 'BH' (alias 'fdr') · Benjamini & Hochberg (1995), JRSS-B 57(1):289-300, doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x (FDR — default BH) · Holm (1979), Scand. J. Statist. 6:65-70 (step-down FWER; dominates Bonferroni) · Benjamini & Yekutieli (2001), Ann. Statist. 29(4), doi:10.1214/aos/1013699998 (FDR under dependence — BY)

cards.method: Binomial GLM (probit/logit) — recession probability (Estrella-Mishkin)
cards.when: a binary outcome (a recession dummy 0/1); estimating P(y=1|x) from predictors (the yield-curve spread) with probit/logit; optionally high-dimensional fixed effects + clustered SE + weights
cards.when_not: a continuous outcome (-> #33, or forecasting); more than two categories (-> an ordered model, or #30); an endogenous dynamic recession state (a dynamic probit, outside the surface); counts (-> Poisson)

alternatives.criterion: you want an odds-ratio interpretation (probit is the Estrella-Mishkin default)
without high-dimensional FE / clustered SE it is equivalent
the recession state is latent/unobserved -> extract regime probabilities (gaussian/lm only)
an autoregressive latent recession probability (outside the wrapper)

output_key_fields: coefficients: named beta on the LINK scale (the index), NOT marginal effects/probabilities
coeftable: term/estimate/std_error/z_value/p_value (z-test; SE clustered if a cluster was supplied)
fitted_probabilities: P(y=1|x) via predict(type=response) — the score that feeds #84
obs_kept: 1-based indices of the retained rows (fixef/separation -> length < nrow; alignment)
pseudo_r2: McFadden pseudo-R2 (ratio of log-likelihoods, fitstat pr2) — NOT an OLS R2
loglik/aic/bic/deviance/nobs: fit stats; link/family/fixef_names: metadata
interpretation_traps: coef = the effect on the latent index, NOT the marginal effect on the probability (which shrinks at the extremes); only the sign & significance are directly readable
do NOT assume length(fitted_probabilities)==nrow; fixef/separation drops rows -> align through obs_kept
pseudo-R2 != R2; a McFadden value of 0.3 is excellent (not '30% of the variance')
perfect/quasi-separation -> coefficients of ±∞ with enormous SE, or a drop (check obs_kept & the SE)
an in-sample AUC (via #84 on the same sample) is optimistic; an out-of-sample/real-time vintage is needed
sources: Bergé 2018 CREA discussion paper (efficient estimation with many fixed effects)
Estrella & Mishkin 1998 Rev. Econ. Stat. 80(1):45-61 (probit recession probability)
Estrella & Hardouvelis 1991 J. Finance 46(2):555-576 (yield curve -> activity)
Kauppi & Saikkonen 2008 Rev. Econ. Stat. 90(4):777-791 (dynamic probit, alt)

cards.method: ROC / AUC — binary forecast evaluation
cards.when: a numeric score/prediction (the fitted_probabilities of #83) + a binary target; threshold-independent discrimination: AUC + DeLong CI + the full ROC curve + the Youden best threshold
cards.when_not: >2 classes (multiclass); a point/interval forecast of a continuous variable (-> RMSE/DM, cat. 15); comparing two curves (roc_test, out of scope); calibration (-> Brier/reliability)

alternatives.criterion: a specific false-alarm/miss cost; you operate at one cutoff (-> best_threshold)

alternatives.alt: bootstrap intervals for sensitivity and specificity
alternatives.criterion: partial AUC or smoothed curves (outside the wrapper; the default is analytic DeLong)
an asymmetric cost, missed recession >> false alarm (Youden weights them equally)
comparing two models/curves (outside the wrapper)

output_key_fields: auc: Area Under Curve in [0,1]; 0.5=random, 1=perfect (the C-statistic)
auc_ci: {low,high,conf_level,method=delong}; low>0.5 -> significantly better than random
roc_curve: data_frame threshold/sensitivity/specificity (chart-ready; the ±Inf sentinels are removed)
best_threshold: named list at the Youden point (threshold/sensitivity/specificity; several rows on ties)
n_cases/n_controls: positives/negatives after dropping missing values; controls_level/cases_level: WHICH label is which
direction: '<' (controls below cases, the normal case for a probability score) or '>'; percent: False
interpretation_traps: CRITICAL label inversion: swapped control/case labels -> AUC=1-AUC; always read controls_level/cases_level; AUC<0.5 is often inverted labels/direction
direction=auto silently picks the orientation with AUC>=0.5, hiding an inversion; for a strict evaluation set direction='<'
an in-sample AUC (a predictor from the same sample) is optimistic; an out-of-sample/real-time evaluation is needed
Youden != operationally optimal (it weights false alarm/miss equally; macro recession-calling is asymmetric)
AUC measures discrimination, NOT calibration; the same AUC can correspond to very different probability calibration

cards.when: a robust combination of 2-7 univariate models (a/e/f/n/s/t/z) on ONE series; a baseline macro forecast where stability matters

there are cross-series dependencies/cointegration that the univariate combination ignores

the weights reflect low error, NOT the structural correctness of the component (a purely predictive criterion)

Alternatives: #30 Markov switching (probabilistic regimes) (you want regime probabilities + endogenous transitions instead of deterministic dates; gaussian/lm only) · HP / band-pass / Hamilton filters (#56/#57/#92, category 10) (you want a continuous cyclical gap instead of discrete turning points) · state space / dynamic factor analysis (#58/#61, category 10) (a latent common cycle from several series) · Monthly Bry-Boschan (monthly data (outside the surface of this card))
Output: states: ts of the regime, +1=expansion / -1=recession per quarter · peaks_index/troughs_index: index positions inside the series (not dates) · peaks_date/troughs_date: peaks/troughs as 'YYYYQn' labels · phases: data_frame type/start/end/duration/state/complete · avg_expansion_duration/avg_recession_duration: the mean duration over complete phases only · n_complete_phases: complete (non-censored) phases · the raw dating fit (a stub once serialised)
Pitfalls: sign convention: +1=expansion, -1=recession — not the reverse, not a z-score · peaks/troughs are position indices, NOT dates; a peak = the end of an expansion/the start of a recession · the edge phases are censored (complete=False); they are excluded from the means — do not compare them with complete ones · an interior gap in average_over_phases is an error, not a silent omission; an entirely empty input is rejected · mincycle/minphase determine the number of turning points; the dating is not unique; mincycle>minphase (gate) · deterministic (v0.9.8, legacy/archived); no RNG

cards.method: inequality indices + Lorenz curve (Gini/Theil/Atkinson/RS/Kolm/CV/entropy)
cards.when: a cross-section of non-negative values (incomes/wealth/shares) → a scalar inequality index or the Lorenz curve as numeric data; descriptive/distributional at one point in time
cards.when_not: a return tail (VaR/ES→#65); a conditional-on-X tail/GaR (→#64); poverty/concentration indices (pov/conc are not exposed); a within/between Theil decomposition by group; time-series dynamics

alternatives.criterion: a headline single number, the most comparable; sensitive mainly to the centre of the distribution
you want an additive within/between decomposition (the GE family); entropy@1==Theil@0==Theil's T/GE(1) (upper tail), entropy@0==Theil@1==mean log deviation/GE(0) (lower tail)
you want an explicit inequality-aversion parameter epsilon (normative/welfare)
you want absolute inequality (invariant to adding a constant), not relative
Ricci-Schutz/Pietra: the share of the total that would have to be redistributed (Robin Hood)
a non-parametric comparison: if curve A lies everywhere above B ⇒ unambiguously less inequality (stronger than a scalar)

alternatives.alt: category 12 (#64 quantile regression / #65 VaR and Expected Shortfall)
alternatives.criterion: a conditional-on-X tail (GaR) or return risk metrics — a different question

output_key_fields: index (compute_inequality): the scalar index; Gini/Atkinson/RS ∈ [0,1] (0 = equality), Theil/entropy >= 0 (NOT a percentage), Kolm in units of x (absolute), var = CV and square_var = CV²
type (compute_inequality): which index was computed (a closed enum, default Gini)
parameter (compute_inequality): blank ⇒ the index default (Atkinson 0.5, Kolm 1, entropy 0.5, Theil 0), NOT 'no parameter'
n (compute_inequality): the sample size
p (lorenz_curve): the cumulative population share (a chart-ready array)
L (lorenz_curve): the ordinary Lorenz curve — the bottom p*100% holds L(p)*100% of the total; relative inequality
L_general (lorenz_curve): the generalized Lorenz curve = L × mean (units of x); it embeds the level → a welfare comparison
gini (lorenz_curve): the Gini of the same series, for consistency; n: the size
interpretation_traps: Theil/entropy are NOT bounded at 1 — do not read them as a percentage; only Gini/Atkinson/RS∈[0,1]
Kolm is absolute (units of x), not a 0-1 relative index — do not compare it with the Gini

in ineq the parameter is inverted between the two types: entropy@1==Theil@0 (==the Theil default; Theil's T/GE(1), upper tail), entropy@0==Theil@1 (mean log deviation/GE(0), lower tail): the same number, a different name/tail
a blank parameter in the output ⇒ the index default, NOT 'no parameter'
non-negativity is enforced ONLY for Gini/Atkinson/Theil/entropy and the Lorenz curve; RS/Kolm/var/square_var accept negatives, and the underlying index routine does not error on them
all zeros: it passes the >=0 gate but Lc divides by 0 → NaN→JSON null; the wrapper blocks it with a sum(x)>0 gate
ordinary L (shape) vs generalized L_general (shape+level): the same L does not mean the same welfare if the mean differs (Shorrocks)
sources: Cowell 2000 Measurement of Inequality (Handbook of Income Distribution)
Theil 1967 Economics and Information Theory (Theil/entropy indices)
Arnold 1987 Majorization and the Lorenz Order, Springer (Lorenz dominance)

cards.method: Density-forecast evaluation — CRPS / LogS / PIT (sample + parametric + tail-weighted)
cards.when: evaluating a predictive DISTRIBUTION (posterior/ensemble draws or parametric) as a whole distribution; proper scoring (CRPS/LogS) + PIT calibration + tail-weighted CRPS for GaR downside risk
cards.when_not: a point-forecast comparison -> #74 Diebold-Mariano; selecting among many point models -> #75 model confidence set; binary AUC -> #84; in-sample fit -> #76/#77; multivariate ES and VS are outside the surface

alternatives.criterion: a robust default for draws; the same units as y
a likelihood-based/local score; BUT sensitive to the KDE bandwidth in the tails
the predictive distribution is explicitly normal/t/mixnorm (an analytic BVAR predictive)
an asymmetric cost in the tail (GaR left-tail focus)
point forecasts only (comparing 2 models)
GaR quantiles -> a full density; then parametric scoring here

output_key_fields: scores: per-observation score vector (chart-data, score per time period)
mean_score: the mean score (the comparative number; LOWER=BETTER)
score: 'CRPS'/'LogS'/'twCRPS'; method (edf/kde) or family (normal/t/mixnorm)
weighted/side/a/b/kind: tail-weighted metadata (twcrps threshold / owcrps outcome)
pit (sr_pit_sample): the PIT values in [0,1]; a histogram close to uniform => good calibration
n / n_draws: number of observations / draws
interpretation_traps: ORIENTATION: CRPS & LogS are NEGATIVELY oriented — LOWER = BETTER (not accuracy)
LogS = -Inf if y falls outside the support of the draws; KDE smooths that but is sensitive to the bandwidth in the tails -> for heavy tails prefer CRPS(edf)
the CRPS of a single observation is in the same units as y -> it is NOT comparable across series of different scale
PIT: a ∪ shape => underdispersed (too tight a distribution); a ∩ shape => overdispersed; uniform => calibrated
a low tail-weighted score may simply reflect few observations in the tail — read the per-obs scores
bw: crps/logs_sample requires a bw vector[1:n]; the wrapper recycles a scalar -> length(y)
sources: Jordan, Krüger & Lerch 2019 JSS 90(12) (evaluating probabilistic forecasts with proper scoring rules)
Gneiting & Raftery 2007 JASA 102:359-378 (proper scoring rules, CRPS/LogS)
Krüger, Lerch, Thorarinsdottir & Gneiting 2021 Int. J. Forecast. (predictive-distribution scoring)
Diebold, Gunther & Tay 1998 Int. Econ. Rev. 39(4):863-883 (PIT calibration evaluation — the basis of sr_pit_sample, custom implementation)
precondition_tools: c03_multivariate_nowcasting/bayesian_var.bvar_predict (or #13/#14/#17/#60: they produce the posterior predictive draws the scores are evaluated on)
c12_distribution_risk/quantile_regression.qr_growth_at_risk (GaR quantiles; the density comes via #95 -> parametric scoring)

cards.method: Skew-t fit to fitted quantiles (ABG Growth-at-Risk «step 2») + density/ES
cards.when: you have conditional quantiles (from #64 GaR) and you want the FULL growth density: quantile matching to a skew-t (Adrian-Boyarchenko-Giannone 2019) -> density/CDF + expected shortfall / downside risk
cards.when_not: you only want the quantiles (stop at #64); you have a raw sample of returns (VaR/ES directly -> #65); you want an MLE skew-t regression on raw data (selm, outside the surface); non-monotone probs (crossing) -> fix that first

alternatives.criterion: you do not need the full density/ES, only the GaR/upside points
you have a raw sample of returns (not conditional quantiles) -> historical/Gaussian/modified VaR
you want a full ML skew-t regression, not quantile matching (outside the wrapper)
a small/noisy quantile set -> lock nu (e.g. 5) for stability

output_key_fields: dp: c(xi=location, omega=scale, alpha=slant, nu=df) — the fitted skew-t parameters
objective/rmse: weighted SSE / rmse of fitted vs target quantiles (small = a good fit)
fitted_quantiles vs target_quantiles: for a visual check of fit quality (chart-data)
st_density: {x, pdf, cdf} grid (chart-ready full density/CDF)
st_shortfall: {var, es, mean, median} — VaR=quantile, es=Expected Shortfall (ABG downside)
convergence: 0 = converged (hard gate: !=0 -> stop)
interpretation_traps: alpha<0 => negative skewness (a heavy left tail) = the ABG «vulnerable growth» case; alpha>0 = right skew
a small nu (->2) => heavy tails => a much more negative ES; nu<=2 is blocked (infinite variance)
quantile CROSSING in the #64 conditional quantiles => non-monotone => gate stop (an invalid distribution) — fix the crossing first
quantile matching != MLE: the fit is to the quantile points, not to raw data; its quality depends on the number of quantiles & their spread
ES = E[X|X<=VaR] (the left tail); the right-side ES is the 'expected longrise' (upper tail)
CONVERGENCE gate: a non-converged optimisation stops (not a silently bad fit, as in #68)
sources: Adrian, Boyarchenko & Giannone 2019 AER 109(4):1263-1289 (Vulnerable Growth: skew-t on GaR quantiles)

cards.method: JSON interchange: parse / serialise / validate / NDJSON stream in-out
cards.when: the JSON/NDJSON data layer; json_parse/json_stream_parse are producers (register); json_write/stream_write are serializers; json_validate is a diagnostic
cards.when_not: CSV -> #96; Excel -> #97; Parquet -> #98; for tabular data prefer #96/#98; file IO belongs to the reader and writer nodes

alternatives.criterion: NDJSON newline-delimited records -> a data_frame; not a single JSON document
purely tabular data (Parquet/CSV) instead of nested/semi-structured JSON

output_key_fields: json_parse: parsed (vector/list/data_frame, registered; df->Parquet otherwise RDS) + type/n
json_stream_parse: data (data_frame -> Parquet) + n/ncol
json_write/json_stream_write: json/ndjson/text strings; json_validate valid/error/offset
interpretation_traps: CRITICAL: the serialiser defaults to 4 significant digits and rounds SILENTLY (pi -> 3.1416) -> the wrapper disables the rounding
auto_unbox=True (the default): length-1 arrays become JSON scalars
fromJSON auto-fetching a URL/path is blocked by the validate-first rule (no SSRF)
sources: Ooms 2014 (arXiv:1403.2805) — a mapping between JSON data and statistical data types
validation_notes: json_parse: txt a single non-empty string; validate FIRST, which blocks both malformed input AND any attempt to fetch a URL or a file
json_write: digits unset means full precision; force=False, so a value with no JSON mapping is a hard error
json_stream_parse: text with no blank entry; EVERY line is validated before the stream; json_stream_write requires at least one row

cards.method: Import/export Stata/SPSS/SAS (.dta/.sav/.sas7bdat) with labelled metadata + labelled-to-categorical materialisation
cards.when: ingest an uploaded .dta/.sav/.sas7bdat -> a long-format frame (register data -> Parquet) + the variable and value labels; sfile_write_stata exports; sfile_labels_to_categorical turns a labelled column into a categorical
cards.when_not: CSV -> #96; Excel -> #97; Parquet -> #98; JSON -> #99; the secondary formats (.por/.xpt, SPSS write); URL or stream inputs (a local path only)

alternatives.criterion: choose by file format (.dta/.sav/.sas7bdat)
categorical analysis/plots on haven_labelled columns before the downstream step

output_key_fields: data: the frame (a registered producer -> Parquet; labelled columns as numeric codes)
var_labels/value_labels/labelled_cols/col_types/dataset_label: JSON-safe metadata
writer: path/written/version/n_rows/n_cols/bytes; as_factor: data/input_type/levels/n
interpretation_traps: the column attribute 'label' PARTIAL-matches 'labels' (the value labels) when the variable label is absent -> an exact lookup everywhere
write_dta version=14.5 is accepted SILENTLY; version=c(14,15) gives a cryptic length error -> a whole-number length-1 gate
as_factor on a plain numeric -> forcats silently produces a factor (silently wrong) -> a labelled-only gate
sources: the Stata .dta, SPSS .sav and SAS .sas7bdat file-format specifications
validation_notes: read path: a string of length 1, NOT a directory, existing; write path: the parent dir exists + a POST-gate that it was written
the data to write must be a frame with at least one column; version a single integer in 8-15; and the label either unset or at most 80 bytes
sfile_labels_to_categorical: a non-df input MUST be labelled (otherwise forcats silently turns every vector into a factor)

cards.when: the rolling-aggregate layer; rolling mean/sum/sd/min/max/median in 4 regimes (positional/index-relative/calendar-period/arbitrary pairs); type-stable throughout
cards.when_not: charts (the frontend); diff/growth/lags -> #103/#104; a free custom reducer (structurally excluded); weighted or exponential rolling -> #107/#109

output_key_fields: values: double vector = chart-data (length=length(x) for slide*, =length(starts) for hop)
n/n_na/reducer/na_rm + the applied arguments
empty windows -> NaN/Inf, reported in n_na (they are not hidden)
interpretation_traps: the reducer is NEVER exposed as a callable — it is a closed enum {mean, sum, sd, min, max, median}, which is a security boundary
win_hop_index returns one value per start (NOT one per observation); in win_slide_period the before/after counts are BLOCKS, not observations
before/after: an integer, or infinity; a negative value looks forward; and a non-empty window requires before+after>=0
sources: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd ed., ch.3 (moving averages and rolling windows)

alternatives.criterion: Excel NETWORKDAYS: the count must start/end on a business day
inclusive counting (it also counts the final business day; +1 against financial=True)
the market roll convention (following vs preceding)
you need a time-series transformation, not calendar arithmetic

bday_adjust: result (rolled Date->ISO) + dates + direction + n_out
bday_sequence: sequence (business days, Date->ISO) + n + from/to
interpretation_traps: weekdays: only the 7 LOWER-CASE English tokens; 'Saturday'/'funday' SILENTLY become business days (silently wrong) -> hard gate
bday_offset: a fractional n returns nothing SILENTLY -> a gate on integers

cards.method: Tidy temporal data frames — an explicit key/index contract + structural gap handling (detect/list/count/fill) + CLOSED-vocabulary calendar aggregation
cards.when: a long frame -> a contract-checked temporal table with an explicit index (and an optional key); detecting and materialising implicit gaps; calendar aggregation to a lower frequency; it feeds #8 and #126
cards.when_not: free-form expressions (excluded); layout-agnostic conversion -> #78; statistical imputation -> #80 (tt_fill_gaps only inserts the empty rows); INCREASING the frequency -> #79; charts (the frontend)

alternatives.criterion: class-agnostic conversion/transformation without the key/index contract (lighter)

tt_gaps: result + any_gaps + n_missing (has=keys with gaps; scan=the missing rows; count=the sum of n)
tt_fill_gaps: n_filled (the rows added, left empty)
interpretation_traps: a raw Date index on monthly/quarterly data -> interval=1D (the GCD of the days) -> SPURIOUS gaps; supply yearmonth/yearquarter; the interval is returned explicitly
tt_index_aggregate with a key SILENTLY merges the keys together; by_key=True (the default) aggregates per key instead
coarsening to a HIGHER resolution than the index (finer than the source) => a clean error (caught), not a silent one
the reducers apply only to NUMERIC measured columns (gated before the cryptic summarise error)
sources: Wang, Cook & Hyndman (2020), A New Tidy Data Structure to Support Exploration and Modeling of Temporal Data, JCGS 29(3):466-478, doi:10.1080/10618600.2019.1695624

trim ∈ [0,0.5); >=0.5 blanks silently; a gap with na_rm=False blanks silently (all gated)

cards.method: Benchmarking a high-frequency indicator to a low-frequency total (two-step Prais-Winsten regression + additive Denton smoothing)
cards.when: a high-frequency indicator is bent so that it sums EXACTLY to a low-frequency target total (the INSEE two-step: Prais-Winsten GLS + additive Denton); annualBenchmark = the default QNA windows
cards.when_not: a broad menu of disaggregation methods (Chow-Lin/Fernandez/Litterman/Denton-Cholette) -> #79; plain aggregation with no consistency constraint -> ts_aggregate (#78); proportional three-rule smoothing (omitted); charts (the frontend)

alternatives.criterion: you want an explicit choice of disaggregation model (chow-lin/fernandez/litterman/denton) or high->low aggregation (ta)
annual->sub-annual with the usual default windows of quarterly national accounts

output_key_fields: benchmarked: the high-frequency series (->{values,start,frequency}) — the MAIN result; = fitted_values + smoothed_part; it sums exactly to lfserie within the window
coefficients/std_errors/rho: the Prais-Winsten regression (constant + the loading on the indicator); rho=0 = no AR term (not a failure)
fitted_values/smoothed_part: the two additive components (ts); n_high/freq_high/freq_low/freq_ratio metadata
model: the fitted twoStepsBenchmark handle (RDS bucket) -> bench_in_sample / coef / se / rho
comparison (bench_in_sample): a two-column frame (benchmark against predicted value), type changes|levels
interpretation_traps: FREQUENCY GATE: the high-frequency series must be STRICTLY faster than the low-frequency one, at an integer ratio; an equal frequency (ratio 1) would be accepted SILENTLY and is degenerate -> hard-blocked
a gap in the low-frequency series silently blanks the coefficients and the benchmark (silently wrong) -> hard-blocked
include_differenciation=1 (a number) would be accepted silently as True -> a strict boolean gate
consistency holds ONLY inside the benchmark window; the extrapolation tail (hf beyond lf) is a projection, not a benchmarked value
sources: Denton 1971, Adjustment of Series to Annual Totals (JASA 66(333):99-102); Prais & Winsten 1954; INSEE/Banque de France two-step benchmarking

cards.method: Fast row/column panel statistics (median/var/sd/quantiles) + a diffusion index (breadth) over a numeric wide panel matrix
cards.when: a wide numeric panel (matrix rows=time, cols=series); fast cross-sectional (per-period) & over-time (per-series) location/spread, quantiles per period (fan chart), and a diffusion index (the share of series that rise)
cards.when_not: a single series or layout handling -> #78; rolling windows -> #105; ACF/PACF/correlation -> #81; grouped or panel-aware work with ids -> #103; it accepts ONLY a plain numeric matrix

alternatives.criterion: grouped/panel-aware aggregation with ids, or speed on very large data
class/frequency plumbing of one or a few series rather than cross-sectional panel statistics

output_key_fields: values: a numeric vector (by row -> n_time cross-sectional, by column -> n_series over time) + margin/stat/na_rm
quantiles: a matrix n_time x len(probs), columns named by prob (drop=False keeps a matrix for a single prob)
index: the diffusion index of length n_time-1 in [0,1] (0.5=balance, >0.5=broad expansion)
interpretation_traps: na_rm=False => a gap PROPAGATES (visible, NOT a silent drop); set it True to ignore gaps
row = per-period cross-sectional; col = per-series over time — do not confuse the axis
a time-indexed object also answers to the matrix check and would be accepted silently -> a hard gate blocks it; supply a plain numeric matrix
a row variance or standard deviation over a single element is blank (the variance of one value), not an error

cards.method: Composite index / dimensionality reduction with PCA (PC1 composite index + loadings + variance decomposition + biplot coordinates + newdata projection + rules for the number of components + KPSS precheck)
cards.when: many correlated indicators -> ONE composite index = PC1 (data-driven loadings); dimensionality reduction; cum_var for the number of components; scale=True (default) for heterogeneous units; biplot chart-data (observation scores + variable arrows in the SAME scaled space) -> pca_biplot_coords; out-of-sample apply: fit on train, project NEW rows with the SAME center/scale -> pca_predict; how many components to keep BY A RULE (Kaiser-Guttman / cum-var / broken-stick) -> pca_n_components; BEFORE PCA on TIME SERIES: KPSS per column -> pca_stationarity_precheck
cards.when_not: charts as DRAWING (the frontend; we supply ONLY coordinates); a latent factor with dynamics, mixed frequency or missing data -> #15 (category 03); explicit or equal weights -> panel_row_stats (#116) / #82; NON-STATIONARY series in LEVELS -> #256 (pn_pca_nonstationary); the elbow or scree plot as a rule (Cattell 1966: it requires VISUAL judgement, not a rule)

alternatives.criterion: a common latent factor with dynamics/mixed frequency/gaps (state space) rather than a static cross-section
you want explicit/audited (equal/expert) weights instead of data-driven loadings
a measurement model with error terms (factor analysis), not maximisation of explained variance
the columns are NON-STATIONARY time series (KPSS rejects) — the standardization of classical PCA is MATHEMATICALLY UNDEFINED there (Hamilton, Ma & Xi, NBER WP 32068)

output_key_fields: composite: PC1 scores = the composite index (numeric of length n, names from row labels)
loadings/scores: matrices (p x k / n x k) -> nested rows + axis labels
var_explained/cum_var: the share & cumulative share per PC1/PC2/..; pc1_var = the share of the composite
sdev, n_obs/n_vars/n_comp, center/scale (the applied arguments)
pca_biplot_coords: obs_coords (n x 2) / var_coords (p x 2) / lambda (the COMMON scale factor) / components / var_explained — NUMBERS ONLY, no drawing (charter §5)

pca_predict: scores_new / composite_new / rotation / center_used / scale_used (fit/apply externalization — a reproducible apply OUTSIDE the node: scale(new, center_used, scale_used) %*% rotation) / scores_train
pca_n_components: k_kaiser + kaiser_threshold + kaiser_basis · k_cum_var + cum_var_threshold · k_broken_stick (sequential) + k_broken_stick_any + broken_stick_expected · k_min/k_max

pca_stationarity_precheck: statistic/p_value/p_at_bound/trunc_lag/nonstationary PER COLUMN · columns_flagged/n_nonstationary/any_nonstationary/small_sample · warning_code/warning_message/recommended_node/recommended_fn/source (a STRUCTURED field, NOT message, NOT stop)
interpretation_traps: PC signs are arbitrary (help Note, they differ by build/BLAS) -> an explicit sign normalization: each PC is flipped so that the max-|loading| is positive; interpret the direction from the loadings
scale=True is a hard gate against a constant or zero-variance column (otherwise 'cannot rescale a constant/zero column'); a gap or an infinity gives a cryptic decomposition error
PC1 is z-score-like (mean ~ 0) with no natural units -> for a base-100 index do a separate rebase; scale=False lets the highest-variance column dominate
the input must be a numeric matrix (NOT a data_frame -> silent character coercion), >=2 columns, >=3 rows

pca_predict matches columns BY NAME only when the rotation carries them — that is, when the training matrix had column names. Without them only the column COUNT is checked, and reordered columns project SILENTLY WRONG (live-verified: the same input, completely different scores) ⇒ pca_predict requires column names on BOTH sides AND an identical ORDER
biplot_scale is NOT the PCA scaling flag: it is the lambda exponent of the biplot. The reference construction only WARNS outside [0,1]; here it is a hard stop (charter §5)

a biplot on a rank-deficient matrix (a duplicate or collinear column): sdev ~ 1.18e-16, NOT exactly 0 -> lam ~ 0 -> silently enormous observation coordinates. Gated with the documented tolerance of the decomposition: sqrt(machine epsilon) * sdev[0]

the Kaiser-Guttman «eigenvalue > 1» rule HOLDS ONLY on a CORRELATION matrix (scale=True, mean eigenvalue == 1). On a COVARIANCE matrix (scale=False) the threshold is the mean of the eigenvalues (Jolliffe 2002 §6.1.2) — which is why kaiser_threshold and kaiser_basis are returned explicitly

broken-stick: «ALL of them pass» is MATHEMATICALLY IMPOSSIBLE (sum(var_explained) == sum(b_j) == 1); k_broken_stick (which stops at the FIRST failure) and k_broken_stick_any DIFFER (e.g. on ~independent columns: k=0 but k_any=2)
kpss_test gives a p-value ONLY within [0.01, 0.10] (interpolation in KPSS 1992 Table 1) and warns at the bounds ⇒ alpha is gated to [0.01, 0.10] + p_at_bound per column
non-stationarity is NOT a stop: the node must stay fully usable on CROSS-SECTION data (countries/firms), where stationarity is not even defined — hence a STRUCTURED warning is returned
sources: Venables & Ripley, Modern Applied Statistics with S (2002); Jolliffe, Principal Component Analysis (2002) §6.1.1/§6.1.2
OECD/JRC Nardo et al., Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (2008) — PCA weighting
the biplot construction (lam = (sdev*sqrt(n))^scale; observations divided by lam, variables multiplied by it) · Gabriel 1971 Biometrika 58(3):453-467
Kaiser HF (1960), Educ. Psychol. Meas. 20:141-151 · Guttman L (1954) — eigenvalue>1 on a correlation matrix
Frontier 1976 · Jackson 1993 Ecology 74(8):2204-2214 — the broken stick, b_j = (1/p) * sum over i from j to p of 1/i
Cattell RB (1966) — elbow/scree is REJECTED as a rule (it requires visual judgement, not a rule)
Hamilton, Ma & Xi, NBER WP 32068 — for a non-stationary variable the population mean is undefined and the sample sd diverges ⇒ PCA standardization is invalid

Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt & Shin 1992, J. Econometrics 54:159-178 · the kpss_test routine (lshort=True ⇒ a truncation lag of floor(4*(n/100)^0.25); Table 1 ⇒ small_sample = n<30; a p-value only within [0.01,0.10])
precondition_tools: pca_stationarity_precheck # ONLY when the input is TIME SERIES (in a cross-section stationarity is undefined)

cards.method: Parametric distributions (normal/student_t) as a numeric grid: quantile bands / cdf / density / moments (fan-chart data)
cards.when: a forecast/scenario from PARAMETERS (mean/sd, df) -> numeric data for the frontend: fan bands per horizon, CDF/tail probability, a density curve, moments
cards.when_not: density-forecast scoring (CRPS/LogS/PIT) -> #94; empirical quantiles from a sample -> #110; FITTING a distribution to data -> #196 (this card takes parameters, it does not fit); charts -> the frontend

alternatives.criterion: density-forecast EVALUATION (CRPS/LogS/PIT) rather than grid generation
fat tails in the scenario -> student_t (a small df); otherwise normal (df->inf)

output_key_fields: dist_fan_quantiles: quantiles (matrix n_dist x n_probs) + probs/family/params + mean/sd
dist_prob_cdf: cdf (n_dist x n_at) in [0,1]; dist_density_grid: density (n_dist x n_at) >=0
dist_moments: mean/variance/sd per distribution
interpretation_traps: probs must be strictly in (0,1): probs>1 => a silent WARN 'NaNs produced' (silently wrong); 0/1 => ±Inf (hard gate)
Student-t: the variance is infinite for df<=2, the mean is undefined for df<=1 => to_mcp null (NOT 0)
sigma is a scale, NOT the sd for a t: sd = sigma*sqrt(df/(df-2)) for df>2; recycling of length 1 or L (otherwise a clean stop)
sources: O'Hara-Wild et al., distributional: Vectorised Probability Distributions

cards.method: US NBER recession chronology — recession-shading intervals + a per-date 0/1 recession dummy
cards.when: the official NBER peak->trough recession intervals as numeric data -> recession-shading bands (frontend) or a 0/1 recession-dummy regressor aligned to a series
cards.when_not: DRAWING the bands (nberShade/ymdShade/romerLines — frontend); DATING turning points from data — these two functions date nothing, they clip and test intervals the caller already has, so a chronology has to exist before either is called; Romer dates (not exposed)

alternatives.criterion: you need the series itself/transformations, not a recession reference
you want a 0/1 dummy per date rather than intervals for shading

output_key_fields: recessions: records df start/end = peak->trough (yyyymmdd int by default, or Date); overlap-clipped to [from,to]
flags: records df date/in_recession 0/1 + n_recession_periods
metadata: n_recessions/n, from/to (yyyymmdd), as_date

vintage: n_intervals + the first and last date read off the chronology THAT ARRIVED — the engine holds no snapshot to describe, so this echoes the caller's input rather than a publisher, a retrieval date or a digest of anything shipped
interpretation_traps: the window is INCLUSIVE at both ends (Start=peak & End=trough are inside the recession); the day after the trough => 0
a recession-free [from,to] => 0 rows (valid, NOT an error)
20200101 is a yyyymmdd INTEGER, NOT a year; from=2020 errors (not an 8-digit date)

the committee dates peaks and troughs to a MONTH, and separately to a QUARTER — it publishes no day. Every day-of-month in a redistributed recession dataset was chosen by whoever repackaged it, not by the NBER, so two chronologies claiming the same recession can disagree on its edges by up to a month. These functions take dates at day precision because their windows and their output are day-precision; that is a convention of the argument, never a claim that the underlying date is known to the day

the answer is only ever as good as the chronology handed in: supply a different one and every interval, flag and count moves with it. Nothing here validates the chronology against the committee's, because nothing here has the committee's to compare against
sources: NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee — US business cycle expansions and contractions (nber.org). Where a caller GETS a chronology, not something this engine ships or retrieves; the committee's own notice grants copying provided the source is attributed, so attribution is the form that use takes

Output: recessions: records df start/end = peak->trough (yyyymmdd int by default, or Date); overlap-clipped to [from,to] · flags: records df date/in_recession 0/1 + n_recession_periods · metadata: n_recessions/n, from/to (yyyymmdd), as_date · vintage: n_intervals + the first and last date read off the chronology THAT ARRIVED — the engine holds no snapshot to describe, so this echoes the caller's input rather than a publisher, a retrieval date or a digest of anything shipped
Pitfalls: the window is INCLUSIVE at both ends (Start=peak & End=trough are inside the recession); the day after the trough => 0 · a recession-free [from,to] => 0 rows (valid, NOT an error) · 20200101 is a yyyymmdd INTEGER, NOT a year; from=2020 errors (not an 8-digit date) · the committee dates peaks and troughs to a MONTH, and separately to a QUARTER — it publishes no day. Every day-of-month in a redistributed recession dataset was chosen by whoever repackaged it, not by the NBER, so two chronologies claiming the same recession can disagree on its edges by up to a month. These functions take dates at day precision because their windows and their output are day-precision; that is a convention of the argument, never a claim that the underlying date is known to the day · the answer is only ever as good as the chronology handed in: supply a different one and every interval, flag and count moves with it. Nothing here validates the chronology against the committee's, because nothing here has the committee's to compare against
Sources: NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee — US business cycle expansions and contractions (nber.org). Where a caller GETS a chronology, not something this engine ships or retrieves; the committee's own notice grants copying provided the source is attributed, so attribution is the form that use takes
