cards.method: Financial-network contagion: DebtRank + Furfine cascades + interbank exposure-matrix reconstruction (Maximum Entropy / Minimum Density)
cards.when: a bilateral network of financial exposures (interbank/counterparty): (a) only the MARGINS are KNOWN (assets per node + liabilities per node) → reconstruct the n×n exposure matrix with Maximum Entropy (dense) or Minimum Density (sparse, realistic); (b) the exposure matrix + capital buffers are KNOWN → measure systemic risk/contagion with DebtRank (continuous stress) or traditional default cascades (a Furfine threshold), identifying the most systemic nodes (too-central-to-fail)
cards.when_not: non-financial networks, or general centrality and community work (-> #55); spillover or connectedness from a VAR and its FEVD of returns (-> #51/#52); you want the tail risk of one series (VaR and ES, #65; Growth-at-Risk, #64); you have only indicators and no network; Bayesian Erdős-Rényi sampling of a network from its margins (-> #223)

alternatives.criterion: you want a fully connected (dense) matrix that maximises entropy subject to the margins; deterministic; it understates concentration/contagion (a known issue: much denser than real interbank networks)
you want a SPARSE, more realistic matrix (few large exposures, Anand et al. 2015); STOCHASTIC → a seed is mandatory for reproducibility
you want a CONTINUOUS measure of systemic importance — how much stress the failure of each node transmits (Bardoscia et al. 2015); single_hit=True selects the older Battiston 2012 variant
you want discrete default cascades (which nodes default in a chain when the losses exceed the buffer), not continuous stress
you want a Bayesian posterior distribution of networks consistent with the margins (ER/Gibbs), not a single ME/MD point estimate
you want general centrality/community/connectivity, not contagion-specific DebtRank/cascade dynamics

output_key_fields: exposure_matrix (nrm_reconstruct_matrix): the reconstructed n×n exposure matrix (rows are lenders and assets, columns borrowers and liabilities; a registered handle for chaining into nrm_contagion)
density/n_links (nrm_reconstruct_matrix): the sparsity of the network (minimum density far below maximum entropy); total_exposure: the total volume
max_rowsum_resid/max_colsum_resid (nrm_reconstruct_matrix): how well the requested margins were honoured — the fit quality
seed (nrm_reconstruct_matrix): the seed that was used, critical for the minimum-density route
results (nrm_contagion): a frame per scenario — scenario/original_stress/additional_stress/original_losses/additional_losses/additional_defaults
additional_stress (nrm_contagion): the unweighted DebtRank of each node when every node is shocked; most_systemic_scenario names the most systemic node
total_additional_defaults (nrm_contagion): the total number of chain defaults beyond the initial shock
weights_defaulted (nrm_contagion): True when equal weights were used, the fallback when none were supplied
user weights in nrm_contagion: a hard gate requires their sum to be strictly positive; a zero sum would divide by zero and give a NaN systemic stress (blocked by the gate)
interpretation_traps: MATRIX ORIENTATION: rowsums=ASSETS (the creditor/lender per row), colsums=LIABILITIES (the debtor/borrower per column); M[i,j]>0 means an «assets network»: i holds a claim/asset on j (i lent to j). exposure_type='liabilities' REVERSES the convention — state correctly which one describes your matrix
BALANCE is mandatory: sum(rowsums)==sum(colsums) (total assets = total liabilities in a closed system); otherwise ME silently rescales the rowsums → a hard gate
MD (min_dens) is STOCHASTIC: a different seed → a different matrix/results; always record/pin the seed; ME/DebtRank/threshold are deterministic
additional_stress is NON-NEGATIVE additional stress (systemic amplification), NOT a z-score; ME understates transmission (too dense a network) — prefer MD for realistic exposures

shock: 'all' = one default scenario per node (a per-node DebtRank); a numeric vector = ONE scenario of a uniform proportional shock in [0,1]; values outside [0,1] are rejected (otherwise contagion silently returns a meaningless 0)
leaving the weights unset trips a bug in the raw routine; the wrapper works around it with equal weights (weights_defaulted=True) — supply total assets as weights for an economic weighting
single_hit=True (the older Battiston 2012 single-hit DebtRank) applies ONLY to method='debtrank'; with 'threshold' it is rejected
sources: Battiston, Puliga, Kaushik, Tasca & Caldarelli 2012 'DebtRank: Too Central to Fail?' Scientific Reports 2:541
Bardoscia, Battiston, Caccioli & Caldarelli 2015 'DebtRank: A Microscopic Foundation for Shock Propagation' PLoS ONE 10(6)
Upper & Worm 2004 'Estimating bilateral exposures in the German interbank market' European Economic Review 48, 827-849 (Maximum Entropy)
Anand, Craig & von Peter 2015 'Filling in the blanks: network structure and interbank contagion' Quantitative Finance 15(4), 625-636 (Minimum Density)
Furfine 2003 'Interbank Exposures: Quantifying the Risk of Contagion' JMCB 35(1) (threshold default cascades)

Pitfalls: MATRIX ORIENTATION: rowsums=ASSETS (the creditor/lender per row), colsums=LIABILITIES (the debtor/borrower per column); M[i,j]>0 means an «assets network»: i holds a claim/asset on j (i lent to j). exposure_type='liabilities' REVERSES the convention — state correctly which one describes your matrix · BALANCE is mandatory: sum(rowsums)==sum(colsums) (total assets = total liabilities in a closed system); otherwise ME silently rescales the rowsums → a hard gate · MD (min_dens) is STOCHASTIC: a different seed → a different matrix/results; always record/pin the seed; ME/DebtRank/threshold are deterministic · additional_stress is NON-NEGATIVE additional stress (systemic amplification), NOT a z-score; ME understates transmission (too dense a network) — prefer MD for realistic exposures · shock: 'all' = one default scenario per node (a per-node DebtRank); a numeric vector = ONE scenario of a uniform proportional shock in [0,1]; values outside [0,1] are rejected (otherwise contagion silently returns a meaningless 0) · leaving the weights unset trips a bug in the raw routine; the wrapper works around it with equal weights (weights_defaulted=True) — supply total assets as weights for an economic weighting · single_hit=True (the older Battiston 2012 single-hit DebtRank) applies ONLY to method='debtrank'; with 'threshold' it is rejected
Sources: Battiston, Puliga, Kaushik, Tasca & Caldarelli 2012 'DebtRank: Too Central to Fail?' Scientific Reports 2:541 · Bardoscia, Battiston, Caccioli & Caldarelli 2015 'DebtRank: A Microscopic Foundation for Shock Propagation' PLoS ONE 10(6) · Upper & Worm 2004 'Estimating bilateral exposures in the German interbank market' European Economic Review 48, 827-849 (Maximum Entropy) · Anand, Craig & von Peter 2015 'Filling in the blanks: network structure and interbank contagion' Quantitative Finance 15(4), 625-636 (Minimum Density) · Furfine 2003 'Interbank Exposures: Quantifying the Risk of Contagion' JMCB 35(1) (threshold default cascades) · wrapper footer IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (c21_systemic_risk/financial_network_contagion)

cards.method: Bayesian interbank-network reconstruction (the Gandy-Veraart Gibbs sampler, an Erdős-Rényi hierarchical model)
cards.when: you know only the MARGINS of an interbank network — the row sums l (the total liabilities of each bank) & the column sums a (the total claims) — and you want to reconstruct the UNKNOWN n×n matrix of bilateral exposures L; Bayesian sampling of all the matrices consistent with the margins -> a posterior mean matrix, the probability of an edge per cell, the network density (an input for contagion/stress tests)
cards.when_not: you ALREADY have the full exposure matrix (go straight to contagion or centrality, category 09, #55/#51); you want network centrality or connectedness rather than reconstruction; non-square margins, or known cells (scoped out); a deterministic maximum-entropy or RAS reconstruction rather than a Bayesian posterior; margins that do not balance (a gate)

alternatives.criterion: you need a valid calibrated model BEFORE the sampler; you tune targetdensity (the expected share of existing edges)
you believe in a dense/interconnected network (a fully connected core); a smaller one -> a sparse network (few large exposures)
you want ONE point estimate (no posterior/uncertainty); it typically overstates interconnection (a fully connected bias) — Gandy-Veraart corrects that with sparsity
the exposure matrix is KNOWN and you want diffusion/centrality metrics, not a reconstruction

output_key_fields: mean_matrix: the n×n posterior MEAN exposure matrix (rowSums==l, colSums==a, a zero diagonal — guaranteed)
prob_link: the n×n posterior probability that an edge EXISTS, P(L[i,j]>0) ∈ [0,1]
sd_matrix / lower_matrix / upper_matrix: the uncertainty per cell (the standard deviation + the quantiles probs)
density: the mean network density (the share of positive off-diagonal edges)
out_degree / in_degree: the expected degree per bank (the sums of prob_link)
row_sum_max_dev / col_sum_max_dev: the maximum deviation from the margins (~0 = a sound reconstruction)
n_moving_cells: the cells that moved in the MCMC (the rest are deterministic/forced)

achieved_density (build_er_model): the REALIZED margin-conditional density (the mean off-diagonal link proportion over seeded sample_HierarchicalModel draws; the same quantity as the density of sample_interbank_network) — NOT the unconditional prior density of genL; directly comparable with targetdensity
model / samples: the raw handles (systemicrisk_er_model / systemicrisk_gv_samples) -> a to_mcp stub, registered for chaining
seed: the reproducibility seed (every stochastic path is seeded)
interpretation_traps: ORIENTATION: l = the row sums = the LIABILITIES (what bank i owes, row i), a = the column sums = the CLAIMS (what is owed to it, column j); L[i,j] = the exposure of i to j — do not transpose l/a; the post-gate rowSums==l & colSums==a catches it
sum(l) MUST equal sum(a) (total liabilities == total claims); a mismatch -> a hard gate 'they do not balance', NOT a silent adjustment

achieved_density can EXCEED targetdensity when the margins force a minimum number of edges (forced links); too LOW a targetdensity -> calibrate_ER ERRORS with 'Could not find feasible matrix', not a warning
both functions are STOCHASTIC (the calibration samples; the Gibbs sampler is MCMC); ALWAYS pass a seed for reproducibility — the same seed -> an identical posterior
the diagonal is always zero (no self-exposure); the diagonal of prob_link == 0
a small nsamples/thin -> a noisy estimate (the MCMC has not converged); raise them for production; the defaults (100/100) are conservative for small networks
mean_matrix is NOT the 'true' matrix — it is the posterior mean; the uncertainty lives in sd_matrix/lower/upper; use prob_link for the structure, not only the mean
sources: Gandy & Veraart 2017 'A Bayesian Methodology for Systemic Risk Assessment in Financial Networks' Management Science 63(12) 4428-4446
Gandy & Veraart 2019 'Adjustable Network Reconstruction with Applications to CDS Exposures' J. Multivariate Analysis 172 193-209

cards.method: tax progressivity & redistribution + subgroup decomposition of inequality (extended/S-Gini · concentration · Atkinson · GEI · Lorenz)
cards.when: a cross-section of non-negative values (income/wealth/tax/expenditure) when you want (a) a single-parameter/extended Gini with an explicit tail weight (param), an Atkinson index (aversion epsilon), a GEI (Theil/MLD), (b) a concentration index ranked by ANOTHER variable → the building blocks of Kakwani progressivity/Reynolds-Smolensky redistribution, (c) the Lorenz curve as numeric data, or (d) a SUBGROUP decomposition into within/between/(overlap|stratif|cross|residual) by a factor
cards.when_not: a plain scalar index with no tail parameter/decomposition → #91 ineq (Gini/RS/Kolm/var); a return tail VaR/ES → #65; a conditional-on-X GaR → #64; poverty indices (FGT) — not exposed; time-series dynamics

alternatives.criterion: a headline scalar Gini/Theil/Atkinson/Kolm WITHOUT a group decomposition and WITHOUT an extended-Gini param — a simpler surface
an extended Gini with an explicit weight on the poor (param=2 is the classic Gini; a larger param → more sensitivity to the lower tail)
you want a FULLY ADDITIVE within+between decomposition (the GE family)
BDA is multiplicative (1-(1-w)(1-b)) with a cross term; DP is additive (within+between+residual) — choose according to your reference framework
Kakwani progressivity = C_tax - G_preTax; Reynolds-Smolensky = G_preTax - C_postTax — the redistributive analysis of taxes/benefits
a non-parametric comparison of distributions (curve A everywhere above B ⇒ unambiguously less inequality)

output_key_fields: index (ineqd_sgini / ineqd_sconc / ineqd_atkinson / ineqd_gei): the scalar index; index_name (SGini/SConc/Atk/GEI); parameter and parameter_name (param/epsilon/alpha); n; weighted
p (ineqd_lorenz): the cumulative population share (n+1 points, chart-ready); L: the ordinary Lorenz curve; L_general: the generalized one, L times the mean, in units of x; plus gini and mean

within/between (the ineqd_decomp_* nodes): the within- and between-group inequality; third_component and third_name (overlap, stratification, cross or residual); between_elmo, the Elbers 'maximum' between-group term (blank when it is not requested, and OUTSIDE the identity)

reconciled_total and reconcile_error (the ineqd_decomp_* nodes): the recomposition check, |total - sum(components)| <= 1e-6; plus decomp_method; groups, a frame per group with group/index/share/weight and optionally contribution; and n_groups
interpretation_traps: the EXTENDED GINI param: param=2 == the classic Gini; param>1 weights the poor; param->1 => 0; 0<param<1 => a NEGATIVE index (a mathematically valid S-Gini, NOT conventional inequality — for a headline figure use param>=1)

the ATKINSON DECOMPOSITION: BDA is MULTIPLICATIVE (total=1-(1-within)(1-between)) — do NOT add within+between+cross (it does not equal the total; the 'cross' term = within+between-total); DP is ADDITIVE (within+between+residual)
the GEI is FULLY ADDITIVE (total=within+between); the SGini BM decomposition is within+between+overlap, YL is within+between+stratif; betweenELMO is NOT part of any identity

KAKWANI/REDISTRIBUTION = the DIFFERENCE between a concentration index and a Gini, NOT a single output: Kakwani progressivity = C_tax - G_preTax (positive=progressive); Reynolds-Smolensky = G_preTax - C_postTax; the wrapper supplies the building blocks, the difference is taken downstream
STRICT POSITIVITY: Atkinson with epsilon==1, and the GEI with alpha in {0,1}, require x>0 — a zero makes the raw routine return nothing at all; other values of epsilon or alpha accept zeros

SILENTLY WRONG (gated by the wrapper): a negative x returns nothing; a gap in x or w is silently removed; a wrong weight length is silently recycled; a non-categorical grouping variable returns nothing; an extreme alpha overflows to infinity
GEI alpha: alpha=1 is Theil-T/GE(1) (the upper tail); alpha=0 is the mean log deviation/GE(0) (the lower tail); alpha=2 is half the CV²
sources: Kakwani N.C. (1977) Measurement of Tax Progressivity, Economic Journal 87(345):71-80 (concentration/progressivity)
Atkinson A.B. (1970) On the Measurement of Inequality, JET 2:244-263
Blackorby C., Donaldson D., Auersperg M. (1981) Canadian J. Economics 14:665-685 (the BDA Atkinson decomposition)
Das T., Parikh A. (1982) Empirical Economics 7:23-48 (the DP Atkinson decomposition)
Bhattacharya N., Mahalanobis B. (1967) JASA 62:143-161 (the BM Gini decomposition); Yitzhaki S., Lerman R. (1991) Review of Income and Wealth 37:313 (YL stratification)
Shorrocks A.F. (1980) The Class of Additively Decomposable Inequality Measures, Econometrica 48:613-625 (GE within/between); Elbers et al. (2005) World Bank WP 3687 (the ELMO maximum between)
Reynolds M., Smolensky E. (1977) Public Expenditure, Taxes and the Distribution of Income (the redistribution effect)

cards.method: drivers of inequality change: RIF (recentered influence function) regressions + regression-based (Fields/Yun) inequality decomposition
cards.when: you want to explain WHAT DRIVES inequality (not merely to measure it): (a) the marginal effect of covariates on a distributional statistic (quantile/gini/variance) through a RIF regression; (b) a decomposition of the Gini/MLD into within/between/overlap by subgroup; (c) a Fields regression-based decomposition of total inequality across several characteristics; (d) a Yun decomposition of the CHANGE in inequality between two years into a price vs a quantity effect. Income micro data with survey weights + covariates
cards.when_not: a plain scalar index or Lorenz curve with no covariates (-> #91); tax progressivity or a single-index decomposition (-> #224); a parametric income distribution (-> #227); a conditional outcome tail or Growth-at-Risk (-> #64); return risk metrics, VaR and ES (-> #65); time-series dynamics

alternatives.criterion: you want the influence of each observation on the index itself (an input for a downstream RIF regression or a health-inequality decomposition); recentering: the weighted mean == the index

alternatives.alt: rif_regression (a deterministic OLS on the RIF)
alternatives.criterion: the marginal effects of covariates on a quantile/gini/variance, fast, without inference; it supports a vector of quantiles (unconditional quantile regression, Firpo-Fortin-Lemieux)
you need statistical inference on the RIF coefficients; ONE quantile only; SEEDED (deterministic)
you want the within/between + overlap (interaction) term of the Gini by one categorical variable; the Gini does NOT decompose cleanly (the overlap != 0 when the group distributions overlap)
you want a CLEAN within+between decomposition (no overlap) by one categorical variable; the mean log deviation = the generalized entropy GE(0), additively decomposable
SEVERAL characteristics at once: the contribution of each covariate (+ the residual) to total inequality (4 indices: gini/mld/theil/var-log); they sum to 100%

you compare two years/datasets: a decomposition of the CHANGE in the variance of log income by characteristic into a price effect (a change in the coefficients) vs a quantity effect (a change in composition)

output_key_fields: rif (rif_influence): the numeric RIF vector (chart-ready); recentered_stat: the index — the weighted mean of the RIF equals the index, verified live; method/quantile/kernel/weighted/n

coefficients (rif_regression): a SINGLE frame (term, quantile, coef, se, t, p) — normalised per quantile, since the raw routine changes shape with the method; adjusted_r2 and df; plus the raw fit as a stub
coefficients (rif_regression_se): a frame (term, coef, lower, upper, se, z_value, p_value, signif); Nboot/confidence/seed echoed; deterministic given the seed

decomposition (gini_decomposition): a named record (gini_total, gini_within, gini_between, gini_overlap — they do NOT add up without the overlap); a by_group frame (gini/contribution/mean/share_pop/share_income/n); gini_group_contribution sums to gini_within

decomposition (mld_decomposition): a named record (mld_total, mld_within, mld_between — within plus between equals the total, with NO overlap); a by_group frame; n_deleted, the non-positive values the logarithm drops; plus a note

inequality_measures (ineq_regression_decomp): a named record (gini, mld, theil, variance_logincome); a decomposition frame (variable, contribution — summing to 1); adjusted_r2/r_squared; n_deleted/n_used; plus a note

variance_logincome (ineq_change_decomp): (year1, year2, change); the change_absolute and change_relative frames (variable, price, quantity, total); residual_absolute/residual_relative; the Yun identity holds: the sum of price and quantity, plus the residual, equals the change
interpretation_traps: a DUAL weights convention: rif/gini_decomp/mld_decomp take weights = a numeric VECTOR; rifr/rifrSE/dineq_rb/dineq_change_rb take weights = a COLUMN NAME (a string) inside data — the wrong type = a silent error/misalignment

rifr CHANGES ITS OUTPUT SHAPE per method (quantile: Coef/SE/t/p matrices; gini/variance: a coefficients matrix + a scalar r2) — the wrapper normalises it into ONE long-format data_frame; do not rely on the raw shape
rifrSE accepts a scalar quantile ONLY (a vector → 'condition has length > 1'); it is a BOOTSTRAP → SEEDED (the same seed = identical results)
the log-based methods (mld/dineq_rb/dineq_change_rb) SILENTLY DROP x<=0 → always read n_deleted/note; if you miss it you overstate n
the Gini overlap term != 0 when the group distributions overlap → within+between do NOT sum to the total (unlike the MLD, which is purely additive); do not ignore the overlap

silently wrong: the raw routine drops incomplete cases in x and z, sets a missing weight to 0, and recycles when the weight or group vector is the wrong length; a zero weight then blanks the RIF silently — the wrapper enforces no gaps, a length equal to n, and weights STRICTLY above 0

gini_decomp does NOT filter negative x → a silently wrong Gini; the wrapper enforces an x>=0 gate (project-side); kernel='rectangular' with a gap around the quantile → dq=0 → Inf (the finite post-gate blocks it)

the formula nodes (rif_regression, rif_regression_se, ineq_regression_decomp, ineq_change_decomp): a gap in ANY covariate is blocked by a gate, because the underlying fit would silently drop those rows while reporting '0 deleted' and an inflated n_used; complete cases are required in every variable of the formula
sources: Firpo, Fortin & Lemieux 2009 (Econometrica 77:953, Unconditional Quantile Regressions — the RIF)
Fields 2003 (Research in Labor Economics 22:1, regression-based inequality decomposition)
Yun 2006 / Brewer & Wren-Lewis 2016 (Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 78:289, accounting for changes in income inequality — price vs quantity)
Mookherjee & Shorrocks 1982 (Economic Journal 92:886, the MLD within/between decomposition)
Heckley, Gerdtham & Kjellsson 2016 (J. Health Economics 48:89, a general RIF decomposition of socioeconomic inequality)

WHEN: you want to explain WHAT DRIVES inequality (not merely to measure it): (a) the marginal effect of covariates on a distributional statistic (quantile/gini/variance) through a RIF regression; (b) a decomposition of the Gini/MLD into within/between/overlap by subgroup; (c) a Fields regression-based decomposition of total inequality across several characteristics; (d) a Yun decomposition of the CHANGE in inequality between two years into a price vs a quantity effect. Income micro data with survey weights + covariates
NOT when: a plain scalar index or Lorenz curve with no covariates (-> #91); tax progressivity or a single-index decomposition (-> #224); a parametric income distribution (-> #227); a conditional outcome tail or Growth-at-Risk (-> #64); return risk metrics, VaR and ES (-> #65); time-series dynamics
Alternatives: rif_influence (the RIF vector) (you want the influence of each observation on the index itself (an input for a downstream RIF regression or a health-inequality decomposition); recentering: the weighted mean == the index) · rif_regression (a deterministic OLS on the RIF) (the marginal effects of covariates on a quantile/gini/variance, fast, without inference; it supports a vector of quantiles (unconditional quantile regression, Firpo-Fortin-Lemieux)) · rif_regression_se (bootstrap SE/CI/Z/P) (you need statistical inference on the RIF coefficients; ONE quantile only; SEEDED (deterministic)) · gini_decomposition (you want the within/between + overlap (interaction) term of the Gini by one categorical variable; the Gini does NOT decompose cleanly (the overlap != 0 when the group distributions overlap)) · mld_decomposition (GE(0)) (you want a CLEAN within+between decomposition (no overlap) by one categorical variable; the mean log deviation = the generalized entropy GE(0), additively decomposable) · ineq_regression_decomp (Fields 2003) (SEVERAL characteristics at once: the contribution of each covariate (+ the residual) to total inequality (4 indices: gini/mld/theil/var-log); they sum to 100%) · ineq_change_decomp (Yun 2006) (you compare two years/datasets: a decomposition of the CHANGE in the variance of log income by characteristic into a price effect (a change in the coefficients) vs a quantity effect (a change in composition))
Output: rif (rif_influence): the numeric RIF vector (chart-ready); recentered_stat: the index — the weighted mean of the RIF equals the index, verified live; method/quantile/kernel/weighted/n · coefficients (rif_regression): a SINGLE frame (term, quantile, coef, se, t, p) — normalised per quantile, since the raw routine changes shape with the method; adjusted_r2 and df; plus the raw fit as a stub · coefficients (rif_regression_se): a frame (term, coef, lower, upper, se, z_value, p_value, signif); Nboot/confidence/seed echoed; deterministic given the seed · decomposition (gini_decomposition): a named record (gini_total, gini_within, gini_between, gini_overlap — they do NOT add up without the overlap); a by_group frame (gini/contribution/mean/share_pop/share_income/n); gini_group_contribution sums to gini_within · decomposition (mld_decomposition): a named record (mld_total, mld_within, mld_between — within plus between equals the total, with NO overlap); a by_group frame; n_deleted, the non-positive values the logarithm drops; plus a note · inequality_measures (ineq_regression_decomp): a named record (gini, mld, theil, variance_logincome); a decomposition frame (variable, contribution — summing to 1); adjusted_r2/r_squared; n_deleted/n_used; plus a note · variance_logincome (ineq_change_decomp): (year1, year2, change); the change_absolute and change_relative frames (variable, price, quantity, total); residual_absolute/residual_relative; the Yun identity holds: the sum of price and quantity, plus the residual, equals the change
Pitfalls: a DUAL weights convention: rif/gini_decomp/mld_decomp take weights = a numeric VECTOR; rifr/rifrSE/dineq_rb/dineq_change_rb take weights = a COLUMN NAME (a string) inside data — the wrong type = a silent error/misalignment · rifr CHANGES ITS OUTPUT SHAPE per method (quantile: Coef/SE/t/p matrices; gini/variance: a coefficients matrix + a scalar r2) — the wrapper normalises it into ONE long-format data_frame; do not rely on the raw shape · rifrSE accepts a scalar quantile ONLY (a vector → 'condition has length > 1'); it is a BOOTSTRAP → SEEDED (the same seed = identical results) · the log-based methods (mld/dineq_rb/dineq_change_rb) SILENTLY DROP x<=0 → always read n_deleted/note; if you miss it you overstate n · the Gini overlap term != 0 when the group distributions overlap → within+between do NOT sum to the total (unlike the MLD, which is purely additive); do not ignore the overlap · silently wrong: the raw routine drops incomplete cases in x and z, sets a missing weight to 0, and recycles when the weight or group vector is the wrong length; a zero weight then blanks the RIF silently — the wrapper enforces no gaps, a length equal to n, and weights STRICTLY above 0 · gini_decomp does NOT filter negative x → a silently wrong Gini; the wrapper enforces an x>=0 gate (project-side); kernel='rectangular' with a gap around the quantile → dq=0 → Inf (the finite post-gate blocks it) · the formula nodes (rif_regression, rif_regression_se, ineq_regression_decomp, ineq_change_decomp): a gap in ANY covariate is blocked by a gate, because the underlying fit would silently drop those rows while reporting '0 deleted' and an inflated n_used; complete cases are required in every variable of the formula
Sources: Firpo, Fortin & Lemieux 2009 (Econometrica 77:953, Unconditional Quantile Regressions — the RIF) · Fields 2003 (Research in Labor Economics 22:1, regression-based inequality decomposition) · Yun 2006 / Brewer & Wren-Lewis 2016 (Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 78:289, accounting for changes in income inequality — price vs quantity) · Mookherjee & Shorrocks 1982 (Economic Journal 92:886, the MLD within/between decomposition) · Heckley, Gerdtham & Kjellsson 2016 (J. Health Economics 48:89, a general RIF decomposition of socioeconomic inequality)

cards.method: Complex-survey-aware inequality & poverty with design-based linearized SE (Gini/QSR/Zenga + FGT/ARPR)
cards.when: you have survey MICRODATA (a microdata data_frame) with sampling weights/strata/clusters and you want an inequality index (gini/qsr/zenga) or a poverty index (FGT/ARPR) WITH a correct design-based (linearized) standard error + CI + degrees of freedom; the node builds the survey design and the linearisation internally
cards.when_not: a plain vector with no complex-survey design -> #91 (a scalar index or Lorenz curve, with no standard errors); replicate-weight designs — not exposed; a return tail VaR or ES -> #65; a conditional Growth-at-Risk -> #64; the other design-based inequality estimators (GEI, Atkinson, Rényi, Watts, the median poverty gap) — future candidates

alternatives.criterion: a headline single-number inequality index with a design-based SE; sensitive mainly to the centre
the Quintile Share Ratio S80/S20 (alpha1=0.2, alpha2=0.8): the ratio of the upper to the lower quantile share; a Eurostat headline indicator
the Zenga (2007) uniformity index ∈[0,1]; sensitive to the whole distribution (a point-by-point comparison of lower/upper means)
Foster-Greer-Thorbecke: g=0 the headcount ratio, g=1 the poverty gap, g=2 the severity (the squared gap); an absolute (abs_thresh) or relative (relq/relm) threshold
the At-Risk-Of-Poverty Rate: the share below a relative threshold (the default is 60% of the median); a Eurostat headline poverty indicator
domain estimation (e.g. by region/group) with correctly reduced degrees of freedom
a plain vector with no survey design/weights — a descriptive index without SE

output_key_fields: estimate: the scalar index (Gini/QSR/Zenga/FGT/ARPR); Gini/Zenga/ARPR/FGT∈[0,1], QSR>=1 (a ratio)
se: the design-based LINEARIZED standard error (a Deville influence function; NOT a naive/iid SE)
ci_lower/ci_upper: a t-based CI at the given level, with the design degrees of freedom (df)
df: degf(design) — the degrees of freedom of the design (they drop in a domain subset)

measure/income: which index, and which variable; n_total/n_used/n_na: the sizes; n_used counts the observations that ACTUALLY enter the estimator (n_total minus n_na, or the count within the domain) and is NOT inflated by the incomes the estimator drops
g/type_thresh/abs_thresh (svy_poverty): the FGT parameters; alpha1/alpha2 (svy_inequality): the QSR quantiles
interpretation_traps: the linearisation step is MANDATORY: svyfgt/svyarpr/svyqsr error without it, BUT svygini/svyzenga compute SILENTLY (with a possibly wrong SE) — the wrapper always runs it
wrong ids/weights/strata → a wrong linearized SE (the estimate may be right while the SE is not); the design must reflect the ACTUAL sampling
a missing income with na_rm=False blanks the coefficient SILENTLY; the wrapper blocks that with a hard gate — set na_rm=True explicitly
the survey-design constructor SILENTLY accepts negative/zero weights; the wrapper requires weights>0
the FGT estimator with a relative threshold SILENTLY ignores abs_thresh — the wrapper requires abs_thresh to be unset unless type_thresh='abs'
FGT monotonicity: severity(g=2) <= gap(g=1) <= headcount(g=0); they differ in their sensitivity to the depth of poverty
ids="1" means ~1 (no clustering); df≈n-1; for a clustered design supply the actual PSU column
sources: Foster, Greer & Thorbecke 1984 Econometrica 52:761 (the FGT poverty measures)
Osier 2009 Survey Methodology 35:193 (the linearization of inequality/poverty estimators)
Zenga 2007 Statistica & Applicazioni 5:3 (the Zenga uniformity index)
Eurostat EU-SILC methodology (ARPR at 60% of the median, the S80/S20 quintile share ratio)

cards.method: GB2 (Generalized Beta of the 2nd kind, 4 parameters a,b,p,q) parametric income-distribution ML fit + analytic Gini/ARPR
cards.when: you have microdata of POSITIVE income (optionally with survey weights) and you want a PARAMETRIC model of the whole distribution: the GB2(a,b,p,q) is fitted by ML (full + profile log-likelihood) and yields CLOSED-FORM analytic indicators (Gini, ARPR, RMPG, QSR) that smooth out sampling noise and allow comparison/simulation; or you already have estimated (a,p,q) and want an analytic Gini/ARPR
cards.when_not: a non-parametric scalar index or a Lorenz curve straight from the sample (→#91 ineq, with no distributional assumption); a RETURN tail VaR/ES (→#65) or a conditional-on-X GaR (→#64); income with zeros/negatives (the GB2 is defined on x>0 — it is rejected); a small sample where the 4-parameter ML does not converge (heavy-tail identifiability); a within/between decomposition by group

alternatives.criterion: you do not want a distributional assumption; a descriptive index straight from the sample at one point in time; the GB2 is preferable when you want smoothing, tail extrapolation, or analytic poverty/welfare metrics from a single model
the most general 4-parameter form; it needs a reasonably large sample for the full ML to converge (the convergence gate blocks it otherwise)
you already have (a,p,q) [+prop] from another source/fit and you want only the scale-free index without refitting
you explicitly want the non-converged result for diagnosis (it comes back with converged=False); NEVER as a production output — a non-converged four-parameter fit is silently wrong

alternatives.alt: category 12 (#64 quantile regression / #65 VaR and Expected Shortfall)
alternatives.criterion: a conditional-on-X tail (GaR) or return risk metrics — a different question from an income distribution

output_key_fields: a, b, p and q (fit_gb2), and params as a named vector: the four estimated GB2 parameters from the FULL ML; a is the tail shape, b the scale, and p and q the Beta-2 shapes; at convergence all are above 0

loglik and loglik_profile (fit_gb2): the CONVENTIONAL TOTAL log-likelihood — the sum of the weighted GB2 log-densities, negative and of order n — directly usable for AIC = -2*loglik + 2k, for BIC, or for a likelihood ratio; it is NOT the raw negated per-observation mean the optimiser reports
converged (fit_gb2): True only when the FULL ML optimisation returns code 0 (a FUNCTIONAL GATE); convergence_full and convergence_profile carry the raw codes (0 = ok, 1 = the iteration limit)
gini (fit_gb2): the analytic Gini(a,p,q) in [0,1] at the fitted parameters; gini_defined=False marks a heavy tail (a*q<=1) where it is undefined, so the value is blank
arpr (fit_gb2): the At-Risk-of-Poverty Rate at prop times the median (default 0.6); arpr_prop is the proportion; arpr_defined is the finiteness flag
n (fit_gb2): the sample size; indicators: a frame comparing the empirical estimate against the full and profile ML (median, mean, ARPR, RMPG, QSR, GINI, a, b, p, q) — a chart-ready comparison
gini (gini_gb2): the analytic Gini of the GB2, scale-free and depending only on a, p and q
arpr (arpr_gb2): the analytic ARPR (scale-free); prop is the poverty line as a proportion of the median
interpretation_traps: CONVERGENCE: a small or heavy-tailed sample stops the FULL ML from converging, and yet it returns parameters as if it had succeeded — the convergence gate blocks that, and converged=False is not a valid output

POSITIVE SUPPORT: zero, negative or missing incomes do NOT raise an error in the ML fit; it proceeds silently. The x>0 and no-gaps gate is imposed by the project, and the reference example itself filters to positive incomes
WEIGHTS: a wrong length of w is recycled silently, zero weights exclude observations — a gate on length==n & w>0

HEAVY-TAIL Gini: with a*q<=1 the Gini is undefined, because the expectation does not exist; the standalone gini_gb2 errors explicitly, while inside fit_gb2 the value is left blank with gini_defined=False — and the fit itself remains valid
prop: the ARPR is monotone in prop; a prop outside (0,1) silently gives a wrong value — a gate on (0,1); it is scale-free (b is irrelevant)
the gini_gb2/arpr_gb2 argument order: (shape1=a, shape2=p, shape3=q); swapping p and q changes the result — do not confuse them

cards.method: affluence/richness indices (the top-tail mirror of poverty indices): the richness headcount ratio, the Chakravarty concave T1 index, the FGT convex T2 index, the Medeiros average affluence gap, the top income share, the Medeiros affluence line — weighted implementations
cards.when: a cross-section of positive incomes (with or without population weights) → how much and how intensely wealth is concentrated in the UPPER tail: the headcount of the rich (a line at k×median), the intensity of affluence (the concave T1 / convex T2 index), the absolute mean affluence gap, the income share of the top (1-p), or constructing a Medeiros affluence line from a poverty line
cards.when_not: the inequality of the WHOLE distribution (Gini, Theil, Atkinson, Lorenz -> #91); POVERTY indices or the lower tail (the FGT family); a return tail VaR or ES (-> #65); a conditional Growth-at-Risk (-> #64); Wolfson polarization, the Palma ratio or the weighted Gini (not exposed — the Gini is covered by #91); bootstrap standard errors (stochastic, not exposed); a subgroup decomposition (not exposed)

alternatives.criterion: how many people are rich — the weighted share of the population above the affluence line (the headcount); it does not capture intensity/distance
an affluence intensity that INCREASES under a rank-preserving progressive transfer among the rich (axiom T1); bounded in [0,1]; the parameter beta>0
an affluence intensity that DECREASES under a progressive transfer among the rich (axiom T2); the parameter alpha>1; it is NOT bounded by 1
the ABSOLUTE mean affluence gap (in income units), not a ratio — the size of the excess income above the line
the share of total income of the richest (1-p) fraction — the most widely used metric (top 1%/10% shares); the threshold is the p-quantile, NOT k×median
you want the affluence LINE (not an index) constructed from a poverty line (Medeiros); 0<k<1
the inequality of the whole distribution, not a focus on the upper tail

output_key_fields: index (richness_index): the affluence index; hc and cha lie in [0,1] as ratios, fgt is non-negative but NOT bounded above, and med is absolute, in income units
index_type (richness_index): hc, cha, fgt or med (a closed enum, default hc)
affluence_line (richness_index): rho = k times the weighted median — the UPPER threshold that was used; median_income is the median itself
count_rich / share_rich / k / n (richness_index): the number of units above rho, the weighted share of the rich, the value of k, and the sample size
income_share (income_share_top): the income share of those above the p-quantile, in [0,1]; threshold_quantile is that quantile; top_fraction is 1-p (p=0.9 gives the top 10%); plus count_top and n
affluence_line: the Medeiros affluence line; median_multiple = rho/median, above 1; median_income; poverty_gap; k; n
interpretation_traps: THRESHOLD DIRECTION (critical): the affluence line is an UPPER threshold. richness_index requires k>1, so that rho = k times the median sits above the median; k<=1 puts the line at or below the median and makes 'everyone rich' (live: k=0.5 gives a headcount of 0.9, k=1 gives 0.4). A gate blocks it
the OPPOSITE meaning of k: in affluence_line, k defines a POVERTY line BELOW the median, so 0<k<1; it mirrors richness_index — do not confuse the two
fgt is NOT bounded by 1 (it is convex, gaps^alpha; live alpha=3 → 1.27, a large alpha + a heavy tail → an overflow to Inf that the post-gate blocks); only hc/cha ∈ [0,1]; med is absolute
alpha>1 for fgt, and beta>0 for cha: the raw routine does NOT check the domain (live, alpha=0.5 was computed silently); the wrapper enforces it, and only for the relevant index
positive income (x>0): the raw routine does NOT error on negative or zero values — live, a negative input still returned a number; the wrapper blocks them, since the cha index divides by x

weights: the same length as x, with no recycling, strictly positive and with no gaps; leaving them unset gives equal weights. The weighted median and quantile use the SAME routine the index calls internally, so the reported rho and quantile are identical to the internal threshold

income_share_top: p is the QUANTILE threshold in (0,1), and the index measures the richest 1-p tail (p=0.9 gives the top 10%); it is not 'the top p%'; the extremes degenerate — p towards 0 gives about 1, p towards 1 gives 0 — and are blocked

affluence_line (Medeiros): the line MUST lie ABOVE the median (median_multiple>1, a hard post-gate); a degenerate line at or below the median is blocked, since it would make everyone 'rich'; an x with zero dispersion, fewer than two distinct values, trips a pre-gate; and a matrix with more than one column trips another — vectors, or a single column, only
sources: Peichl, Schaefer, Scheicher 2008 IZA Discussion Paper 3790 (measuring richness — affluence indices, axioms T1/T2)
Chakravarty 1983 Mathematical Social Sciences 6:307-313 (the concave index, the T1 mirror)
Foster, Greer, Thorbecke 1984 Econometrica 52:761-766 (the FGT decomposable family, the convex T2 mirror)
Medeiros 2006 Social Indicators Research 78:1-18 (an affluence line constructed from the poverty line)
Brzezinski 2010 Social Indicators Research 99:285-299 (income affluence in Poland; the richness headcount & top income share)

WHEN: a cross-section of positive incomes (with or without population weights) → how much and how intensely wealth is concentrated in the UPPER tail: the headcount of the rich (a line at k×median), the intensity of affluence (the concave T1 / convex T2 index), the absolute mean affluence gap, the income share of the top (1-p), or constructing a Medeiros affluence line from a poverty line
NOT when: the inequality of the WHOLE distribution (Gini, Theil, Atkinson, Lorenz -> #91); POVERTY indices or the lower tail (the FGT family); a return tail VaR or ES (-> #65); a conditional Growth-at-Risk (-> #64); Wolfson polarization, the Palma ratio or the weighted Gini (not exposed — the Gini is covered by #91); bootstrap standard errors (stochastic, not exposed); a subgroup decomposition (not exposed)
Alternatives: index='hc', the richness headcount (how many people are rich — the weighted share of the population above the affluence line (the headcount); it does not capture intensity/distance) · index=cha (Chakravarty, T1 concave) (an affluence intensity that INCREASES under a rank-preserving progressive transfer among the rich (axiom T1); bounded in [0,1]; the parameter beta>0) · index=fgt (FGT, T2 convex) (an affluence intensity that DECREASES under a progressive transfer among the rich (axiom T2); the parameter alpha>1; it is NOT bounded by 1) · index=med (the Medeiros gap) (the ABSOLUTE mean affluence gap (in income units), not a ratio — the size of the excess income above the line) · income_share_top (the share of total income of the richest (1-p) fraction — the most widely used metric (top 1%/10% shares); the threshold is the p-quantile, NOT k×median) · affluence_line (you want the affluence LINE (not an index) constructed from a poverty line (Medeiros); 0<k<1) · #91 ineq (Gini/Theil/Atkinson/Lorenz) (the inequality of the whole distribution, not a focus on the upper tail)
Output: index (richness_index): the affluence index; hc and cha lie in [0,1] as ratios, fgt is non-negative but NOT bounded above, and med is absolute, in income units · index_type (richness_index): hc, cha, fgt or med (a closed enum, default hc) · affluence_line (richness_index): rho = k times the weighted median — the UPPER threshold that was used; median_income is the median itself · count_rich / share_rich / k / n (richness_index): the number of units above rho, the weighted share of the rich, the value of k, and the sample size · income_share (income_share_top): the income share of those above the p-quantile, in [0,1]; threshold_quantile is that quantile; top_fraction is 1-p (p=0.9 gives the top 10%); plus count_top and n · affluence_line: the Medeiros affluence line; median_multiple = rho/median, above 1; median_income; poverty_gap; k; n
Pitfalls: THRESHOLD DIRECTION (critical): the affluence line is an UPPER threshold. richness_index requires k>1, so that rho = k times the median sits above the median; k<=1 puts the line at or below the median and makes 'everyone rich' (live: k=0.5 gives a headcount of 0.9, k=1 gives 0.4). A gate blocks it · the OPPOSITE meaning of k: in affluence_line, k defines a POVERTY line BELOW the median, so 0<k<1; it mirrors richness_index — do not confuse the two · fgt is NOT bounded by 1 (it is convex, gaps^alpha; live alpha=3 → 1.27, a large alpha + a heavy tail → an overflow to Inf that the post-gate blocks); only hc/cha ∈ [0,1]; med is absolute · alpha>1 for fgt, and beta>0 for cha: the raw routine does NOT check the domain (live, alpha=0.5 was computed silently); the wrapper enforces it, and only for the relevant index · positive income (x>0): the raw routine does NOT error on negative or zero values — live, a negative input still returned a number; the wrapper blocks them, since the cha index divides by x · weights: the same length as x, with no recycling, strictly positive and with no gaps; leaving them unset gives equal weights. The weighted median and quantile use the SAME routine the index calls internally, so the reported rho and quantile are identical to the internal threshold · income_share_top: p is the QUANTILE threshold in (0,1), and the index measures the richest 1-p tail (p=0.9 gives the top 10%); it is not 'the top p%'; the extremes degenerate — p towards 0 gives about 1, p towards 1 gives 0 — and are blocked · affluence_line (Medeiros): the line MUST lie ABOVE the median (median_multiple>1, a hard post-gate); a degenerate line at or below the median is blocked, since it would make everyone 'rich'; an x with zero dispersion, fewer than two distinct values, trips a pre-gate; and a matrix with more than one column trips another — vectors, or a single column, only
Sources: Peichl, Schaefer, Scheicher 2008 IZA Discussion Paper 3790 (measuring richness — affluence indices, axioms T1/T2) · Chakravarty 1983 Mathematical Social Sciences 6:307-313 (the concave index, the T1 mirror) · Foster, Greer, Thorbecke 1984 Econometrica 52:761-766 (the FGT decomposable family, the convex T2 mirror) · Medeiros 2006 Social Indicators Research 78:1-18 (an affluence line constructed from the poverty line) · Brzezinski 2010 Social Indicators Research 99:285-299 (income affluence in Poland; the richness headcount & top income share)

cards.method: Real-time data-revision analysis (vintages: a triangle, revision statistics, news-vs-noise/efficiency tests, a state-space nowcast)
cards.when: successive releases/vintages of the SAME macro series (real-time data) -> a revision triangle, revision summary statistics, news-vs-noise/bias/efficiency tests, or a state-space efficient final-estimate nowcast
cards.when_not: a single release (no vintage dimension); business-cycle dating (#88); plain forecast evaluation without vintages (#74-77); data ingestion (a file upload — a frontend route, not a node)

alternatives.criterion: you want a simple overview/heatmap of the revision table (wide: reference periods x publication dates)
you want the VALUES of the revisions relative to one reference; nth_release='latest' => the total revision (to the final release)
you want statistics + tests: bias/MAR/noise-to-signal/correlation/Theil and news-vs-noise (Mankiw-Shapiro)
you want to find the first release that is unbiased & efficient (b0=0 & b1=1, HAC)
you want a state-space 'efficient' estimate of the final value (Jacobs-van Norden news/noise or Kishor-Koenig)

output_key_fields: triangle: a matrix of reference periods against vintages, plus n_obs_per_period, the number of observed values per period
revisions: a frame {pub_date, time, revision} plus a summary (mean/sd/MAR/min/max, n_revisions counting the observed ones, n_missing)

sign_convention (compute_revisions): a mode-dependent string that travels WITH the numbers — 'revision = final - release' when nth_release='latest', against 'revision = reference - vintage (older - newer)' for an interval, a small nth_release, or a reference date; the OPPOSITE polarity from the sign_convention of analyze_revisions, which is 'final - initial'
revision_summary: a data_frame with one row per release (Bias(mean), MAR, noise/signal, Correlation, Theil's U, the news/noise test coefficient + p)
first_efficient_release: e, 0-indexed and blank when there is none, plus a tests frame {release, F_stat, p_value, efficient}
nowcast: the states and params frames, loglik/aic/bic/convergence/converged, and the raw fit as a stub
interpretation_traps: TWO different sign conventions: compute_revisions revision = REFERENCE - VINTAGE (nth_release='latest' => final - initial; interval/a small nth_release => NEGATIVE values for an upward-trending series); analyze_revisions revision = final - initial

news/noise polarity: the News test = a regression of the revision on the INITIAL value; the Noise test = a regression on the FINAL value (the coefficient point estimates coincide with a plain lm; HAC changes ONLY the SE/p-value)
the get_revision_analysis columns depend on the degree (1=magnitude/bias, 2=correlation, 3=news/noise, 4=Theil/sign, 5=all 38)
first_efficient_release: e is 0-indexed, so 0 means the first release is already efficient; when there is none it comes back blank with a warning — a valid result, not an error
nowcast: e MUST be >0 AND e<n_releases; the MLE is deterministic (identical when seeded); a small sample -> boundary/degenerate parameters
the node handles ONE series: several id values are blocked by a gate; unobserved revisions do NOT inflate n, since n_revisions counts only the observed ones
diagnose WAS OMITTED (a console-printing helper); the same statistics are exposed machine-readably by analyze_revisions
sources: Mankiw-Shapiro 1986 'News or Noise? An Analysis of GNP Revisions' Survey of Current Business (news vs noise)
Aruoba 2008 'Data Revisions Are Not Well Behaved' Journal of Money, Credit and Banking 40(2-3) 319-340 (the efficient release / Mincer-Zarnowitz test)
Jacobs & van Norden 2011 'Modeling data revisions: Measurement error and dynamics of true values' Journal of Econometrics 161(1) 101-109 (the jvn nowcast)
Kishor & Koenig 2012 'VAR Estimation and Forecasting When Data Are Subject to Revision' Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 30(2) 181-190 (the kk nowcast)

cards.method: Heterogeneous-panel VAR/SVAR: (P)MG estimation, panel cointegration rank tests, structural identification (+MG-IRF/MG-FEVD), bootstrap IRF confidence bands
cards.when: a panel of N individuals × K macro variables (heterogeneous, a common lag p) -> a (pooled) mean-group panel VAR or a rank-restricted VECM; testing the panel cointegration rank (combining the K×N individual statistics); structural identification (recursive/ICA/proxy/long-run) with an MG-IRF & MG-FEVD; confidence bands through a panel/individual moving-block bootstrap or mean-group inference
cards.when_not: a single time series or individual (a single-country VAR or SVAR -> categories 03/04); a micro-panel regression with no VAR dynamics (-> #46/#47); a pure cross-section with no time dimension; data ingestion (a file upload — a frontend route, not a node)

alternatives.criterion: a stationary/level panel -> a mean-group VAR in levels (Canova-Ciccarelli 2013; Pesaran-Smith 1995 MG)
a cointegrated panel of known rank r -> a (pooled) mean-group rank-restricted VECM (Pesaran-Shin-Smith 1999 PMG; Breitung 2005)
an unknown cointegration rank -> a panel rank test (JO=the Johansen trace panel test; BR=Breitung pooled; SL=Saikkonen-Luetkepohl; CAIN=Arsova-Oersal); RUN IT BEFORE model=VEC in order to choose r

structural shocks: chol=recursive (a known causal ordering); cvm/dc=statistical ICA (non-gaussian shocks); iv=external instruments/a proxy; grt=long/short-run restrictions on an SVEC; -> an MG-IRF (Gambacorta et al. 2014) + an MG-FEVD

IRF confidence bands: pmb=a panel moving-block bootstrap (full inference); mg=the mean-group spread over the N individuals (fast, no bootstrap); mb=an individual moving-block bootstrap for one selected individual

output_key_fields: pv_estimate: A (the lined-up MG coefficient matrices), beta (the cointegrating matrix; VEC), dim_K/dim_N/dim_r, individuals, variables, estimator; fit=pvarx (register -> a raw_handle, a to_mcp stub)

pv_cointegration: panel_stats & panel_pvals (matrices: rows=the combination methods LRbar/Choi_P/Choi_Pm/Choi_Z, columns=r_H0=0.K-1), individual_stats/pvals, ranks_tested, combination_tests, csd_present

pv_identify: B (the (K×S) structural impact matrix, MG), irf (a data_frame V1=horizon + impulse->response columns), fevd_mg (a named list per response variable; the matrices sum to ~100 per row under full identification), shock_names; fit=pid (register -> a raw_handle)

pv_bootstrap: irf_point/irf_lower/irf_upper as frames (V1 plus the impulse-to-response columns, at the (1-level)/2 and 1-(1-level)/2 quantiles), n_boot as actually run, level, horizon, impulse_response, and the individual index for the moving-block route
interpretation_traps: the Breitung panel cointegration test FAILS when the type arrives as a vector; the wrapper enforces a scalar through a closed enum; the SL and CAIN variants ignore det_case and use 'SL_trend'

a panel-level FEVD is NOT defined — it works per individual only; fevd_mg is the mean group of the individual FEVDs; under partial identification (an instrument with fewer shocks than variables) the rows do NOT necessarily sum to 100
the mean-group IRF (the default) is the average of the INDIVIDUAL IRFs (Gambacorta et al. 2014); it is NOT the IRF of the mean-group VAR, which is a different quantity
recursive-design bootstrap bands (pmb/mb) do NOT necessarily contain the point estimate (a small-sample bias); mg gives the spread across the N individuals, NOT a genuine bootstrap
cvm/dc identification is STOCHASTIC (DEoptim/steadyICA); the pmb/mb bootstraps are too; determinism comes from seeding (identical confirmed); chol/mg use no RNG

chaining: pv_estimate -> pv_identify -> pv_bootstrap; pv_identify requires an UNIDENTIFIED fit and blocks an already-identified one; pv_bootstrap requires an identified fit; the long-run route requires a VEC fit
sources: Canova & Ciccarelli 2013 'Panel Vector Autoregressive Models: A Survey' Advances in Econometrics 32, 205-246
Pesaran & Smith 1995 'Estimating Long-Run Relationships from Dynamic Heterogeneous Panels' J. Econometrics 68, 79-113 (mean group)
Pesaran, Shin & Smith 1999 'Pooled Mean Group Estimation of Dynamic Heterogeneous Panels' JASA 94, 621-634 (PMG); Breitung 2005 Econometric Reviews 24, 151-173 (two-step panel cointegration)
Gambacorta, Hofmann & Peersman 2014 JMCB 46, 615-642 (the mean-group IRF); Herwartz & Wang 2024 J. Applied Econometrics 39(4), 620-639 (panel ICA identification)

Mertens & Ravn 2013 AER 103, 1212-1247 & Jentsch & Lunsford 2021 JBES 40, 1876-1891 (the proxy SVAR); Empting et al. 2025 (the panel proxy SVAR); Kilian 1998 REStat 80, 218-230 (bootstrap-after-bootstrap)

cards.method: Quantifying QUALITATIVE survey expectations (up/same/down shares -> a numeric expectations series): the balance approach, Carlson-Parkin (+limen/distribution extensions), the regression approach, conditional expectations
cards.when: you have a QUALITATIVE expectations survey (the shares/counts of respondents expecting a rise/no change/a fall in a macro variable y, typically inflation) + the ACTUAL series y, and you want a NUMERIC series of quantified expectations for downstream analysis/charts
cards.when_not: QUANTITATIVE expectations that are already numeric (survey point forecasts) -> analyse them directly; density or fan-chart forecasts -> category 12; anchoring or disagreement regressions -> #33, or plain OLS; data ingestion (a file upload — a frontend route, not a node)

alternatives.criterion: you want the simplest indicator: a scaling of the balance (up-down) with theta calibrated to the actual change in y; minimal distributional assumptions
you want the probability method with indifference limens; limen_type selects Carlson-Parkin, Weber-Fechner, a constant, or a symmetric or asymmetric series, and distrib_type the normal, logistic or t
you want time-invariant ASYMMETRIC upper and lower limens estimated by OLS, plus a symmetry test (White, or the small-sample heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors)
you want a method with NO assumption of symmetric/parametric limens: expectations built on the empirical distribution of past realizations (a moving/fixed experience horizon)

output_key_fields: qn_balance: y_e_mean_abs / y_e_mean_perc (chart-data: the quantified expectation in levels, the abs & the perc version) + delta_y_e_mean/sd_abs/perc + theta_abs/theta_perc (the scaling) + nob/mae/rmse
qn_carlson_parkin: y_e_mean_abs/perc (chart-data) + limen_abs/limen_perc (the indifference limen per period) + delta_y_e_* + nob/mae/rmse + the limen_type/distrib_type echo
qn_regression: y_e_mean_abs/perc (chart-data) + upper_limen_abs/lower_limen_abs (+perc) + symmetry_abs/symmetry_perc (the p-value of the symmetry test) + nob/mae/rmse
qn_conditional_expectations: y_e (chart data — the quantified expectation, full length and blank outside the window) plus nob/mae/rmse and the exp_horizon_type and distrib_param echo
all of them: the forecast_horizon/first_period/last_period echo of the period window
interpretation_traps: abs vs perc: each of bal/cp/ra gives TWO versions — expectations of the ABSOLUTE change (y_e_mean_abs) vs of the PERCENTAGE change (y_e_mean_perc); choose according to whether the question concerns a level or a rate
y_e is full-length and aligned to the input, blank outside [first_period, last_period]; nob counts only the quantified periods — do not confuse the length of y_e with nob

the shares must be NON-NEGATIVE: the raw routine SILENTLY accepts negative shares and produces plausible-but-wrong output (the balance theta came out inflated) -> a hard gate requires up, same and down to be non-negative; they need not sum to 100, since 'Don't know' is allowed
cp does NOT need first_period>forecast_horizon (source-verified: cp calibrates against the FUTURE change y[t+h] vs y[t]); the ONLY constraint is last_period+forecast_horizon<=n

qn_conditional_expectations degenerates when the experience window is too short: it SILENTLY returns nob=0, or an entirely blank y_e; the fix is for fix_horizon_end to reach roughly first_period-1. A post-check gate blocks it, and an even shorter window raises an internal error

the DISTRIBUTION root: the Carlson-Parkin and regression routes with distrib_type='t' need distrib_t_df>0, defaulting to last minus first; the logistic uses a location and a scale, the normal a mean and a standard deviation
DETERMINISM: analytic/OLS methods, NO RNG (identical verified) -> no seed
sources: the balance, Carlson-Parkin, regression-adjusted and cross-entropy quantifiers (arguments and value fields verified live)
Batchelor, R.A. (1984) 'Quantitative vs. qualitative measures of inflation expectations' Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics 48(2) 99-120 (the balance approach)
Carlson, J.A. & Parkin, M. (1975) 'Inflation expectations' Economica 42, 123-138 (the Carlson-Parkin probability method)
Henzel, S. & Wollmershaeuser, T. (2005) 'Quantifying inflation expectations with the Carlson-Parkin method' Journal of Business Cycle Measurement and Analysis 2, 321-352 (the Weber-Fechner limen)
Nardo, M. (2003) 'The quantification of qualitative survey data: a critical assessment' Journal of Economic Surveys 17(5) 645-668 (the zero-share correction)
Pesaran, M. (1984) 'Expectations formation and macroeconomic modelling' in Contemporary macroeconomic modelling, 27-55 (the regression approach)
MacKinnon, J.G. & White, H. (1985) 'Some heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimators' Journal of Econometrics 29, 305-325 (the symmetry-test SE)
Zuckarelli, J. (2015) 'A new method for quantification of qualitative expectations' Economics and Business Letters 3(5) 123-128 (conditional expectations)

Alternatives: qn_balance (Batchelor 1984) (you want the simplest indicator: a scaling of the balance (up-down) with theta calibrated to the actual change in y; minimal distributional assumptions) · qn_carlson_parkin (Carlson-Parkin 1975) (you want the probability method with indifference limens; limen_type selects Carlson-Parkin, Weber-Fechner, a constant, or a symmetric or asymmetric series, and distrib_type the normal, logistic or t) · qn_regression (Pesaran 1984) (you want time-invariant ASYMMETRIC upper and lower limens estimated by OLS, plus a symmetry test (White, or the small-sample heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors)) · qn_conditional_expectations (Zuckarelli 2015) (you want a method with NO assumption of symmetric/parametric limens: expectations built on the empirical distribution of past realizations (a moving/fixed experience horizon))
Output: qn_balance: y_e_mean_abs / y_e_mean_perc (chart-data: the quantified expectation in levels, the abs & the perc version) + delta_y_e_mean/sd_abs/perc + theta_abs/theta_perc (the scaling) + nob/mae/rmse · qn_carlson_parkin: y_e_mean_abs/perc (chart-data) + limen_abs/limen_perc (the indifference limen per period) + delta_y_e_* + nob/mae/rmse + the limen_type/distrib_type echo · qn_regression: y_e_mean_abs/perc (chart-data) + upper_limen_abs/lower_limen_abs (+perc) + symmetry_abs/symmetry_perc (the p-value of the symmetry test) + nob/mae/rmse · qn_conditional_expectations: y_e (chart data — the quantified expectation, full length and blank outside the window) plus nob/mae/rmse and the exp_horizon_type and distrib_param echo · all of them: the forecast_horizon/first_period/last_period echo of the period window
Pitfalls: abs vs perc: each of bal/cp/ra gives TWO versions — expectations of the ABSOLUTE change (y_e_mean_abs) vs of the PERCENTAGE change (y_e_mean_perc); choose according to whether the question concerns a level or a rate · y_e is full-length and aligned to the input, blank outside [first_period, last_period]; nob counts only the quantified periods — do not confuse the length of y_e with nob · the shares must be NON-NEGATIVE: the raw routine SILENTLY accepts negative shares and produces plausible-but-wrong output (the balance theta came out inflated) -> a hard gate requires up, same and down to be non-negative; they need not sum to 100, since 'Don't know' is allowed · cp does NOT need first_period>forecast_horizon (source-verified: cp calibrates against the FUTURE change y[t+h] vs y[t]); the ONLY constraint is last_period+forecast_horizon<=n · qn_conditional_expectations degenerates when the experience window is too short: it SILENTLY returns nob=0, or an entirely blank y_e; the fix is for fix_horizon_end to reach roughly first_period-1. A post-check gate blocks it, and an even shorter window raises an internal error · the DISTRIBUTION root: the Carlson-Parkin and regression routes with distrib_type='t' need distrib_t_df>0, defaulting to last minus first; the logistic uses a location and a scale, the normal a mean and a standard deviation · DETERMINISM: analytic/OLS methods, NO RNG (identical verified) -> no seed
Sources: the balance, Carlson-Parkin, regression-adjusted and cross-entropy quantifiers (arguments and value fields verified live) · Batchelor, R.A. (1984) 'Quantitative vs. qualitative measures of inflation expectations' Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics 48(2) 99-120 (the balance approach) · Carlson, J.A. & Parkin, M. (1975) 'Inflation expectations' Economica 42, 123-138 (the Carlson-Parkin probability method) · Henzel, S. & Wollmershaeuser, T. (2005) 'Quantifying inflation expectations with the Carlson-Parkin method' Journal of Business Cycle Measurement and Analysis 2, 321-352 (the Weber-Fechner limen) · Nardo, M. (2003) 'The quantification of qualitative survey data: a critical assessment' Journal of Economic Surveys 17(5) 645-668 (the zero-share correction) · Pesaran, M. (1984) 'Expectations formation and macroeconomic modelling' in Contemporary macroeconomic modelling, 27-55 (the regression approach) · MacKinnon, J.G. & White, H. (1985) 'Some heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimators' Journal of Econometrics 29, 305-325 (the symmetry-test SE) · Zuckarelli, J. (2015) 'A new method for quantification of qualitative expectations' Economics and Business Letters 3(5) 123-128 (conditional expectations) · wrapper footer IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (c25_expectations_surveys/quantifying_qualitative_survey)

cards.method: Design-based complex-survey estimation (means/totals/quantiles/domains) with correct design variances (stratification, clustering, weights, fpc)
cards.when: estimating means/totals/quantiles/domains from survey microdata (expectation/consumer/business tendency surveys, e.g. Michigan, the ECB SPF) where the sampling DESIGN (strata/clusters/weights/fpc) must enter the variance; the naive s²/n understates it (clustering) or ignores the sampling weights -> a wrong CI
cards.when_not: informal or equally weighted data with no design (a plain mean or quantile); a regression on a survey design (a future node); calibration, post-stratification, raking, or a replicate-weight bootstrap (a different family); estimating category proportions, which changes the output shape; time-series or aggregate data rather than microdata; qualitative tendency surveys (-> #231) or small-area estimation (-> #233)

alternatives.criterion: ALWAYS FIRST: declare the complex-survey design from a df_handle + column names (ids/strata/weights/probs/fpc); ids='1' => no clusters; it returns a raw_handle that feeds the consumers
you want the design-based weighted MEAN of numeric variables + a correct SE/CI/cv/deff
you want an estimate of a population TOTAL (a weighted sum) + a design SE
you want weighted QUANTILES (the median etc.) with a design CI/SE; the quantiles must lie strictly in (0,1)
you want an estimate per DOMAIN/subgroup (a mean or a total per level of a grouping variable) with a correct design SE per domain

output_key_fields: srv_design: design (register -> a raw_handle) + metadata (n_obs, n_variables, numeric_vars, n_strata, has_strata/has_fpc/has_clusters, weighted, weight_min/max/mean/total = a summary of the design weights 1/prob)

srv_mean/srv_total: an estimates df {variable, estimate, SE, cv, ci_lower, ci_upper[, deff]} + coefficients + SE + vcov (a matrix with axis labels) + statistic('mean'/'total') + the raw fit (to_mcp -> a stub)
srv_quantile: an estimates df {variable, quantile, estimate, SE, ci_lower, ci_upper} (newsvyquantile: a matrix per variable, with columns quantile/ci.2.5/ci.97.5/se) + n_quantiles
srv_by_domain: an estimates df (records per domain, with the columns produced by svyby: the grouping + estimate + se) + n_groups + group_levels + statistic
interpretation_traps: the design effect is Var_design/Var_SRS; above 1 it means clustering or unequal weighting INCREASES the variance relative to a simple random sample of the same n; the column appears ONLY when deff=True
weights AND probs are mutually exclusive (probs = 1/weights); with neither => an equally weighted SRS (weight_min==weight_max); non-positive weights -> a hard gate (invalid estimates)
nest=True applies ONLY when the cluster ids are reused within strata, so that they need relabelling per stratum; otherwise the strata come out wrong

svyquantile (survey 4.5 'newsvyquantile'): a list per variable, matrix columns {quantile, ci.2.5, ci.97.5, se}, row labels=the probs; quantiles of 0/1 -> infinities -> a gate (strictly (0,1)); in small samples the CI can be NaN (the linearization df) -> to_mcp maps them to null
the variables MUST be numeric: a categorical one would give PROPORTIONS per level, a different output shape -> a hard gate here rejects non-numeric variables

the finite population correction REDUCES the standard error when the sample is a large fraction of the population; leaving it unset means sampling with replacement — no correction, and a conservative standard error
PURELY ANALYTIC (Horvitz-Thompson/linearization) -> no RNG/seed; identical output across two calls (a seed would be needed only for a replicate-weights bootstrap, which is out of scope)
sources: the complex-survey estimators (design, mean, total, quantile, by-group, standard error, CV, design effect) (live-verified, the engine)
Lumley 2010 'Complex Surveys: A Guide to Analysis Using the reference' (Wiley) — design-based estimation, design effects, domain estimation
Lumley 2004 JSS 9(1) (analysis of complex survey samples)
Horvitz & Thompson 1952 JASA 47:663-685 (the design-based estimator of totals)

cards.method: Small-area estimation (SAE): the Fay-Herriot area-level EBLUP (+ the analytic Prasad-Rao MSE) & the Battese-Harter-Fuller unit-level EBLUP
cards.when: estimating an indicator per small area/domain (regions, age/subgroups of a survey) when the per-area sample is too small for a reliable DIRECT estimate -> 'borrowing strength' through a model of auxiliary variables + a random effect; eblupFH when you have ONLY aggregate direct estimates + their sampling variances (area level); eblupBHF when you have UNIT-level micro data + the population means of the auxiliary variables (unit level); mseFH for an analytic MSE/CV of reliability
cards.when_not: large per-area samples (the direct estimate suffices); unknown sampling variances for FH; spatial/spatio-temporal correlation between areas (eblupSFH/eblupSTFH, separate methods); non-normal/EB under a transformation (ebBHF); a plain regression with no domain structure

alternatives.criterion: you have ONE direct estimate theta_hat_i per area + its sampling VARIANCE psi_i (vardir); you want a shrinkage estimate (a point estimate)

alternatives.alt: sae_mse_fh (the FH EBLUP + an analytic MSE + CV%)
alternatives.criterion: you want ALSO the analytic (Prasad-Rao g1+g2+g3) MSE/RMSE estimate + the CV% for reliability per area (with an optional seeded bootstrap goodness-of-fit test, B>0)
you have UNIT-level micro data (a nested-error regression) + the population means/sizes of the auxiliary variables per area; you want the EBLUP of the area MEANS

output_key_fields: eblup: a numeric vector of small-area estimates (chart-data); direct: the direct estimates (the model response); n_areas/n_domains
coefficients (FH): a data_frame {beta,std_error,tvalue,pvalue}; fixed (BHF): a named beta vector
variance components: refvar (the between-area sigma_u^2); errorvar (the within-area sigma_e^2, BHF); icc = refvar/(refvar+errorvar) (BHF); convergence/iterations/goodness (loglike/AIC/BIC/KIC, FH)
sae_mse_fh: mse (a numeric vector; Prasad-Rao) + cv = 100*sqrt(mse)/eblup (the CV%); bootstrap = B
sae_eblup_bhf: domain/sampsize/random(u_i)/residuals/loglike (the heavy merMod summary is deliberately removed)
interpretation_traps: vardir is the sampling VARIANCE (SD^2), NOT the SD -> the wrong scale gives silently wrong shrinkage; the wrapper blocks vardir<0 (a hard gate) because eblupFH accepts negative values and returns an apparently valid EBLUP
sae_eblup_bhf: when a target area is missing from the population means or sizes, the routine emits ONLY a warning and silently returns a blank EBLUP -> a hard gate on full coverage

vardir and dom are resolved as column NAMES when data is supplied, so they must be given as strings rather than as expressions or values; the wrapper copies them into fixed sae_vardir and sae_dom columns

the EBLUP = a shrinkage gamma_i*direct + (1-gamma_i)*regression with gamma_i = A/(A+psi_i); areas with a large psi_i (a small sample) shrink more towards the model; read the CV% per area for reliability
seed: only the bootstrap goodness-of-fit path (B>0) in mseFH/eblupFH is stochastic; the EBLUP/analytic MSE are deterministic (identical when seeded, verified)
sources: the small-area estimators (Fay-Herriot EBLUP, its MSE, and the unit-level BHF EBLUP)
Fay & Herriot 1979 'Estimates of Income for Small Places: An Application of James-Stein Procedures to Census Data' JASA 74(366) 269-277 (area-level FH)
Battese, Harter & Fuller 1988 'An Error-Components Model for Prediction of County Crop Areas Using Survey and Satellite Data' JASA 83(401) 28-36 (unit-level BHF)
Prasad & Rao 1990 'The Estimation of the Mean Squared Error of Small-Area Estimators' JASA 85(409) 163-171 (the analytic MSE)
Rao & Molina 2015 'Small Area Estimation' 2nd ed, Wiley (the textbook)

cards.method: Textual sentiment pipeline (corpus -> lexicon sentiment -> time aggregation -> elastic-net sparse-regression forecasting)
cards.when: you have time-stamped TEXT (news/reports/tweets) {id,date,texts,+features} and you want to turn it into numeric sentiment indicators and forecast a macro variable: (a) build the corpus, (b) compute the lexicon-based document sentiment, (c) aggregate it over time into several measures (lexicon×feature×time scheme), (d) run a sparse elastic-net regression of y on the measures
cards.when_not: you have no text, only numeric series (-> #219/#220); you want a general sparse regression with no textual sentiment (-> #216/#219); word embeddings or transformer NLP (outside the surface); data ingestion (a file upload — a frontend route, not a node)

alternatives.criterion: the first step: a df {id,date,texts,+numeric features} -> a sento_corpus (a register handle for the chain)
lexicon-based document sentiment with >=1 built-in lexicons (LM_en/HENRY_en/GI_en/FEEL/..) and a within-document weighting
the temporal aggregation of the document sentiment into measure time series; how_time (equal_weight/linear/almon/beta/exponential) — ALL of them are tried -> nmeasures=lexicons×features×time

a sparse elastic-net regression of y on the measures; the alpha and lambda pair is selected by an information criterion (gaussian only), or by out-of-sample cross-validation, which also covers classification

output_key_fields: snt_corpus: corpus (a register raw_handle) + n_documents/date_min/date_max/features/n_features
snt_sentiment: sentiment (a registered raw handle; the per-document records are the chart data) + sentiment_columns (lexicon and feature), lexicons, and how
snt_measures: measures (a register raw_handle) + measures_table (date + the measure columns = chart-data) + measure_names/n_measures/n_dates/dates/dimensions(features,lexicons,time)

snt_model: a coefficients frame {term, coefficient}, with a class column in the multinomial case; alpha and the selected lambda; n_predictors; n_selected, the non-zero ones excluding the intercept; a discarded frame; ic_criterion, blank under cross-validation; fit_dates; and the raw fit as a stub
interpretation_traps: a 4-stage CHAIN: each stage REGISTERS the raw object as a handle (a raw_handle) that feeds the next one; snt_model is TERMINAL
the information criteria (type=BIC/AIC/Cp) apply ONLY to model='gaussian'; binomial/multinomial REQUIRE type='cv' (with train_window/test_window)
y MUST be aligned with the measure dates (length == n_dates); gaussian numeric; binomial 2 values; multinomial >=3 values
how_time and alphas are vectors, and ALL of their entries are tried — they are not a single enumerated choice; a custom weight matrix is not supported
alpha=0=ridge, alpha=1=lasso (the elastic-net mixing); n_selected = the sparse (non-zero) coefficients; a higher lambda => a sparser model
the seed pins the cross-validation fold draw (defence in depth; the information-criterion path is deterministic anyway)
sources: Ardia, Bluteau, Boudt, Borms & Vrontos 2021 JSS 99(2) (computing, aggregating and predicting with textual sentiment)
Ardia, Bluteau & Boudt 2019 'Questioning the news about economic growth: Sparse forecasting using thousands of news-based sentiment values' International Journal of Forecasting 35(4) 1370-1386

Loughran & McDonald 2011 'When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10-Ks' Journal of Finance 66(1) 35-65 (the LM lexicon); Henry 2008 (the HENRY lexicon); Stone et al. General Inquirer (the GI lexicon)
Zou & Hastie 2005 JRSS-B 67(2):301-320 (regularization and variable selection via the elastic net); Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010 JSS 33(1) (regularization paths via coordinate descent)
