cards.method: Mixed and random-parameters logit for panel choice data
cards.when: repeated choices by the same individuals, or taste heterogeneity you want to estimate rather than assume away; relaxes IIA without imposing a nesting structure
cards.when_not: you have one choice per person and no basis for heterogeneity; market-level shares only (-> BLP)

alternatives.criterion: no heterogeneity and IIA is acceptable
heterogeneity is discrete rather than continuous
you observe shares rather than individual choices

output_key_fields: params: mean and standard deviation of each random coefficient
individual_params: posterior means per chooser, where a panel identifies them
wtp: willingness to pay when a price coefficient is present
loglike, aic, n_draws: the simulation size the estimate rests on
interpretation_traps: the estimate is SIMULATED; too few draws produce a likelihood surface with spurious local optima, and the reported standard error does not include simulation noise

cards.method: Willingness to pay, compensating variation and consumer welfare from discrete choice
cards.when: converting estimated demand into money: what a characteristic is worth, and what a price or choice-set change does to consumer surplus
cards.when_not: the price coefficient is insignificant or wrong-signed, which makes every money-metric meaningless; you want producer welfare only

alternatives.criterion: the question is substitution rather than money
you want the exact closed-form surplus under logit
the model has random coefficients and no closed form

output_key_fields: wtp: characteristic coefficient divided by the price coefficient, with a delta-method interval
compensating_variation: per-chooser money-metric change
consumer_surplus_change: aggregate change, in the price numeraire
log_sum: the inclusive value before and after

cards.method: Propensity-score estimation with common-support trimming
cards.when: reducing a many-dimensional covariate vector to one score so treated and control units can be compared, under selection on observables
cards.when_not: treatment is randomised (no score needed); selection is on unobservables (-> IV or DiD); there is no overlap to trim to

alternatives.criterion: few covariates and you want exact comparability
you want protection against a misspecified score
you want to keep the whole sample rather than match

output_key_fields: pscore: the fitted propensity per unit
common_support: the retained overlap region and how many units each arm lost
overlap_diagnostics: score distributions by arm and the minimum/maximum of the common range
auc: discrimination, which should be moderate -- not high
interpretation_traps: a HIGH propensity-score AUC is bad news, not good: near-perfect prediction of treatment means no overlap and nothing to compare
trimming changes the estimand -- the effect is now for the retained overlap population, not the original one, and that must be reported
the score is only as good as the covariates in it; balancing the score does not balance anything omitted from it

cards.method: Nearest-neighbour, caliper, kernel and radius matching
cards.when: constructing a comparison group by pairing treated units with similar controls, when you want a transparent design rather than a regression adjustment
cards.when_not: overlap is poor and matching would discard most of the sample; the covariate set is high dimensional (-> weighting or double ML)

alternatives.criterion: you want to retain the full sample
poor matches must be refused rather than accepted at any distance
you want to use many controls per treated unit for efficiency

output_key_fields: att/atc/ate: the matched effect for the requested estimand
matched_pairs: the pairing, so the design is auditable
n_unmatched: treated units dropped for want of a match inside the caliper
se: standard error, which must account for the matching, not the naive one
interpretation_traps: the naive standard error over matched pairs is WRONG -- matching is not sampling and the estimated score adds variance (-> the bias-corrected estimator)
matching with replacement reuses good controls, which lowers bias and raises variance; without replacement the answer depends on the ORDER units are processed
unmatched treated units silently change the estimand from ATT to ATT-on-the-matchable
sources: Dehejia & Wahba 2002 (Review of Economics and Statistics 84:151)

cards.method: Abadie-Imbens bias-corrected matching with valid standard errors
cards.when: you need matching estimates whose standard errors are actually valid, and a correction for the bias that matching on a continuous score leaves behind
cards.when_not: matching is exact so there is no bias to correct; the design is weighting rather than matching

alternatives.criterion: you accept the bias and do not need valid inference
you would rather have double robustness than a bias correction
the outcome model is credible on its own

bias_correction: the size of the adjustment, which reveals how poor the matches were
se: the Abadie-Imbens variance, which accounts for matching and for the estimated score
n_matches_used: match multiplicity per treated unit
interpretation_traps: the bootstrap is INVALID for nearest-neighbour matching -- Abadie and Imbens proved it fails, so a bootstrapped standard error here is simply wrong
a large bias correction is a warning that the matches were poor, not a sign the correction worked
matching on an ESTIMATED score adds variance that the naive formula omits entirely

cards.when: estimating an average effect by reweighting rather than matching, and buying insurance against misspecification by combining the weight model with an outcome model
cards.when_not: overlap is so poor that weights explode; treatment is continuous without a dose-response model

alternatives.criterion: you prefer an explicit paired design
the treatment model is credible and you want simplicity
you want a substitution estimator with the same double robustness

output_key_fields: ate/att: the point estimate for the requested estimand
weights: per-unit weights, stabilised where asked
max_weight, ess: the largest weight and the effective sample size -- the diagnostics that matter
se, conf_int: influence-function based inference
interpretation_traps: a handful of extreme weights can drive the entire estimate; ALWAYS read the effective sample size, which is often a small fraction of n
doubly robust means consistent if EITHER model is right -- it does not mean consistent if both are wrong, and it does not fix poor overlap
stabilised weights fix the variance, not the bias; if the treatment model is wrong, stabilising hides the symptom

Pitfalls: a handful of extreme weights can drive the entire estimate; ALWAYS read the effective sample size, which is often a small fraction of n · doubly robust means consistent if EITHER model is right -- it does not mean consistent if both are wrong, and it does not fix poor overlap · stabilised weights fix the variance, not the bias; if the treatment model is wrong, stabilising hides the symptom
Sources: Robins, Rotnitzky & Zhao 1994 (JASA 89:846-866) · Hernan & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If · Chernozhukov et al. 2018 (Econometrics Journal 21:C1) · doubleml

cards.method: Balance diagnostics: standardised differences, variance ratios and love plots
cards.when: checking whether a matching or weighting design actually achieved comparability, which is the only thing that licenses the causal reading
cards.when_not: the design is randomisation with a large sample, where balance is guaranteed in expectation

alternatives.criterion: the standard, sample-size-free summary
means balance but spread may not
the whole distribution matters, not the first two moments

output_key_fields: smd_before/smd_after: standardised difference per covariate
variance_ratio: treated-to-control variance per covariate
love_plot_data: covariates ordered by post-adjustment imbalance, ready to plot
worst_covariate: the covariate that remains least balanced
interpretation_traps: a t-test of balance is the WRONG instrument -- it conflates imbalance with sample size, so trimming makes it 'pass' by losing power
balancing means says nothing about higher moments or interactions; a design can balance every mean and still compare different populations
balance can only be checked on OBSERVED covariates; it is silent about the ones that drive selection

cards.method: Propensity stratification and subclassification
cards.when: you want a transparent design that uses the whole sample: split on the score into strata, estimate within each, and aggregate
cards.when_not: the score has poor overlap so some strata contain one arm only; you need unit-level pairing

alternatives.criterion: you want explicit pairs rather than blocks
you want a continuous weight rather than blocks
you want exact strata on covariates rather than on the score

output_key_fields: stratum_effects: the effect and count within each stratum
ate/att: the aggregate, weighted by stratum size or by treated count
balance_by_stratum: standardised differences within each stratum
n_strata_dropped: strata lacking one arm
interpretation_traps: five strata is a convention, not a result; the number of strata is a bias-variance choice and the estimate moves with it

cards.method: Sensitivity to hidden bias: Rosenbaum bounds and the E-value
cards.when: asking how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to overturn the finding -- the only honest answer to 'but what about omitted variables'
cards.when_not: the design is randomised; the effect is already null, in which case there is nothing to overturn

alternatives.criterion: the design is matched and you want a p-value under bias
you want a single transportable number on the risk-ratio scale
the design is regression with observable selection

output_key_fields: gamma_critical: the odds of differential assignment at which significance is lost
bounds: p-value bounds across the gamma grid
e_value: the minimum confounder association that would explain away the estimate
e_value_ci: the same for the confidence limit, which is the more conservative reading
interpretation_traps: these bound the effect of an unmeasured confounder; they do NOT test whether one exists and cannot
a gamma near 1 means the finding is fragile to very mild hidden bias -- report it, do not bury it
the E-value is on the risk-ratio scale; applying it to a coefficient without converting is meaningless

cards.method: G-computation, standardisation and targeted maximum likelihood
cards.when: estimating a causal effect by modelling the outcome and averaging predictions over the covariate distribution, with a targeting step that restores valid inference
cards.when_not: there is no overlap; the outcome model cannot be fitted credibly and no machine learner helps

alternatives.criterion: you want the same double robustness in an estimating-equation form
the outcome model is credible and you accept model-based inference
the treatment model is the one you trust

output_key_fields: ate/att: the standardised effect
potential_outcomes: mean outcome under each arm, averaged over the covariate distribution
influence_curve_se: inference from the influence function, valid after targeting
initial_vs_targeted: how far the targeting step moved the estimate
interpretation_traps: plain g-computation with a machine-learned outcome model has NO valid standard error -- that is exactly the gap the targeting step exists to close
a large gap between the initial and targeted estimate signals a poorly specified initial model, not a successful correction
the estimand is defined by the covariate distribution you average over; averaging over the treated gives ATT, over everyone gives ATE, and the difference is not cosmetic
sources: van der Laan & Rubin 2006 (International Journal of Biostatistics 2:11)

cards.method: Kernel regression: Nadaraya-Watson, local linear and local polynomial with mixed data
cards.when: estimating a conditional mean without committing to a functional form, when the shape of the relationship is the object of interest
cards.when_not: the sample is small or the covariate dimension above three or four -- the curse of dimensionality makes the estimate noise; you need parameters to interpret

alternatives.criterion: the default: no boundary bias, unlike Nadaraya-Watson
you want a basis expansion you can put in a regression
several covariates, additive structure acceptable

output_key_fields: fitted: the estimated conditional mean on the evaluation grid
bandwidth: the bandwidth actually used, per covariate
conf_band: pointwise band, which is not a uniform band
r_squared: the nonparametric goodness of fit
interpretation_traps: Nadaraya-Watson is badly biased at the BOUNDARY of the support; local linear is not, which is why it is the default
the pointwise band does not cover the whole curve simultaneously -- reading it as a uniform band overstates precision
bandwidth choice dominates every other decision here; a cross-validated bandwidth on dependent data is too small
sources: Nadaraya 1964 (Theory of Probability and Its Applications 9:141); Watson 1964 (Sankhya A 26:359)
Fan & Gijbels 1996, Local Polynomial Modelling and Its Applications

cards.method: Bandwidth selection: cross-validation, plug-in and rule of thumb
cards.when: the bandwidth is the single choice that determines a nonparametric estimate, and it should be made by a stated rule rather than by eye
cards.when_not: the estimator supplies its own bandwidth internally and you have no reason to override it

alternatives.criterion: the target is the regression function
you want speed and the density is roughly smooth
a quick first look only -- it assumes near-normality

output_key_fields: bandwidth: the selected value per covariate
criterion_curve: the objective over the searched grid, so a flat or multi-modal objective is visible
method: which rule produced the answer
interpretation_traps: cross-validation on SERIALLY DEPENDENT data selects a bandwidth that is far too small; use a blocked or modified criterion for time series
the rule of thumb assumes approximate normality and is badly wrong for skewed or multimodal data
a flat criterion curve means the bandwidth is barely identified and the estimate is unstable across near-equivalent choices
sources: Silverman 1986, Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis

cards.method: Multivariate and conditional kernel density estimation
cards.when: estimating a joint or conditional density without a parametric family -- for distributional questions, mode finding and density-based diagnostics
cards.when_not: you need tail probabilities far beyond the data (-> extreme value theory); the dimension is high

alternatives.criterion: one variable and you only need a shape
the object is the distribution of y given x, not the joint
you want interpretable components rather than a smooth surface

bandwidth: bandwidth per dimension

in more than two or three dimensions the estimate is dominated by sparsity, whatever the bandwidth

cards.method: Nonparametric conditional quantiles
cards.when: the whole conditional distribution matters, not the mean, and you are unwilling to impose linearity on the quantile function
cards.when_not: a linear quantile regression is adequate; the sample is too small for tail quantiles to be estimable

alternatives.criterion: linearity is acceptable and you want coefficients
many covariates and interactions
you want a full parametric conditional distribution

output_key_fields: quantiles: the estimated conditional quantile per requested level
crossing_detected: whether the fitted quantile curves cross, which is a specification failure
prediction_interval: the interval implied by the requested quantile pair
interpretation_traps: separately estimated quantile curves CAN CROSS, which is logically impossible for a distribution function -- check the flag rather than assuming it away
extreme quantiles need far more data than central ones; a 1% conditional quantile from a few hundred observations is noise
quantile forests give conditional quantiles under an implicit smoothness assumption from the tree structure, not a distribution-free guarantee

cards.method: Series and sieve estimation with polynomial and spline bases
cards.when: you want nonparametric flexibility inside an ordinary regression, so the estimate has closed-form inference and composes with instrumental variables
cards.when_not: the basis dimension needed exceeds what the sample supports; the relationship is genuinely local (-> kernel methods)

alternatives.criterion: you want a local estimate rather than a global basis
you want smoothness chosen by a penalty rather than by basis size
the function is smooth and low order suffices

output_key_fields: fitted: the fitted conditional mean
basis: the constructed design matrix, reusable in any downstream regression
k_selected: the basis dimension chosen and the criterion that chose it
params, bse: coefficients on the basis, which have no direct interpretation
interpretation_traps: basis coefficients are NOT interpretable individually -- only the fitted function and its derivatives are
high-order global polynomials oscillate wildly near the boundary (Runge's phenomenon); splines are the fix, not a higher degree
the basis dimension must grow with the sample for consistency, and selecting it on the same data invalidates the naive standard error
sources: Chen 2007, Large sample sieve estimation of semi-nonparametric models (Handbook of Econometrics 6B)

cards.method: Partially linear models by the Robinson double-residual method
cards.when: one coefficient is the object of interest and everything else is a nuisance you would rather not specify -- the semiparametric workhorse behind modern double machine learning
cards.when_not: every covariate is of interest; the nuisance dimension is small enough for a fully parametric model

alternatives.criterion: the nuisance is high dimensional and you want machine learners with cross-fitting
the nuisance functional form is known
you want each nuisance term visible and additive

output_key_fields: theta: the parametric coefficient of interest, root-n consistent
se, conf_int: inference that already accounts for the nuisance estimation
nuisance_r2: fit of the two first-stage regressions
n_folds: the cross-fitting used, which is what makes the inference valid
interpretation_traps: WITHOUT cross-fitting the estimate is biased by overfitting in the nuisance step; a single-fold implementation is not the same estimator
the double-residual construction requires BOTH first stages to converge fast enough; a badly fitting nuisance model breaks the root-n claim silently
theta is a partial effect holding the nuisance function fixed -- it is not a total derivative
sources: Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey & Robins 2018 (Econometrics Journal 21:C1)

cards.when: you want dimension reduction without full nonparametrics: a single linear index passed through an unknown link, or coefficients that vary smoothly with one modifier

bandwidth: the smoothing used for the link or the coefficient paths

cards.when_not: strong interactions dominate and additivity is false; you need a single index (-> single index)

cards.when: asking whether a parametric model is adequate, with a test whose alternative is 'some smooth function' rather than another parametric form
cards.when_not: you are comparing two specific parametric models (-> non-nested tests); the sample is too small for a nonparametric alternative to have power

alternatives.criterion: a cheap parametric screen for neglected nonlinearity
the alternative is a specific rival model
you want diagnosis rather than a formal test

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: the specification test
bootstrap_p: wild-bootstrap p-value, which is the one to report in small samples
parametric_fit, nonparametric_fit: the two fits being compared
interpretation_traps: the asymptotic null distribution is a poor approximation in small samples; the wild bootstrap version is the usable one
rejection says the parametric form is inadequate; it does not say which nonparametric alternative is right
power depends on the bandwidth of the alternative, so a non-rejection at one bandwidth is not a non-rejection

cards.method: General nonlinear GMM: one-step, two-step, iterated and continuously-updated
cards.when: the model is defined by moment conditions rather than a likelihood -- Euler equations, rational-expectations restrictions, any orthogonality the theory implies
cards.when_not: a likelihood is available and correctly specified (use it, it is efficient); the moments are linear in parameters and a 2SLS closed form exists

alternatives.criterion: the standard default once a weighting matrix can be estimated
better small-sample behaviour, at the cost of a harder optimisation
the full distribution is known and you want efficiency

dependence within known groups

cards.method: Overidentification and moment-selection tests
cards.when: deciding which moment conditions to believe when the overidentification test rejects, rather than dropping instruments until it stops rejecting
cards.when_not: the model is exactly identified so no test exists; you have no candidate subset in mind

alternatives.criterion: an omnibus test of all overidentifying restrictions
you want to test one specific subset of moments
you want a ranking over many candidate subsets

c_statistic: the difference-in-Sargan for the nominated subset
selected_moments: the subset a criterion prefers
msc: the moment-selection criterion value per candidate

cards.method: Classical and efficient minimum distance
cards.when: you have a set of reduced-form estimates and a structural mapping, and want the structural parameters plus a test that the mapping fits
cards.when_not: the structural parameters can be estimated directly in one step; the reduced-form covariance is unavailable

alternatives.criterion: the reduced-form covariance is well estimated

alternatives.alt: classical minimum distance with identity weighting
alternatives.criterion: the covariance estimate is poor and efficiency is not worth the noise

alternatives.alt: one-step GMM on the structural moments
alternatives.criterion: you can write the structural moments directly

distance_statistic, p_value: the specification test of the mapping
weighting_matrix: the matrix used

cards.method: Empirical likelihood and generalised empirical likelihood
cards.when: you want GMM's moment-based identification with better small-sample behaviour and an internally studentised likelihood-ratio test
cards.when_not: the sample is large enough that GMM's asymptotics are reliable and the optimisation cost is not worth paying

alternatives.criterion: large sample, and you want speed
a member of the same family with different small-sample behaviour
you want a different member of the GEL family

el_ratio, p_value: the empirical-likelihood ratio test, which needs no variance estimate
probabilities: the implied observation weights, which should be near 1/n
converged: inner and outer convergence
interpretation_traps: the inner optimisation can fail when the moment conditions cannot be satisfied by any convex weighting -- that is the empty-set problem, not a numerical glitch

cards.method: Simulated method of moments and indirect inference
cards.when: the model can be simulated but its moments have no closed form -- structural models with latent states, discrete choice dynamics, agent-based models
cards.when_not: analytic moments exist (use GMM); simulation is too slow for the optimiser to converge in reasonable time

alternatives.criterion: the moments are analytic
you want to match the parameters of an auxiliary model rather than raw moments
the likelihood can be simulated and you want efficiency

output_key_fields: params, bse: the estimate, with the simulation-noise inflation factor applied
objective: the distance at the optimum
n_sim: simulation draws per evaluation, which sets the noise floor
auxiliary_params: the auxiliary model's parameters under data and under simulation
interpretation_traps: the SAME random draws must be used at every parameter evaluation -- redrawing makes the objective discontinuous and the optimiser will wander forever
standard errors must include the simulation noise via the (1 + 1/S) inflation; omitting it understates uncertainty
too few simulation draws make the objective surface bumpy, and the optimiser will report a local minimum as a solution
sources: Gourieroux, Monfort & Renault 1993 (Journal of Applied Econometrics 8:S85)

cards.method: Constrained estimation, numerical derivatives and the optimiser layer
cards.when: the estimation problem has bounds, equality or inequality constraints, or a badly scaled objective, and the default optimiser silently returns a non-solution
cards.when_not: the problem is unconstrained, smooth and well scaled, where the estimator's own default is fine

alternatives.criterion: the objective is noisy or non-smooth, as with simulation
the objective is smooth and derivatives are available
the problem can be written as a convex programme and solved exactly

converged, message, n_evaluations: whether and how the search terminated
gradient, hessian: numerical derivatives at the optimum
active_constraints: which bounds or constraints bind, which changes inference
interpretation_traps: a parameter AT its bound has a non-standard sampling distribution -- the usual standard error and t-test do not apply

cards.method: Partial identification: Manski bounds, Lee bounds and moment-inequality sets
cards.when: the data do not point-identify the parameter and you would rather report the set that is consistent with them than a point that is not
cards.when_not: the parameter is point identified; the identified set is so wide it is uninformative and you should say so instead

alternatives.criterion: selection is unrestricted and you want the assumption-free bound
attrition or sample selection with a monotone response
the model implies inequalities rather than equalities

confidence_set: a set with the requested coverage, for the parameter or for the set
width: how informative the bounds are -- the number that decides whether this was worth doing
assumptions_used: which restrictions narrowed the set
interpretation_traps: a confidence set for the PARAMETER and one for the identified SET are different objects with different coverage; report which one you computed
worst-case bounds are almost always wide -- that is the honest answer, not a failure of the method

cards.method: IID and residual bootstrap with BCa and percentile-t intervals
cards.when: the sampling distribution of a statistic is unknown or its asymptotic approximation is poor, and the observations are independent
cards.when_not: the data are serially dependent (-> block or sieve bootstrap); the statistic is non-smooth, such as a nearest-neighbour matching estimator, where the bootstrap is known to fail

alternatives.criterion: serial dependence
the statistic is biased or skewed
a variance estimate is available and you want second-order accuracy

output_key_fields: estimate, bias, se: the point estimate, bootstrap bias and standard error
conf_int: interval by the requested method
replications: the bootstrap distribution itself
method: which interval construction produced the answer
interpretation_traps: the plain percentile interval is only first-order accurate and is badly wrong for skewed statistics -- BCa or percentile-t is the default worth having
the bootstrap FAILS for non-smooth statistics: nearest-neighbour matching, the maximum, parameters on a boundary
bootstrapping a t-statistic requires a variance estimate at every replication, which is what makes percentile-t expensive and accurate
sources: Efron & Tibshirani 1993, An Introduction to the Bootstrap

cards.method: Moving-block and circular-block bootstrap
cards.when: resampling serially dependent data by taking contiguous blocks, so the short-run dependence survives the resample
cards.when_not: the data are independent (-> iid bootstrap); the dependence is long memory, where blocks of any feasible length lose it

alternatives.criterion: you want to avoid the end effects of fixed blocks
the dependence is well captured by an autoregression
the series is short and end effects would dominate

output_key_fields: estimate, se, conf_int: as for the iid bootstrap
block_length: the length used and the rule that chose it
replications: the bootstrap distribution
interpretation_traps: the BLOCK LENGTH is the whole method: too short destroys the dependence, too long leaves too few blocks to resample
the moving-block bootstrap under-weights observations at the ends of the sample; the circular version fixes that by wrapping
block bootstraps are inconsistent for statistics depending on long-range dependence

cards.when: block resampling with geometrically random block lengths, so the resampled series is itself stationary
cards.when_not: the data are independent; the statistic requires blocks of a fixed known length

alternatives.criterion: you want deterministic block lengths

the statistic converges at an unknown rate

cards.when: the dependence is well described by a linear autoregression, so resampling its residuals reproduces the dynamics without blocking
cards.when_not: the dependence is nonlinear or the series has conditional heteroskedasticity the autoregression cannot capture

alternatives.criterion: the dependence is not well approximated by an autoregression

cards.method: Wild bootstrap with Rademacher, Mammen and Webb weights
cards.when: regression errors are heteroskedastic of unknown form and you want inference that does not rely on the asymptotic sandwich
cards.when_not: the errors are homoskedastic; the design is clustered, where the cluster-level wild bootstrap is required instead

alternatives.criterion: errors are correlated within clusters
the regressors are stochastic and you want to resample them too
the sample is large and asymptotics are reliable

output_key_fields: estimate, se, conf_int: wild-bootstrap inference
p_value: bootstrap p-value for the tested restriction
weights: which auxiliary distribution was used
replications: the bootstrap distribution of the statistic
interpretation_traps: Rademacher weights take only two values, so with very few clusters or observations the bootstrap distribution has a COARSE support and the p-value cannot fall below a floor
Webb weights exist precisely to fix that floor when there are six or fewer clusters
the restriction must be imposed on the null when resampling; the unrestricted version has poor size

interpretation_traps: with fewer than about five clusters NO method restores correct size; report the cluster count prominently rather than a p-value that looks precise
Rademacher weights impose a floor of 2^(1-G) on the p-value; with G=5 nothing below 0.0625 is attainable, so a reported 0.01 is impossible
the null must be imposed when resampling; the unrestricted variant over-rejects, which is the failure it was meant to cure
sources: Cameron, Gelbach & Miller 2008 (Review of Economics and Statistics 90:414-427)

cards.method: Randomisation and permutation inference
cards.when: the design assigned treatment by a known randomisation, so inference can rest on that design rather than on a sampling model or an asymptotic approximation
cards.when_not: assignment was not random and the permutation distribution has no design justification; the sample is a population and there is nothing to permute

alternatives.criterion: you want a sampling-based rather than design-based interval
the outcome is binary and the table is small
the sample is large and the design is simple

output_key_fields: p_value: the exact or approximate randomisation p-value
null_distribution: the permutation distribution of the statistic
n_permutations: exhaustive or sampled, and how many
conf_int: interval by test inversion, where requested
interpretation_traps: the permutation must respect the ACTUAL randomisation -- permuting freely when assignment was blocked or clustered gives a p-value for an experiment that was never run
the sharp null of no effect for any unit is stronger than the null of no average effect; the test is exact only for the former
with a small number of possible assignments the p-value has a coarse, bounded support

cards.method: Subsampling and jackknife
cards.when: the bootstrap is invalid or the convergence rate is unknown, and you need a resampling scheme that survives both
cards.when_not: the statistic is smooth and the bootstrap works -- it is more efficient here

alternatives.criterion: the statistic is smooth and regular
the convergence rate is unknown or the bootstrap is inconsistent
the statistic is non-smooth and delete-1 fails

output_key_fields: estimate, bias, se: resampling summaries
conf_int: subsampling or jackknife interval
subsample_size: b, the size used, and the rate assumed
pseudo_values: jackknife pseudo-values, for influence diagnostics
interpretation_traps: subsampling is consistent under far weaker conditions than the bootstrap, but it needs b to grow more slowly than n and the answer is sensitive to b
the DELETE-1 jackknife is inconsistent for non-smooth statistics such as the median; delete-d is the fix
jackknife pseudo-values identify influential observations, which is often more useful than the interval itself

cards.method: Multiple testing: Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg and Romano-Wolf stepdown
cards.when: many hypotheses are tested at once -- multiple outcomes, subgroups or specifications -- and the unadjusted p-values guarantee false discoveries
cards.when_not: there is one pre-registered primary hypothesis; the tests are so few that adjustment is not credible either way

alternatives.criterion: you must control the family-wise error rate and tests may be dependent
you can tolerate a proportion of false discoveries among rejections
the tests are dependent and you want power that exploits that dependence

output_key_fields: p_adjusted: adjusted p-values in the order supplied
rejected: which hypotheses survive at the requested level
n_rejected: the count before and after adjustment
method: the procedure applied
interpretation_traps: FWER and FDR control DIFFERENT things; Holm bounds the probability of any false rejection, Benjamini-Hochberg bounds their expected share, and they are not interchangeable
Benjamini-Hochberg assumes independence or positive dependence; under arbitrary dependence the Benjamini-Yekutieli correction is needed and is much more conservative
Romano-Wolf requires resampling the joint distribution -- it cannot be applied to a list of p-values alone

cards.method: Data-generating-process simulators for ARMA, VAR, GARCH, panel and factor models
cards.when: you need data with known properties to check an estimator, size a study or demonstrate a method
cards.when_not: you have real data and no need for a controlled experiment

alternatives.criterion: you want realism rather than a known truth
the truth must be known exactly
the process is not describable in closed form

output_key_fields: simulated: the generated data
true_params: the parameters used, so an estimator can be scored against them
seed: the seed, without which nothing here is reproducible
interpretation_traps: the burn-in must be long enough for the process to reach stationarity, or the first observations carry the initial condition
a simulated series is only as informative as the process is realistic; a study on a well-behaved ARMA says nothing about a break-ridden real series

cards.method: Size and power studies with rejection frequencies
cards.when: quantifying whether a test actually holds its nominal level and how often it detects a given alternative, before it is used on real data
cards.when_not: the test is standard and its properties in your design are already documented

alternatives.criterion: a closed-form power function exists
the test is complex or the design is non-standard
the test over-rejects and you want a corrected critical value

output_key_fields: size: rejection frequency under the null, which should equal alpha
power: rejection frequency under each alternative
size_corrected_power: power at the empirical rather than nominal critical value
mc_se: Monte Carlo standard error of each frequency
interpretation_traps: comparing POWER between tests that do not have the same size is meaningless -- size-corrected power is the only fair comparison
every reported frequency has Monte Carlo error; with 1000 replications a 5% rate has a standard error near 0.7 percentage points
a test that over-rejects under the null will look powerful under the alternative for exactly the wrong reason
sources: Davidson & MacKinnon 2004, Econometric Theory and Methods, ch.4

cards.method: Coverage and calibration checks
cards.when: an interval or a predictive distribution claims a coverage level, and that claim should be checked rather than assumed
cards.when_not: the procedure is exact by construction, such as a randomisation interval in a finite design

alternatives.criterion: you have a known truth to cover
the object is a predictive distribution rather than an interval
the object is a probability forecast

output_key_fields: coverage: realised coverage per nominal level
coverage_error: realised minus nominal, with its Monte Carlo error
mean_width: interval width, since coverage alone can be bought with width
pit: probability-integral-transform values, uniform under correct calibration
interpretation_traps: coverage and width must be read TOGETHER; a trivially wide interval covers perfectly and says nothing
an under-covering interval is a bigger problem than a wide one, because it makes false claims rather than weak ones
PIT uniformity is necessary but not sufficient for calibration -- a badly wrong forecast can still be marginally calibrated

cards.method: Global sensitivity analysis: Sobol, Morris, FAST and delta
cards.when: a model has many inputs and you want to know which ones actually drive the output, over the whole input space rather than at one point
cards.when_not: the model is cheap and linear, where local derivatives suffice; there are only one or two inputs

alternatives.criterion: many inputs and you only need to rank them cheaply
you want variance shares including interactions
the model is near-linear around one point

output_key_fields: first_order: the variance share attributable to each input alone
total_order: the share including every interaction the input takes part in
interaction: total minus first order, which is where the structure hides
conf_int: bootstrap intervals on each index
interpretation_traps: a LOCAL derivative is not a global sensitivity; for a nonlinear model the two routinely disagree about which input matters
first-order indices summing to well below one means interactions dominate -- read the total-order indices, not the first-order ones
Sobol needs a specific sample design; feeding it an arbitrary sample gives numbers that are not Sobol indices
sources: Saltelli et al. 2008, Global Sensitivity Analysis: The Primer

cards.method: Experimental designs: Latin hypercube, factorial, Box-Behnken and Plackett-Burman
cards.when: choosing WHERE to evaluate an expensive model or run an experiment, so the runs you can afford answer the question
cards.when_not: the input space is one dimensional; you can afford to evaluate everywhere

alternatives.criterion: continuous inputs and a space-filling sample
few discrete factors and you want every combination
many factors, screening main effects only

output_key_fields: design: the generated design matrix
n_runs: how many evaluations the design costs
resolution: which effects are confounded with which, for fractional designs
discrepancy: space-filling quality for the sampling designs
interpretation_traps: a fractional factorial CONFOUNDS effects by construction; the resolution says which, and ignoring it means attributing an interaction to a main effect
Plackett-Burman screens main effects only and its interaction aliasing is complex -- it is a screen, not an analysis
Latin hypercube is space-filling in projection but a bad draw can still cluster; check the discrepancy

cards.when: deciding how large a trial must be before running it, or reporting honestly what a completed trial could ever have detected
cards.when_not: the study is already run and you are tempted by post-hoc power, which is a function of the p-value and adds nothing

alternatives.criterion: a standard two-arm design
randomisation is at group level
the design is non-standard

output_key_fields: n_required: sample size for the requested power
power: attained power at a given size and effect
mde: the minimum detectable effect at the design's size
design_effect: the cluster inflation factor, 1 + (m-1)*icc
interpretation_traps: POST-HOC power computed from the observed effect is a monotone function of the p-value and tells you nothing -- do not report it
cluster randomisation inflates the required sample by the design effect; ignoring the intra-cluster correlation understates the needed size by a large multiple
the number of CLUSTERS, not the number of individuals, drives power in a cluster design

cards.method: Quasi-random and low-discrepancy sequences
cards.when: Monte Carlo integration converges slowly; a low-discrepancy sequence fills the space more evenly and converges faster for smooth integrands
cards.when_not: the integrand is discontinuous or very high dimensional, where the advantage disappears; you need genuine randomness for a randomisation test

alternatives.criterion: you need independence, as in a randomisation test
smooth integrand, moderate dimension
you want quasi-random accuracy plus an error estimate

output_key_fields: sample: the generated points
discrepancy: how evenly the points fill the space
scrambled: whether randomisation was applied, which is what permits an error estimate
interpretation_traps: an UNSCRAMBLED low-discrepancy sequence gives no error estimate at all, because the points are deterministic
the advantage decays with dimension and is usually gone well before a hundred dimensions
taking a non-power-of-two prefix of a Sobol sequence breaks its balance properties
sources: Niederreiter 1992, Random Number Generation and Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods

cards.when: testing whether a portfolio earns a return the known factors cannot explain -- the alpha is the object of interest
cards.when_not: the test assets are individual stocks with short histories; you want cross-sectional risk prices (-> Fama-MacBeth)

alternatives.criterion: the question is the price of risk rather than a portfolio alpha
you have many portfolios and want one test of all alphas

betas: factor loadings with standard errors
t_alpha, p_alpha: the test of zero alpha
r_squared, residual_vol: how much the factors explain
interpretation_traps: alpha is the excess return the model cannot explain and is only as meaningful as the factor set is complete
the standard errors need a HAC correction; returns are heteroskedastic and mildly autocorrelated
testing many portfolios one at a time guarantees false alphas -- that is what the joint test exists for

cards.method: The GRS joint test of zero alphas
cards.when: you have many test portfolios and want ONE test of whether the model prices them all, instead of many individually mined alphas
cards.when_not: the number of assets approaches the number of periods, where the test is undefined or badly sized; the residuals are far from normal

alternatives.criterion: you care about one specific portfolio
the classic exact test under normality
you want to relax normality and homoskedasticity

df1, df2: degrees of freedom, which show how close to infeasible the test is

sharpe_ratio_gain: how much the test assets improve the tangency portfolio
interpretation_traps: the test REQUIRES more time periods than assets, and its power collapses as the two approach each other

cards.when: estimating the cross-sectional PRICE of risk -- what the market pays per unit of exposure -- rather than a single portfolio's alpha
cards.when_not: you only need time-series alphas; the betas are estimated on so little data that the errors-in-variables problem dominates

alternatives.criterion: the question is alpha, not the price of risk

[#318] Fama-MacBeth two-pass regression with the Shanken correction
Category: 37-asset-pricing-factors
Nodes: ap_fama_macbeth
WHEN: estimating the cross-sectional PRICE of risk -- what the market pays per unit of exposure -- rather than a single portfolio's alpha
NOT when: you only need time-series alphas; the betas are estimated on so little data that the errors-in-variables problem dominates
Alternatives: time-series factor regression (the question is alpha, not the price of risk) · GMM one-step (you want to estimate both passes jointly and avoid the correction) · portfolio sorts (you want a model-free look at the same cross-sectional pattern)
Output: lambda: the estimated risk prices, one per factor · t_shanken: t-statistics after the errors-in-variables correction · t_naive: uncorrected t-statistics, always larger -- shown so the difference is visible · r_squared_cs: cross-sectional fit per period and on average
Pitfalls: the naive Fama-MacBeth standard error IGNORES that betas were estimated; the Shanken correction is not optional and always widens the interval · using individual stocks rather than portfolios makes the beta estimates noisy and biases the risk price toward zero · a significant risk price on a factor that does not span the test assets is a common artefact of a poorly chosen cross-section
Sources: Fama & MacBeth 1973 (Journal of Political Economy 81:607-636) · Shanken 1992 (Review of Financial Studies 5:1-33) · linearmodels.asset_pricing

cards.when: the factors are macroeconomic rather than portfolio returns, so the risk price cannot be read off a mean and must be estimated from the pricing kernel
cards.when_not: every factor is a traded excess return, where the risk price is just the factor mean

alternatives.criterion: all factors are excess returns
factors are macro variables
you want the two-pass estimate with its familiar diagnostics

lambda: implied risk prices
j_statistic, p_value: the overidentification test of the pricing restrictions
pricing_errors: per-asset alpha under the model
interpretation_traps: for a NON-TRADED factor the risk price is not the factor mean, and treating it as such is a common and serious error
the SDF coefficient b and the risk price lambda are different parameters related by the factor covariance; reporting one as the other inverts conclusions
with many test assets the J statistic almost always rejects, which says more about the asset count than the model

cards.when: a model-free look at whether a characteristic predicts returns, by sorting assets on it and reading the spread

cards.method: Financial event studies: abnormal returns, CAR and BHAR
cards.when: measuring the return impact of a dated corporate or policy event, net of what the market would have delivered anyway
cards.when_not: the event is not sharply dated; events cluster in calendar time so abnormal returns are cross-correlated and the usual tests fail

alternatives.criterion: short horizons, additive aggregation
long horizons, compounding matters
events cluster and cross-correlation invalidates event-time tests

output_key_fields: ar: abnormal return per event per day
car, bhar: cumulative and buy-and-hold aggregates over the window
test_statistics: parametric and rank tests over the cross-section
estimation_diagnostics: fit of the normal-return model per event
interpretation_traps: EVENT CLUSTERING in calendar time makes abnormal returns cross-correlated, and every standard test assumes they are not -- this is the single most common failure
CAR and BHAR answer different questions and diverge more the longer the window; long-horizon BHAR inference is notoriously fragile
the estimation window must not overlap the event window, or the normal-return model absorbs the effect
sources: Kothari & Warner 2007, Econometrics of event studies (Handbook of Corporate Finance 1)

cards.method: Performance analytics: Sharpe, Sortino, information ratio, drawdown and turnover
cards.when: summarising a return stream in the risk-adjusted terms an investment committee actually reads
cards.when_not: the return series is too short for any of these ratios to be estimated with useful precision

alternatives.criterion: symmetric risk and a single summary
downside risk is the concern
performance is measured against a benchmark

output_key_fields: sharpe, sortino, information_ratio, calmar: the ratio family, annualised
max_drawdown, drawdown_duration: the path-dependent risk measures
turnover: portfolio churn, the cost driver
se_sharpe: standard error of the Sharpe ratio, which is rarely small

cards.method: Mean-variance optimisation and the efficient frontier under constraints
cards.when: turning return and risk estimates into portfolio weights, with the constraints a real mandate imposes
cards.when_not: the inputs are estimated from a short sample without shrinkage, where the optimiser will amplify estimation error into extreme weights

alternatives.criterion: you distrust the return estimates entirely
you want to blend views with a market-implied prior
you want weights that survive input uncertainty

output_key_fields: weights: the optimal portfolio
frontier: risk and return along the efficient set
expected_return, volatility, sharpe: the optimum's characteristics
status: whether the solver actually reached optimality
interpretation_traps: mean-variance is an ERROR MAXIMISER: it loads on assets whose returns are most overestimated, which is why raw sample means give unusable weights
the covariance matrix must be well conditioned; with more assets than periods it is singular and the optimum is arbitrary
a solver status other than optimal means the weights are not a solution, whatever they look like

cards.method: Covariance and return estimation with shrinkage and denoising
cards.when: the sample covariance is the weakest link in any allocation; shrinkage and denoising make it usable when assets are many and history is short
cards.when_not: you have far more periods than assets and the sample estimate is already well conditioned

alternatives.criterion: a well-tested default with an analytic intensity
you want to strip eigenvalues indistinguishable from noise
a factor structure is credible and you want the implied matrix

output_key_fields: covariance: the estimated matrix
shrinkage_intensity: how far the estimate was pulled toward the target
condition_number: before and after -- the number that says whether it worked
eigenvalues: the spectrum, for the denoising diagnostic
interpretation_traps: a shrinkage intensity near one means the sample covariance carried almost no usable information; that is a finding, not a fix
shrinking the covariance while using raw sample MEANS leaves the larger problem untouched -- means are far harder to estimate than covariances
denoising changes the eigenvalue spectrum and therefore every risk decomposition computed from it
sources: Laloux, Cizeau, Bouchaud & Potters 1999 (Physical Review Letters 83:1467)
Lopez de Prado 2020, Machine Learning for Asset Managers

cards.method: Black-Litterman with investor views
cards.when: blending a market-implied equilibrium prior with explicit views, so the optimiser produces weights that differ from the market only where you have an opinion
cards.when_not: you have no views, in which case the answer is the market portfolio; the market capitalisations needed for the prior are unavailable

alternatives.criterion: you trust your return estimates directly
you want the market as a prior and views as an update
the views are on non-linear functions or higher moments

output_key_fields: posterior_returns: the blended expected returns
posterior_covariance: the blended covariance
weights: the implied optimal portfolio
view_impact: how far each view moved the posterior
interpretation_traps: the prior comes from REVERSE-OPTIMISING market weights; feeding it arbitrary weights silently discards the method's whole logic
tau, the prior scaling, is barely identified and the posterior is sensitive to it -- report the value used
a view with high stated confidence and little supporting data dominates the posterior; the confidence parameter is an assumption, not evidence
sources: He & Litterman 1999, The intuition behind Black-Litterman model portfolios (Goldman Sachs)

cards.method: Risk parity, equal risk contribution and risk budgeting
cards.when: allocating by risk rather than by capital, when return forecasts are not trusted but the covariance is
cards.when_not: you have credible return views that the method would ignore by construction

alternatives.criterion: you do trust the return estimates
no view at all beyond risk
you want to allocate risk in stated proportions

output_key_fields: weights: the risk-parity portfolio
risk_contributions: each asset's share of total risk, equal by construction for ERC
converged: whether the nonlinear problem solved
leverage: the gross exposure implied, often above one
interpretation_traps: risk parity IGNORES expected returns entirely -- that is the design, and it is also its main weakness
the solution is invariant to leverage, so it usually needs scaling to a risk target, which reintroduces a decision the method was meant to avoid
risk contributions are computed from an ESTIMATED covariance and inherit all of its error
sources: Maillard, Roncalli & Teiletche 2010 (Journal of Portfolio Management 36:60-70)

cards.method: Hierarchical risk parity and hierarchical equal risk contribution
cards.when: allocating without inverting a covariance matrix at all, by clustering assets and splitting risk down the tree -- robust when the matrix is near-singular
cards.when_not: the asset set is small and well conditioned, where a direct optimiser is fine and more transparent

alternatives.criterion: no hierarchy is credible
many correlated assets and an unstable covariance
you want the hierarchy but with an explicit risk measure at each split

output_key_fields: weights: the hierarchical allocation
linkage: the dendrogram the allocation followed
quasi_diagonal_order: the reordering that makes the correlation matrix near block-diagonal
clusters: the cluster assignment at the chosen cut
interpretation_traps: the answer depends on the LINKAGE and the distance metric; single linkage chains and produces very different trees from ward
no matrix inversion is the selling point -- so a near-singular covariance that would break mean-variance does not break this, but it does not become informative either
the tree is estimated from the same data as the weights, and that estimation error is not in any reported interval

cards.method: CVaR, CDaR, mean-semivariance and Kelly optimisation
cards.when: variance is the wrong risk measure when returns are skewed or the mandate is written in terms of losses, not dispersion
cards.when_not: returns are near-symmetric and variance is an adequate proxy; the sample is too short to estimate a tail measure

alternatives.criterion: returns are near-normal
the tail is the mandate's concern
the objective is long-run growth rather than a risk target

output_key_fields: weights: the optimal portfolio under the chosen measure
risk_value: the realised CVaR, CDaR or semideviation at the optimum
status: solver status
comparison: the same portfolio's variance-based risk, for reference
interpretation_traps: CVaR at a given level is estimated from the observations BEYOND that level -- at 99% on monthly data that is a handful of points, and the estimate is correspondingly unstable
full Kelly maximises long-run growth but produces violent drawdowns; fractional Kelly is what is actually used
CDaR is path dependent, so it depends on the ORDER of returns and is not invariant to resampling

cards.when: the inputs are estimates, and you want weights chosen to perform acceptably across a stated set of plausible inputs rather than optimally for one

cards.method: Walk-forward backtesting with turnover and transaction costs
cards.when: estimating what an allocation rule would actually have delivered, using only information available at each rebalancing date and charging for trading
cards.when_not: you intend to evaluate on the same data the rule was fitted to, which measures nothing

alternatives.criterion: never, for a rule with estimated parameters
the honest default
you want many paths and control of leakage

output_key_fields: returns_net: the backtested return stream after costs
turnover: trading per rebalance
cost_drag: the return given up to costs, which often reverses the ranking of rules
weights_path: the weight history, so the rule is auditable
interpretation_traps: any use of full-sample information -- covariances, breakpoints, even the asset universe -- is LOOK-AHEAD BIAS and inflates every result
transaction costs frequently reverse the ranking of allocation rules; a backtest without them is not a backtest
survivorship in the asset universe is a bias no rebalancing scheme can undo

Nodes: pf_walk_forward · pf_backtest_summary
WHEN: estimating what an allocation rule would actually have delivered, using only information available at each rebalancing date and charging for trading
NOT when: you intend to evaluate on the same data the rule was fitted to, which measures nothing
Alternatives: in-sample evaluation (never, for a rule with estimated parameters) · walk-forward (the honest default) · combinatorial purged cross-validation (you want many paths and control of leakage)
Output: returns_net: the backtested return stream after costs · turnover: trading per rebalance · cost_drag: the return given up to costs, which often reverses the ranking of rules · weights_path: the weight history, so the rule is auditable
Pitfalls: any use of full-sample information -- covariances, breakpoints, even the asset universe -- is LOOK-AHEAD BIAS and inflates every result · transaction costs frequently reverse the ranking of allocation rules; a backtest without them is not a backtest · survivorship in the asset universe is a bias no rebalancing scheme can undo
Sources: Bailey & Lopez de Prado 2014 (Journal of Portfolio Management 40:94) · Harvey & Liu 2015 (Journal of Portfolio Management 42:13) · Lopez de Prado 2018, Advances in Financial Machine Learning · skfolio

cards.method: Risk contribution and factor risk attribution
cards.when: decomposing portfolio risk into the assets or factors that generate it, which is what a risk report has to say
cards.when_not: the portfolio is a single asset; there is no factor model to attribute to

alternatives.criterion: you want per-asset shares of total risk
you want risk by systematic factor
you want risk under stated scenarios rather than a decomposition

output_key_fields: risk_contributions: per-asset shares, summing to total risk
factor_contributions: risk by factor plus a specific-risk residual
marginal_risk: the derivative of risk with respect to each weight
concentration: how far contributions are from equal
interpretation_traps: risk contributions sum to total risk only for HOMOGENEOUS risk measures; that holds for volatility and CVaR but not for every measure
a large factor contribution can come from a small exposure to a very volatile factor -- exposure and contribution are not the same thing
the decomposition inherits every error in the estimated covariance or factor model, and reports none of it
sources: Meucci 2007, Risk contributions from generic user-defined factors (Risk 20:84)
Roncalli 2013, Introduction to Risk Parity and Budgeting

cards.method: OHLC spread estimators: Roll, Corwin-Schultz, Abdi-Ranaldo and EDGE
cards.when: estimating the effective bid-ask spread from daily open-high-low-close data when trade-and-quote data is unavailable or unaffordable
cards.when_not: you have trade and quote data, where the spread can be measured directly rather than estimated

alternatives.criterion: you have quote data
high-low data available and you want a well-tested estimator
you want the current best-performing OHLC estimator

output_key_fields: spread: the estimated proportional effective spread per period
estimator: which construction produced it
n_negative: periods where the estimate came out negative, which happens often

cards.when: measuring how much price a trade moves, or how thin a market is, from daily data available for any listed asset

cards.method: Noise-robust realised measures: two-scale, kernel and pre-averaged
cards.when: estimating integrated variance from high-frequency returns, where naive realised variance is dominated by microstructure noise rather than by volatility
cards.when_not: the sampling frequency is low enough that noise is negligible; you only have daily data

alternatives.criterion: a crude but transparent noise control
you want a consistent estimator with a simple construction
you want the efficient noise-robust estimator

output_key_fields: realised_variance: the estimate at the chosen construction
noise_variance: the estimated microstructure noise, which is the diagnostic
optimal_frequency: the sampling interval the signature plot implies
jump_component: the separated jump contribution where requested
interpretation_traps: naive realised variance at the highest available frequency estimates the NOISE, not the volatility -- it diverges as the interval shrinks

cards.when: diagnosing the intraday shape of volatility and choosing the sampling frequency at which a realised measure is actually informative

alternatives.criterion: choosing a sampling interval
removing the U shape before modelling

cards.when: decomposing the cost of a trade into what the market maker keeps and what the informed trader takes, and locating where price discovery happens across venues
cards.when_not: there is one venue and one price series, so there is nothing to attribute across markets

alternatives.criterion: the question is transaction cost decomposition
several venues quote the same asset
you prefer the permanent-transitory decomposition

output_key_fields: effective_spread: twice the signed distance from the midpoint

price_impact: effective minus realised, the adverse-selection component

cards.method: Black-Scholes and Bachelier pricing, Greeks and implied-volatility inversion
cards.when: pricing a vanilla option, computing its sensitivities, or backing out the volatility the market price implies
cards.when_not: the option is path dependent or American with early exercise that matters (-> a lattice or Monte Carlo); the underlying can go negative and the model is lognormal

alternatives.criterion: the underlying can be negative, as with spreads and some rates
early exercise matters
the smile must be fitted, not assumed away

output_key_fields: price: the model value
delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho: the Greeks
implied_volatility: the inverted volatility, None where no solution exists
moneyness, time_to_expiry: the inputs, echoed for auditability
interpretation_traps: implied volatility DOES NOT EXIST when the price violates the no-arbitrage bounds; returning None is correct and a returned number in that case is a solver artefact
deep in- and out-of-the-money inversions are numerically ill-conditioned because vega goes to zero -- small price errors become large volatility errors
Black-Scholes and Bachelier volatilities are in different units and are not comparable

cards.method: Implied-volatility surface fitting with SVI and SABR, and arbitrage checks
cards.when: building a smooth, arbitrage-free volatility surface from discrete quoted options, so any strike and maturity can be priced consistently
cards.when_not: you only need one option's implied volatility; the quote set is too sparse for a surface to be identified

alternatives.criterion: a slice-wise parameterisation with known arbitrage conditions
you want a dynamic model consistent with smile movement
you only need to fill gaps and do not need a model

output_key_fields: params: the fitted surface parameters per slice
fitted_iv: implied volatility on the requested grid
butterfly_arbitrage, calendar_arbitrage: violation flags and where they occur
rmse: fit quality against the quotes
interpretation_traps: a surface that fits well can still admit ARBITRAGE; the butterfly and calendar checks are not diagnostics of fit, they are constraints on validity
SVI in raw parameterisation has parameter combinations that guarantee butterfly arbitrage -- fitting without the constraint routinely lands there
extrapolating the surface beyond the quoted strike range is unconstrained by data and is where most pricing errors originate

cards.method: Risk-neutral density extraction by Breeden-Litzenberger
cards.when: recovering the market's implied distribution of the underlying from a cross-section of option prices -- the density behind every option-implied uncertainty measure
cards.when_not: the strike grid is too coarse or too noisy for a second derivative to be estimated; you need the physical rather than risk-neutral measure

alternatives.criterion: you want a smooth family rather than a nonparametric density
the standard route: smooth first, differentiate second
you want an interpretable multi-modal fit

output_key_fields: density: the risk-neutral density on the strike grid
cdf: the implied distribution function
quantiles: implied quantiles, which are the usable summary
negative_mass: where the density came out negative, which signals arbitrage or over-fitting
interpretation_traps: the density is a SECOND DERIVATIVE of price in strike, so it amplifies quote noise enormously -- differentiating raw quotes is never acceptable
negative density values mean the fitted price function is not convex, i.e. butterfly arbitrage; they are a validity failure, not a rounding issue
the recovered density is RISK-NEUTRAL and is not the market's physical forecast; the difference is the risk premium
sources: Figlewski 2010, Estimating the implied risk-neutral density (Volatility and Time Series Econometrics)

cards.method: Model-free implied variance and variance swaps
cards.when: computing the VIX-style expected variance from an option strip without assuming any pricing model
cards.when_not: the strike range is too narrow for the integral to converge; you want a model-based volatility instead

alternatives.criterion: a single quick proxy
the model-free expectation under the risk-neutral measure
the physical rather than risk-neutral quantity

output_key_fields: implied_variance: the model-free variance for the maturity
implied_volatility: its annualised square root
truncation_error: the contribution the missing strike wings would have made
variance_risk_premium: implied minus realised, where realised is supplied
interpretation_traps: the integral requires strikes over the WHOLE positive axis; a finite strike range truncates it and systematically understates variance, especially in stressed markets
the VIX construction interpolates two maturities to a constant horizon; comparing a raw single-maturity figure with VIX is not like for like
implied variance is risk-neutral and exceeds expected realised variance by the variance risk premium -- it is not a forecast

cards.method: Risk-neutral moments as uncertainty proxies
cards.when: summarising the option-implied distribution in variance, skewness and kurtosis -- the standard market-based measures of uncertainty and crash fear
cards.when_not: the option cross-section is too thin for higher moments, which need the wings most of all

alternatives.criterion: only the second moment is needed
asymmetry and crash risk are the question
you want the whole distribution rather than moments

output_key_fields: variance, skewness, kurtosis: the risk-neutral moments
skew_measure: the strike-based skew slope, an alternative summary
wing_contribution: how much of each moment comes from the extrapolated wings
interpretation_traps: higher moments are dominated by the WINGS, which is exactly where quotes are sparsest and extrapolation is least reliable -- report the wing contribution
risk-neutral skewness is not physical skewness; it embeds the price of crash risk

cards.method: Stochastic-volatility models: Heston, log-normal SV and rough volatility, with calibration
cards.when: the smile and its dynamics matter, so volatility must be a process rather than a number
cards.when_not: a single vanilla price is all you need (-> Black-Scholes); the option data is too sparse to identify several parameters

alternatives.criterion: closed-form characteristic function and fast calibration
you want volatility to stay positive by construction
the short-maturity smile is steeper than any classical model can fit

output_key_fields: params: the calibrated parameters
fit_rmse: calibration error against the quoted surface
feller_satisfied: whether the Heston variance can reach zero
implied_surface: the model surface, for comparison with the market

cards.method: Rating and state transition matrices, generators and long-run behaviour
cards.when: summarising migration between rating or risk states, and projecting it forward to a multi-period or continuous-time horizon
cards.when_not: there are no discrete states; the sample has too few migrations for the off-diagonal cells to be estimated

alternatives.criterion: simple, uses period-end states only
uses the exact timing of every migration and is far more efficient
you need continuous-time or non-integer horizons

generator: the continuous-time generator, where one exists
stationary_distribution: the long-run state shares

cards.method: Credit scorecards: optimal binning, weight of evidence and monotonic constraints
cards.when: building a transparent, monotone, regulator-defensible credit score from borrower characteristics
cards.when_not: interpretability is not required and pure predictive power is the only objective; the default count is too small for binning to be stable

alternatives.criterion: prediction matters more than explanation
no binning wanted and relationships are near-linear
a scorecard that must be explained and signed off

woe, iv: weight of evidence per bin and information value per variable
scorecard: points per attribute
monotonic: whether each variable's default rate is monotone in its bins
interpretation_traps: INFORMATION VALUE is a univariate screen; a variable with high IV can be useless after controlling for another, and one with low IV can matter

cards.method: Probability-of-default calibration, discrimination and reliability
cards.when: checking that a credit model both RANKS obligors correctly and produces probabilities at the right level -- two different requirements
cards.when_not: the model output is a score with no probability interpretation and none is wanted

alternatives.criterion: discrimination -- can the model rank
level -- are the probabilities right
a formal calibration test, though it is sensitive to binning

calibration_curve: predicted against realised default rate by bucket
brier, reliability, resolution: the Brier decomposition
binomial_test: per-grade test that the realised rate matches the assigned PD
interpretation_traps: DISCRIMINATION AND CALIBRATION ARE INDEPENDENT: a model can rank perfectly (AUC 1.0) while every probability is wrong by a factor of ten
a model calibrated on a benign period is systematically under-calibrated in a downturn; through-the-cycle and point-in-time PDs are different objects
Hosmer-Lemeshow depends on the number of groups chosen and can be made to pass or fail by that choice
sources: Hosmer & Lemeshow 2000, Applied Logistic Regression, 2nd ed.

cards.method: Loss given default and exposure at default models
cards.when: modelling the other two components of expected loss, whose distributions are bounded, bimodal and badly served by ordinary regression
cards.when_not: recovery data is absent and a regulatory floor is being applied instead

alternatives.criterion: the outcome is a proportion strictly inside the unit interval
the outcome includes exact zeros and ones
a mass at zero or one plus a continuous part

output_key_fields: params: coefficients on the chosen link
fitted: predicted loss given default or credit conversion factor
distribution_fit: how well the bounded distribution matches the observed shape
downturn_lgd: the stressed value where a downturn indicator is supplied
interpretation_traps: observed recovery is strongly BIMODAL -- clustered near zero and near one -- so a model fitting only the conditional mean misses the shape entirely
linear regression on a bounded outcome predicts outside the unit interval, and truncating the prediction is not a fix
downturn LGD is a regulatory concept requiring a stressed estimate; the through-the-cycle average is not it

cards.method: Time-to-default hazard models and lifetime PD term structures
cards.when: producing a PD for every future year rather than one year ahead -- the requirement behind lifetime expected credit loss
cards.when_not: only a one-year PD is needed; the panel is too short for a term structure to be estimated rather than extrapolated

alternatives.criterion: only the next year matters
the panel is annual and the natural model is a hazard
ratings are available and the matrix can be powered up

output_key_fields: marginal_pd: the default probability in each future period
cumulative_pd: the survival-implied cumulative probability
term_structure: the PD curve over the lifetime
conditioning: how macroeconomic scenarios shifted the curve
interpretation_traps: cumulative PD is ONE MINUS the survival probability, not a sum of marginal PDs; adding them overstates lifetime risk and the error compounds with horizon
extrapolating a term structure beyond the observed panel is an assumption about duration dependence, and it dominates long-horizon loss
point-in-time conditioning on macro scenarios makes the curve move procyclically, which is the intent but also a source of volatility in reported loss
sources: Lando 2004, Credit Risk Modeling: Theory and Applications

cards.when: aggregating obligor-level risk into a portfolio loss distribution, where correlation rather than average PD drives the tail
cards.when_not: the portfolio is a single exposure; correlations cannot be estimated or assumed with any credibility

alternatives.criterion: the regulatory closed form, one systematic factor
sector or geographic concentration matters
you want tail accuracy without full simulation

output_key_fields: loss_distribution: the simulated or analytic distribution

var, es: tail measures at the requested level
concentration: the share of tail loss attributable to the largest exposures
interpretation_traps: the ASSET CORRELATION drives the tail far more than the average PD does; a small change in correlation moves capital by a large multiple

cards.when: decomposing an observed change in the debt ratio into the interest-growth differential, the primary balance and the residual that reconciles the stock with the flows
cards.when_not: you want a forecast rather than an accounting decomposition; the stock-flow adjustment is unavailable and the identity cannot close

alternatives.criterion: the question is forward-looking
you want the distribution rather than a path
you want behavioural response rather than accounting

snowball: the interest-growth differential effect
sfa: the residual that closes the identity
debt_ratio: the level series the decomposition explains
interpretation_traps: the STOCK-FLOW ADJUSTMENT is a residual, not an explanation; a large one means the identity does not close and the data need checking before anything is concluded
the identity is exact only when the interest rate, growth rate and deflator are on consistent bases -- mixing nominal and real is the standard error
foreign-currency debt adds a valuation effect that appears inside the residual unless it is modelled explicitly

cards.when: projecting the debt ratio forward under stated assumptions, and under the standard shocks a sustainability assessment is expected to report

the standard, transparent presentation

cards.when: putting a probability distribution around a debt projection, driven by the joint historical behaviour of growth, rates and the balance
cards.when_not: the historical sample is too short or too structurally broken for a joint distribution to mean anything

alternatives.criterion: you want transparency over probability
you want the joint distribution taken from the data
you want the dynamics as well as the contemporaneous correlation

shock_correlation: the joint distribution the fan rests on
n_simulations: draws behind the bands
interpretation_traps: the bands inherit the CORRELATION between growth, rates and the balance; simulating them independently badly understates the tail
historical shock distributions embed the policy reactions of the past, so a fan chart is not a counterfactual for a different policy
fan charts are frequently misread as forecast intervals for a fixed policy; the central path is conditional and should be labelled as such
sources: Berti 2013, Stochastic public debt projections (European Economy Economic Papers 480)

interpretation_traps: a positive response coefficient is SUFFICIENT for sustainability in Bohn's sense but says nothing about the level of debt or its political feasibility
the response weakens or reverses at high debt in many samples, so a linear estimate averages two regimes and can conclude sustainability where none holds
the balance responds to the cycle as well as to debt; omitting the output gap biases the debt coefficient
sources: Ghosh, Kim, Mendoza, Ostry & Qureshi 2013 (Economic Journal 123:F4-F30)

cards.method: Fiscal multipliers by local projection and state-dependent local projection
cards.when: estimating how much output responds to a fiscal impulse, and whether that response differs in recessions and expansions
cards.when_not: the fiscal shock is not credibly identified, in which case the multiplier is a correlation

alternatives.criterion: flexible horizon-by-horizon response, robust to misspecification
you want a full system and efficiency
the multiplier is thought to differ by state

output_key_fields: irf: the output response per horizon
multiplier: cumulative output response per unit of fiscal impulse
state_multipliers: the multiplier in each state, where a state variable is supplied
conf_band: bands, which must be robust to the induced serial correlation
interpretation_traps: local-projection residuals are SERIALLY CORRELATED by construction at horizons beyond one; standard errors must be HAC or the bands are far too narrow
the cumulative multiplier depends on the normalisation of the shock; reporting it without stating the normalisation makes it uncomparable
state-dependent estimates split an already short sample and their differences are often not statistically distinguishable
sources: Auerbach & Gorodnichenko 2012 (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 4:1-27)
