cards.method: Likelihood-ratio tests of restrictions on beta and alpha, and weak exogeneity
cards.when: testing whether a cointegrating vector takes the form theory predicts, and whether a variable can be treated as weakly exogenous
cards.when_not: the cointegrating rank is zero, so there is no beta to restrict; the restrictions are not over-identifying and no test exists

alternatives.criterion: theory predicts the long-run relationship
you want to test weak exogeneity or exclusion
both are predicted together

output_key_fields: lr_statistic, p_value, df: the restriction test
beta_restricted: the estimated vector under the restriction
weak_exogeneity: per-variable test that its adjustment coefficient is zero
identified: whether the restrictions just-identify or over-identify
interpretation_traps: beta is identified only up to NORMALISATION; a restriction that merely re-normalises is not testable, and testing it produces a meaningless zero statistic
weak exogeneity means the variable does not adjust to the long-run relationship -- it does not mean the variable is exogenous in any broader sense
the chi-squared distribution requires the restrictions to be over-identifying; with just-identifying restrictions there is nothing to test
sources: Johansen 1995, Likelihood-Based Inference in Cointegrated Vector Autoregressive Models

asymmetric adjustment around a threshold

cards.when: estimating a cointegrating vector with a transformation that removes the endogeneity and serial-correlation bias of ordinary least squares
cards.when_not: there is more than one cointegrating vector (-> Johansen); the correction cannot be estimated because the long-run covariance is unstable

alternatives.criterion: the same aim by a different correction

cards.when: the autocorrelation of squared returns decays hyperbolically rather than exponentially, which no GARCH or IGARCH can reproduce
cards.when_not: the persistence is due to neglected structural breaks, which mimic long memory almost exactly; the sample is too short to distinguish the two

alternatives.criterion: persistence is exponential
shocks are fully permanent
the long memory is spurious and driven by breaks

d: between 0 and 1 for genuine long memory
forecast_variance: which decays hyperbolically
loglike, aic, bic
interpretation_traps: STRUCTURAL BREAKS MASQUERADE AS LONG MEMORY -- an estimated d near 0.4 is entirely consistent with a stable process containing two variance breaks
FIGARCH is not covariance stationary for many parameter values yet still has a well-defined conditional variance; the usual stationarity intuition does not carry

[#437] FIGARCH and HYGARCH long-memory volatility
Category: 06-volatility-regimes
Nodes: vr_figarch
WHEN: the autocorrelation of squared returns decays hyperbolically rather than exponentially, which no GARCH or IGARCH can reproduce
NOT when: the persistence is due to neglected structural breaks, which mimic long memory almost exactly; the sample is too short to distinguish the two
Alternatives: GARCH (persistence is exponential) · IGARCH (shocks are fully permanent) · break-adjusted GARCH (the long memory is spurious and driven by breaks)

Pitfalls: STRUCTURAL BREAKS MASQUERADE AS LONG MEMORY -- an estimated d near 0.4 is entirely consistent with a stable process containing two variance breaks · FIGARCH is not covariance stationary for many parameter values yet still has a well-defined conditional variance; the usual stationarity intuition does not carry · the infinite lag polynomial must be truncated, and the truncation length affects both estimates and forecasts

cards.when: a one-parameter variance recursion that needs no estimation -- the industry default for fast risk updates

alternatives.criterion: you want mean reversion and estimated parameters
speed and no estimation
intraday data available

lambda_: the decay factor used
half_life: the implied memory in periods

cards.method: Realised GARCH and HEAVY models
cards.when: combining a daily return model with a realised measure from intraday data, which reacts to volatility changes far faster than returns alone
cards.when_not: no intraday data is available; the realised measure is noisy enough that it adds variance rather than information

alternatives.criterion: no intraday data
a measurement equation links the two
separate dynamics for the return and realised components

output_key_fields: params: including the measurement-equation parameters
conditional_variance: the fitted path
measurement_residuals: which diagnose the realised measure's bias
loglike, aic
interpretation_traps: the measurement equation must account for the realised measure covering only TRADING HOURS while the return covers the full day; omitting that biases the level
a noisy realised measure degrades the model rather than improving it -- use a noise-robust estimator upstream
the leverage function is part of the measurement equation, so its parameters are not comparable with an EGARCH leverage term
sources: Hansen, Huang & Shek 2012 (Journal of Applied Econometrics 27:877-906)

cards.method: High-frequency jump tests: bipower variation and Lee-Mykland
cards.when: separating the continuous and jump components of price variation, which have different implications for risk and for option pricing
cards.when_not: the data are daily, where jumps cannot be separated from volatility; microstructure noise dominates at the sampling frequency used

alternatives.criterion: a daily test that jumps occurred
you need the individual jump times
you want a simple truncation-based separation

output_key_fields: jump_statistic, p_value: the daily test
jump_times: dated jumps, where the intraday test is used
continuous_variation, jump_variation: the decomposition
jump_share: proportion of total variation attributable to jumps
interpretation_traps: MICROSTRUCTURE NOISE inflates every jump test at high sampling frequencies and produces spurious jumps; the sampling interval is not a detail
the intraday periodicity of volatility must be removed first, or the opening and closing periods generate false jump detections
bipower variation is itself biased by jumps in finite samples, which is why the ratio statistics use corrections

cards.method: ICSS variance change-point detection
cards.when: dating shifts in unconditional variance, which otherwise show up as spurious persistence in a GARCH model
cards.when_not: the variance is plainly stable; the series is short enough that the algorithm's asymptotics do not apply

alternatives.criterion: the classic iterated cumulative sums of squares
you want a modern penalised segmentation
you prefer latent regimes to dated breaks

output_key_fields: break_dates: the detected variance change points
segment_variances: the variance within each segment
n_breaks: how many were found
persistence_before_after: GARCH persistence with and without break dummies
interpretation_traps: IGNORING VARIANCE BREAKS INFLATES GARCH PERSISTENCE toward one; an estimated alpha+beta of 0.99 very often means unmodelled breaks rather than genuine near-integration
ICSS assumes independent observations and over-detects breaks when the data are conditionally heteroskedastic; the corrected versions exist for that
each detected break costs degrees of freedom; a segmentation with many short segments is fitting noise
sources: Sanso, Arago & Carrion 2004 (Revista de Economia Financiera 4:32)

cards.method: Time-varying transition-probability Markov switching
cards.when: the probability of leaving a regime depends on observable conditions, rather than being a constant the model estimates once
cards.when_not: there is no credible driver of the transition probabilities; the sample has too few switches to identify their dependence

alternatives.criterion: no driver available
an observable shifts the switching odds
the regime is determined by the observable rather than probabilistic

output_key_fields: transition_probabilities: the fitted time-varying probabilities
params: regime parameters and the transition equation coefficients
smoothed_probabilities: regime probabilities at each date
expected_duration: which now varies over time
interpretation_traps: identifying the transition equation needs ENOUGH SWITCHES; with two or three regime changes in sample the coefficients are estimated on almost nothing
the label-switching problem is worse here because the transition equation's sign flips with the labelling
the driver must be predetermined; using a contemporaneous variable makes the transition endogenous
sources: Filardo 1994 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 12:299-308)
Diebold, Lee & Weinbach 1994, Regime switching with time-varying transition probabilities (Nonstationary Time Series Analysis and Cointegration)

cards.method: Advanced stochastic volatility: log-normal, Heston and rough volatility calibration
cards.when: volatility is a latent process with its own shocks, which a GARCH -- where volatility is a deterministic function of past returns -- cannot represent
cards.when_not: a GARCH fits adequately and the extra estimation cost is not justified; the sample is too short for the latent process to be identified

alternatives.criterion: deterministic conditional variance, far cheaper
latent volatility with its own shock
the short-horizon behaviour needs a Hurst parameter below one half

output_key_fields: params: volatility-process parameters
latent_volatility: the filtered or smoothed volatility path
hurst: the roughness parameter, where a rough model is fitted
diagnostics: convergence of the sampler or filter
interpretation_traps: stochastic volatility models have NO CLOSED-FORM LIKELIHOOD; every estimate comes from simulation or filtering, and its convergence must be checked rather than assumed
GARCH and stochastic volatility parameters are not comparable -- persistence means different things in a deterministic and a latent recursion
rough volatility with a Hurst parameter well below one half makes standard discretisation schemes fail; a specialised scheme is required
sources: Kim, Shephard & Chib 1998 (Review of Economic Studies 65:361-393)

cards.method: Synthetic difference-in-differences
cards.when: one or a few treated units and a donor pool, where neither synthetic control nor difference-in-differences alone is convincing
cards.when_not: there is no pre-treatment period long enough to fit unit weights; the donor pool contains units affected by the treatment

alternatives.criterion: one treated unit, exact pre-treatment match wanted
parallel trends is credible without weighting
you want unit and time weights plus a DiD structure

output_key_fields: att: the estimated effect
unit_weights, time_weights: the two weightings that define the estimator
se: jackknife or placebo standard error
pre_treatment_fit: how well the weighted control tracked before treatment
interpretation_traps: synthetic DiD is a WEIGHTED DiD, so it relaxes parallel trends but does not remove the assumption -- it only makes it more plausible
inference with one treated unit rests on placebo distributions, not asymptotics; the p-value is bounded below by one over the donor count
a poor pre-treatment fit invalidates the whole design and cannot be fixed by more donors
sources: Arkhangelsky, Athey, Hirshberg, Imbens & Wager 2021 (American Economic Review 111:4088-4118)

cards.method: Heterogeneity-robust staggered DiD: Sun-Abraham, ETWFE, stacked, did2s and LP-DiD
cards.when: treatment starts at different times for different units, where two-way fixed effects can produce an estimate of the wrong sign entirely
cards.when_not: treatment starts at one date for everyone, where ordinary DiD is fine; there are no never-treated or not-yet-treated units to serve as controls

alternatives.criterion: you want an event study free of contamination
you want a regression-based estimator with the same robustness
you want a transparent design or a two-stage estimator

output_key_fields: att: the overall effect and the effect by cohort and by relative period
event_study: dynamic effects around the treatment date
negative_weights: whether the naive TWFE estimator carries them
cohorts: the treatment timing groups
interpretation_traps: TWO-WAY FIXED EFFECTS WITH STAGGERED TIMING USES ALREADY-TREATED UNITS AS CONTROLS, which can produce negative weights and an estimate opposite in sign to every underlying effect
an event-study plot from a naive interacted regression is contaminated across relative periods; the interaction-weighted estimator exists to fix exactly that
the comparison group -- never treated versus not yet treated -- changes the estimand, and both should be reported

cards.method: Regression-discontinuity manipulation and density tests
cards.when: checking whether units sorted around the cut-off, which would invalidate the entire discontinuity design
cards.when_not: the running variable is coarsely discretised so a density test is not meaningful; assignment is verifiably outside the units' control

alternatives.criterion: the classic binned test
a local polynomial density test with no pre-binning
a complementary check

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: the manipulation test
density_left, density_right: estimated densities either side
discontinuity: the estimated jump in the density
bandwidth: the bandwidth used
interpretation_traps: A DENSITY DISCONTINUITY INVALIDATES THE DESIGN; this test is not a robustness check to be relegated to an appendix

cards.when: treating a narrow window around the cut-off as a randomised experiment, which needs no continuity assumption and no extrapolation
cards.when_not: no window is narrow enough for randomisation to be credible; the running variable is continuous and the design has plenty of data for a local polynomial

the running variable is discrete or the sample is small
manipulation itself is the object of study

cards.method: Binscatter with valid inference
cards.when: showing a conditional relationship without imposing a functional form, with bands that are actually valid rather than decorative
cards.when_not: you need the parameter of a specific functional form; the sample is too small for binning to leave anything in each bin

alternatives.criterion: exploratory only
you want a defensible plot with valid bands
you want the curve rather than the bins

output_key_fields: bins: bin means of the outcome and the running variable

the assignment mechanism is known

cards.when: the instruments are weak, where two-stage least squares is biased toward the ordinary least squares estimate and its confidence interval has no coverage
cards.when_not: the first stage is strong by any measure and conventional inference is fine

alternatives.criterion: fully robust to weak instruments, exact coverage
robust and more powerful than Anderson-Rubin
less biased point estimates under many weak instruments

output_key_fields: ar_statistic, clr_statistic: weak-instrument-robust tests

first_stage_f: the effective F statistic
liml, jive: alternative point estimates
interpretation_traps: AN UNBOUNDED CONFIDENCE SET IS THE CORRECT ANSWER when instruments are weak -- it is information, not a failure, and reporting a tight 2SLS interval instead is the error
an EMPTY confidence set means the model is rejected at that level, which is also informative
the rule-of-thumb first-stage F of 10 is not valid with multiple endogenous regressors or non-homoskedastic errors; use the effective F
sources: Andrews, Stock & Sun 2019 (Annual Review of Economics 11:727)

Pitfalls: AN UNBOUNDED CONFIDENCE SET IS THE CORRECT ANSWER when instruments are weak -- it is information, not a failure, and reporting a tight 2SLS interval instead is the error · an EMPTY confidence set means the model is rejected at that level, which is also informative · the rule-of-thumb first-stage F of 10 is not valid with multiple endogenous regressors or non-homoskedastic errors; use the effective F
Sources: Anderson & Rubin 1949 (Annals of Mathematical Statistics 20:46-63) · Moreira 2003 (Econometrica 71:1027) · Andrews, Stock & Sun 2019 (Annual Review of Economics 11:727) · linearmodels

cards.method: Changes-in-changes and quantile treatment effects
cards.when: the treatment may shift the whole distribution rather than just its mean, and the mean can hide offsetting effects at different quantiles
cards.when_not: you only need the mean effect; the sample is too small for quantile estimates at the tails

alternatives.criterion: the mean is the object of interest
a nonlinear DiD that respects the distribution
you want the effect at specified quantiles

output_key_fields: qte: the effect at each requested quantile
conf_band: bands, which must be uniform if the whole curve is interpreted
distributional_test: test of a constant effect across quantiles
counterfactual_distribution: the untreated distribution for the treated
interpretation_traps: a QUANTILE TREATMENT EFFECT IS NOT THE EFFECT ON A GIVEN UNIT unless ranks are preserved; it compares distributions, not individuals
changes-in-changes replaces parallel trends with a monotonicity assumption -- weaker in some respects, stronger in others, not simply better
pointwise quantile bands read as a curve overstate precision; a uniform band is needed for statements about the shape

cards.method: Meta-learners for conditional average treatment effects: S, T, X, residual and doubly-robust
cards.when: the effect varies across units and you want to estimate that variation with machine learning rather than pre-specified interactions
cards.when_not: the sample is too small for the effect surface to be estimated; you only need the average effect

alternatives.criterion: one model with treatment as a feature; simplest, biased toward zero heterogeneity
separate models per arm; unbiased but noisy with imbalanced arms
doubly robust, the usual default

output_key_fields: cate: the estimated effect per unit
ate: the average, which should agree with a direct estimate
heterogeneity_test: whether the effect genuinely varies
feature_importance: which covariates drive the variation
interpretation_traps: THE S-LEARNER SHRINKS HETEROGENEITY TOWARD ZERO because a single model can ignore the treatment feature; a flat CATE from it is not evidence of homogeneity
individual CATE estimates are very noisy; they support group-level statements, not unit-level decisions, without further calibration

cards.method: Policy learning and optimal assignment rules
cards.when: turning heterogeneous effect estimates into a decision rule about who should be treated, subject to a budget or a simplicity constraint
cards.when_not: the effect is homogeneous, where the rule is trivial; the CATE estimates are too noisy to support any rule

alternatives.criterion: no constraint, simplest rule
you need an interpretable rule
only a share can be treated

output_key_fields: policy: the learned assignment rule
value: estimated policy value against the baseline
regret: distance from the infeasible optimal rule
treated_share: the share the rule assigns
interpretation_traps: POLICY VALUE ESTIMATED ON THE SAME DATA THAT LEARNED THE POLICY IS OPTIMISTIC; honest evaluation needs a held-out sample or cross-fitting
a rule built from noisy CATE estimates can be worse than treating everyone or no one; always compare against both baselines
constraining a rule to be interpretable costs policy value, and that cost should be quantified rather than ignored

cards.method: Panel event-study construction and pre-trend testing
cards.when: building the relative-time indicators an event study needs and testing the pre-trends the design depends on
cards.when_not: there is no panel dimension; treatment timing is not observed at unit level

alternatives.alt: event-study plot with leads and lags
alternatives.criterion: the standard presentation
a formal test rather than a visual one
you want to relax parallel trends rather than test it

output_key_fields: coefficients: effect per relative period, with the omitted base period stated
pretrend_test: joint test that pre-treatment coefficients are zero
event_window: the relative periods estimated
binned_endpoints: whether distant periods were binned

the omitted base period is a normalisation; changing it shifts every coefficient and can flip the visual impression entirely
distant relative periods are estimated on few units and must usually be binned, which is a choice that affects the picture

cards.when: turning coefficients from a nonlinear model into quantities that can be read -- effects on the outcome scale, at stated covariate values
cards.when_not: the model is linear with no interactions, where the coefficient already is the marginal effect

alternatives.criterion: the average derivative across the sample
the derivative at one representative point
comparisons between stated covariate profiles

contrasts: differences between specified profiles
predictions: fitted values at stated covariate values
at: the covariate values the effects were evaluated at

cards.method: High-dimensional fixed-effect absorption
cards.when: the design has several high-dimensional fixed effects -- firm, worker, year -- that cannot be estimated as dummies
cards.when_not: there is one low-dimensional fixed effect, where dummies are simpler and give the coefficients directly

alternatives.criterion: few levels
one fixed effect
several high-dimensional effects

output_key_fields: params: coefficients on the non-absorbed regressors
absorbed: the fixed effects removed and their level counts
converged: whether the projection algorithm converged
connected_components: identification structure across the effect dimensions
interpretation_traps: with two or more high-dimensional effects the parameters are identified only WITHIN CONNECTED COMPONENTS of the bipartite mobility graph; a disconnected sample identifies less than it appears to
absorbed fixed effects are not estimated, so they cannot be reported or interpreted -- if you need them, do not absorb them
the alternating-projection algorithm converges slowly with weakly connected data, and a loose tolerance leaves bias in the coefficients
sources: Correia 2017, Linear models with high-dimensional fixed effects (unpublished manuscript)

cards.method: Correlated random effects: Mundlak and Hausman-Taylor
cards.when: you want the efficiency of random effects and the consistency of fixed effects, or you need coefficients on time-invariant regressors that fixed effects wipes out
cards.when_not: there are no time-invariant regressors of interest and fixed effects is adequate; no valid instruments exist for Hausman-Taylor

alternatives.criterion: consistency and no time-invariant coefficients needed
a transparent way to allow correlated effects
time-invariant coefficients wanted and some regressors are exogenous

output_key_fields: params: including coefficients on time-invariant regressors
mundlak_test: joint test of the group means, which is the Hausman test in another form
instrument_validity: over-identification test for Hausman-Taylor
efficiency_gain: against the fixed-effects estimator
interpretation_traps: THE MUNDLAK TEST OF THE GROUP MEANS IS EQUIVALENT TO THE HAUSMAN TEST but is robust and never produces a negative statistic, which the classical Hausman form frequently does
Hausman-Taylor requires you to classify regressors as exogenous or endogenous, and that classification is an assumption the data cannot check
time-invariant coefficients are identified only through that classification, so they are the most fragile numbers in the output

cards.method: Mean group, pooled mean group and common correlated effects
cards.when: the panel has a long time dimension and slopes that plausibly differ across units, where pooling imposes a homogeneity that biases everything
cards.when_not: the time dimension is short, where per-unit estimates are hopeless; homogeneity is credible

cd_test: cross-sectional dependence in the residuals

common correlated effects handles factor dependence by augmenting with cross-sectional averages, and needs enough units for those averages to be informative

cards.when: estimating a cross-sectional relationship period by period and averaging, which handles cross-sectional correlation without modelling it
cards.when_not: the cross-section is small, where per-period estimates are noise; the dependence is in the time dimension rather than the cross-section

alternatives.criterion: you want one regression
cross-sectional correlation, many periods
the unobserved heterogeneity is at unit level

period_estimates: the per-period coefficients

cards.when: several equations share correlated errors, and estimating them jointly is more efficient than one at a time
cards.when_not: the equations have identical regressors, where joint estimation gives exactly the equation-by-equation result

cards.method: Singular spectrum analysis
cards.when: decomposing a series into trend, oscillations and noise without assuming a parametric model, using the spectrum of its trajectory matrix
cards.when_not: you need a model for forecasting with intervals; the series is too short for the embedding window

alternatives.criterion: the components are seasonal and additive
the oscillations are not at a fixed known period
you want a time-frequency view

output_key_fields: components: the reconstructed components
eigenvalues: the singular spectrum, which shows how many components matter
grouping: which singular triples were grouped into each component
window_length: the embedding window used
interpretation_traps: THE GROUPING OF SINGULAR TRIPLES INTO COMPONENTS IS A JUDGEMENT, not an estimate; different groupings give different trends from identical eigenvalues
the embedding window length determines what can be separated and is bounded by half the sample
components are ordered by variance, not by interpretability; the first is not necessarily the trend
sources: Golyandina, Nekrutkin & Zhigljavsky 2001, Analysis of Time Series Structure: SSA and Related Techniques

cards.method: Boosted Hodrick-Prescott filter
cards.when: the ordinary HP filter leaves systematic structure in its cycle, and boosting removes it by refiltering the residual until a stopping rule fires
cards.when_not: you have already rejected HP on principle; the stopping rule cannot be justified for the series

alternatives.criterion: the conventional filter with its known problems
you want HP but with the leftover trend removed
you want to avoid HP entirely

output_key_fields: trend, cycle: the boosted components
n_iterations: boosting rounds, and the stopping rule that ended them
stopping_criterion: the criterion value path
comparison: the plain HP components for reference
interpretation_traps: BOOSTING DOES NOT FIX HP'S END-POINT PROBLEM; the last observations are still revised heavily as data arrive, and boosting can amplify that
the stopping rule determines how much trend is extracted; running to convergence removes almost everything into the trend
lambda still has to be chosen, and the conventional values remain conventions

cards.method: Recursive least squares with CUSUM paths
cards.when: watching coefficients and residuals evolve as the sample grows, to see instability that a full-sample regression averages away
cards.when_not: the sample is too short for recursive estimates to stabilise; you want a formal break test at an unknown date instead

alternatives.criterion: you want to see the coefficient paths
you want a formal stability band
you want a fixed window rather than an expanding one

output_key_fields: recursive_coefficients: the coefficient paths with bands
cusum, cusum_squared: the cumulative sum paths
bounds: the significance bands the paths must stay inside
first_crossing: where a path leaves the band, if it does
interpretation_traps: EARLY RECURSIVE ESTIMATES ARE ESTIMATED ON VERY FEW OBSERVATIONS and swing wildly; the early part of the path is not evidence of instability
CUSUM has low power against a break that does not shift the mean of the residuals; CUSUM-squared complements it by targeting variance shifts
the bands are pointwise in construction and are frequently read as if they were joint

cards.method: Unobserved components with correlated trend and cycle innovations
cards.when: the standard assumption that trend and cycle shocks are uncorrelated is not innocuous, and relaxing it changes the estimated gap substantially
cards.when_not: the correlation is not identified in your specification; the sample is too short to estimate it

alternatives.criterion: the conventional restriction
the restriction is relaxed and tested
perfect negative correlation, the opposite extreme

output_key_fields: trend, cycle: the components under the estimated correlation
rho: the trend-cycle innovation correlation
restriction_test: likelihood-ratio test that rho is zero
cycle_amplitude: which changes sharply with rho
interpretation_traps: THE ZERO-CORRELATION RESTRICTION IS WHAT MAKES THE CYCLE LARGE; relaxing it typically produces a much smaller, BN-like cycle, and the difference is the entire substantive debate
rho is weakly identified and the likelihood can be nearly flat in it -- a point estimate without a profile likelihood is not informative
the estimated output gap is not comparable across specifications with different rho
sources: Morley, Nelson & Zivot 2003 (Review of Economics and Statistics 85:235-243)

cards.method: Ensemble Kalman and square-root filters
cards.when: the state-space model is nonlinear or high dimensional, where the standard Kalman recursion is unstable or infeasible
cards.when_not: the model is linear and low dimensional, where the exact filter is better and cheaper

alternatives.criterion: linear and low dimensional
numerical stability is the issue
high dimensional or nonlinear

output_key_fields: filtered_state, smoothed_state: the state estimates
covariance: state uncertainty, guaranteed positive definite by the square-root form
ensemble_size: draws behind an ensemble filter
loglike: where the filter provides it
interpretation_traps: THE STANDARD KALMAN COVARIANCE RECURSION CAN LOSE POSITIVE DEFINITENESS numerically, which the square-root form prevents by construction -- this is a real failure mode in long or ill-conditioned models
ensemble filters underestimate covariance with small ensembles, which is why inflation and localisation exist
a nonlinear filter's log-likelihood is a simulation estimate and is not directly comparable across ensemble sizes
sources: Durbin & Koopman 2012, Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods, 2nd ed.

cards.method: Growth accounting and Tornqvist-Divisia total factor productivity
cards.when: splitting output growth into contributions from measured inputs and the residual, which is the standard framing for productivity analysis
cards.when_not: the input shares are unavailable; the residual would absorb so much that it explains nothing

alternatives.criterion: shares are stable
shares move and you want a superlative index
you want elasticities rather than shares

output_key_fields: tfp_growth: the residual
contributions: growth attributed to each input
shares: the factor shares used, period by period
index: the Tornqvist or Divisia index level
interpretation_traps: THE SOLOW RESIDUAL IS A RESIDUAL: it absorbs measurement error, capacity utilisation, markups and mismeasured input quality, and calling it technology is an interpretation
using fixed shares when shares actually move introduces a substitution bias that the Tornqvist index exists to remove
capital services and the capital stock are different concepts; using the stock understates input growth

cards.method: Stochastic frontier analysis
cards.when: separating inefficiency from noise when measuring how far a unit is from best practice, which a simple residual cannot do
cards.when_not: there is no reason to expect one-sided inefficiency; the sample is too small to identify the two error components

alternatives.criterion: you want a deterministic, non-parametric frontier
noise must be separated from inefficiency
efficiency is not the question

output_key_fields: params: frontier coefficients
efficiency: per-unit technical efficiency scores
lambda_: ratio of inefficiency to noise variance -- the identification diagnostic
one_sided_test: test that inefficiency is present at all
interpretation_traps: IF LAMBDA IS NEAR ZERO THE INEFFICIENCY COMPONENT IS NOT IDENTIFIED and the efficiency scores are noise dressed as estimates
the test of no inefficiency sits on the boundary of the parameter space, so the naive p-value is wrong and a mixture distribution is required
efficiency scores depend on the assumed inefficiency distribution -- half-normal, truncated normal, exponential -- and rankings change with it

cards.method: Data envelopment analysis with scale and technical decomposition
cards.when: measuring efficiency against a deterministic best-practice frontier built from the data, with no functional form assumed
cards.when_not: the data contain material noise, which DEA attributes entirely to inefficiency; the sample is small relative to the number of inputs and outputs

alternatives.criterion: noise must be separated
scale efficiency is not of interest
you want to separate pure technical from scale efficiency

output_key_fields: efficiency: per-unit scores
technical, scale: the decomposition under variable returns
peers: the reference units defining each unit's frontier segment
returns_to_scale: increasing, constant or decreasing per unit
interpretation_traps: DEA ATTRIBUTES ALL DEVIATION TO INEFFICIENCY; a single mismeasured unit can shift the frontier and change every other unit's score
with many inputs and outputs relative to units, almost everything is efficient by construction -- the dimensionality rule of thumb is not optional
scores are relative to the sample, so adding or removing units changes them
sources: Charnes, Cooper & Rhodes 1978 (European Journal of Operational Research 2:429-444)

cards.method: Multilateral and scanner-data price indices: GEKS and time-product dummy
cards.when: high-frequency scanner data where products enter and leave constantly, and a bilateral index chains drift badly
cards.when_not: the product set is stable, where a bilateral index is fine; the data have no expenditure weights

alternatives.criterion: stable product set
multilateral, transitive by construction
a regression-based multilateral index

output_key_fields: index: the price index series
method: which multilateral form produced it
window: the estimation window and the splicing method
churn: product entry and exit rates, which motivate the method
interpretation_traps: CHAIN DRIFT is the problem these methods solve: a bilateral chained index over high-frequency scanner data can drift by tens of percent with no underlying price change
multilateral indices must be extended over time by splicing, and the splicing choice -- movement, window, mean -- changes the series
the estimation window length trades transitivity against responsiveness and is a substantive choice
sources: de Haan & Krsinich 2014 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 32:341)

cards.method: Shift-share regional growth decomposition
cards.when: splitting a region's growth into what national growth, its industry mix and its own competitiveness contributed
cards.when_not: the industry classification is inconsistent over the period; there is no national benchmark to compare against

alternatives.criterion: the standard decomposition
weights update over time
you want an instrument rather than a decomposition

output_key_fields: national, industry_mix, competitive: the three contributions
total: the sum, which must equal observed regional growth
by_industry: contributions per industry
residual: zero by construction in the classic form
interpretation_traps: THE COMPETITIVE COMPONENT IS A RESIDUAL and absorbs everything the classification does not capture -- it is not a measure of competitiveness in any causal sense
the decomposition is sensitive to the level of industry aggregation; finer classifications shift variation from competitive to industry mix
using shift-share as an instrument requires an entirely separate exogeneity argument about the initial shares

distributional gaps, no functional form

cards.when: attributing a change in output, emissions or value added to changes in technology, final demand structure and demand level, through the supply chain
cards.when_not: you only have aggregate factors (-> index decomposition); the tables are not comparable between the two periods

alternatives.criterion: aggregate factors only, no supply chain
input-output tables for both periods
partial table detail

residual: interaction terms not attributed
decomposition_form: which of the many equivalent forms was used

cards.method: VaR and ES backtesting: Kupiec, Christoffersen, dynamic quantile and traffic light
cards.when: a risk model produces quantile forecasts, and whether those forecasts were any good is a testable question the regulator will ask
cards.when_not: there are too few exceedances for any test to have power -- at 99% on one year of daily data you expect two or three

alternatives.criterion: does the exceedance rate match
are exceedances also independent over time
regression-based, or for expected shortfall

output_key_fields: exceedances: count and rate against the expected
kupiec, christoffersen, dq: the test statistics and p-values
independence: whether exceedances cluster
traffic_light: the supervisory zone
interpretation_traps: CLUSTERED EXCEEDANCES ARE THE REAL FAILURE: a model can hit its unconditional rate exactly while concentrating every breach in one week, which Kupiec alone cannot detect
expected shortfall is not elicitable on its own, which is why its backtests are constructed differently and are less powerful
with a one-year window at 99% the tests have almost no power; a pass is very weak evidence

Alternatives: stock-flow-consistent model (monetary and financial accounting must close) · system dynamics (feedback structure is the focus) · DSGE (optimisation and expectations are the focus)
Output: solution: the simulated stocks and flows · accounting_check: whether every balance sheet and transaction matrix closes · steady_state: the long-run position, where one exists · convergence: solver convergence per period
Pitfalls: THE ACCOUNTING CHECK IS THE MODEL'S MAIN VALIDATION: a non-zero residual in the transaction-flow matrix means the model is wrong, not merely imprecise · these models have no optimising agents, so behavioural equations are assumptions rather than derived; their parameters are not structural in the Lucas sense · results are sensitive to the closure -- which variable adjusts to clear each market -- and the closure must be stated

aggregate feedback without agent detail

cards.method: LOO-CV, WAIC, model comparison and stacking weights
cards.when: comparing Bayesian models by their predictive performance rather than by in-sample fit, and combining them when none dominates
cards.when_not: the models have different likelihoods or different data, where the criteria are not comparable

alternatives.criterion: the default, with a built-in reliability diagnostic
cheaper but less reliable
you want a combination rather than a selection

output_key_fields: elpd_loo, elpd_waic: expected log predictive density with standard errors
pareto_k: the reliability diagnostic -- values above 0.7 mean the estimate is untrustworthy
weights: stacking or pseudo-BMA weights
comparison: models ranked with differences and their standard errors
interpretation_traps: PARETO K ABOVE 0.7 MEANS THE LOO ESTIMATE IS UNRELIABLE for that observation, and reporting elpd without checking k is the standard misuse of this diagnostic
the standard error of a difference in elpd is what decides whether models are distinguishable; a ranking without it is not evidence

cards.method: Bayes factors, Savage-Dickey ratios and ROPE decisions
cards.when: quantifying evidence for a point null, or deciding whether an effect is practically equivalent to zero
cards.when_not: the priors are vague, where Bayes factors are dominated by the prior width and are not interpretable

alternatives.criterion: evidence for a point null against an alternative
nested models, cheap to compute from the posterior
you want a practical-equivalence decision rather than evidence

output_key_fields: bayes_factor: evidence ratio, with the prior it depends on stated
savage_dickey: the prior-to-posterior density ratio at the null
rope_probability: posterior mass inside the region of practical equivalence
decision: accept, reject or undecided
interpretation_traps: BAYES FACTORS ARE ACUTELY SENSITIVE TO THE PRIOR WIDTH on the tested parameter -- widening a vague prior can move the factor by orders of magnitude with no change in the data
the ROPE must be set from substantive knowledge before seeing the posterior; choosing it afterwards makes the decision circular
the Savage-Dickey ratio needs the prior density at the null to be well estimated, which fails for improper priors
sources: Kruschke 2018 (Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1:270)

cards.method: Variational inference, Pathfinder and Laplace approximation
cards.when: the posterior is needed faster than sampling allows, or the model is too large for a Markov chain to mix
cards.when_not: you need accurate tail or correlation estimates, which every approximation here understates

alternatives.criterion: accuracy matters more than speed
a fast approximate posterior
the posterior is near-Gaussian around the mode

output_key_fields: approximation: the fitted approximate posterior
elbo: the evidence lower bound path, whose convergence must be checked
psis_k: diagnostic for how good the approximation is
comparison: against a short MCMC run where available
interpretation_traps: MEAN-FIELD VARIATIONAL INFERENCE SYSTEMATICALLY UNDERSTATES POSTERIOR VARIANCE and destroys correlations between parameters -- credible intervals from it are too narrow, often severely
a converged ELBO does not mean a good approximation; it means the optimiser stopped, and the PSIS diagnostic is what actually assesses quality
Laplace approximation is only defensible when the posterior really is near-Gaussian, which multimodality and boundaries break
sources: Zhang, Carpenter, Gelman & Vehtari 2022 (Journal of Machine Learning Research 23:1)

cards.method: Prior elicitation and prior-predictive checks
cards.when: choosing priors deliberately and checking what they imply about the data before any data is seen
cards.when_not: the priors are fixed by convention or a referee; the model is too complex to simulate from the prior

alternatives.criterion: check what the prior implies for observables
you know plausible ranges, not distributions
you want minimal influence

output_key_fields: prior_predictive: simulated observables under the prior
elicited: the distribution matching stated quantiles
implied_range: what the prior implies for the data scale
warnings: priors implying impossible or absurd observables
interpretation_traps: A 'VAGUE' PRIOR ON A COEFFICIENT CAN BE WILDLY INFORMATIVE ON THE OUTCOME SCALE, especially with a nonlinear link -- the prior predictive check is how that is caught
priors that put mass on impossible observables (negative prices, probabilities above one) are common and are not harmless
eliciting from quantiles requires the elicited quantiles to be internally consistent, which they frequently are not

cards.method: Bayesian additive regression trees
cards.when: you want flexible nonparametric regression with honest uncertainty, without choosing a functional form or tuning a penalty
cards.when_not: the relationship is known to be linear; interpretability of individual terms is required

alternatives.criterion: the form is known
flexible, with posterior uncertainty
prediction only, no uncertainty needed

output_key_fields: posterior_predictive: draws of the fitted surface

partial_dependence: marginal effect curves with credible bands
convergence: chain diagnostics on the tree ensemble

cards.method: Gaussian-process regression and Bayesian nonparametric trends
cards.when: a smooth latent function with calibrated uncertainty, where the uncertainty must widen honestly away from the data
cards.when_not: the sample is large enough that the cubic cost is prohibitive without approximation; the function is not smooth

alternatives.criterion: cheaper, similar smoothness
you want a full posterior over functions
the sample is large

output_key_fields: posterior_mean, posterior_band: the latent function and its uncertainty
hyperparameters: length scale, amplitude and noise
log_marginal_likelihood: for kernel comparison
extrapolation_warning: where the posterior reverts to the prior
interpretation_traps: A GAUSSIAN PROCESS REVERTS TO ITS PRIOR MEAN AWAY FROM THE DATA, so extrapolated forecasts drift to the mean with wide bands -- that is correct behaviour and is frequently mistaken for a bug
the kernel is the model; a squared-exponential kernel assumes infinite differentiability, which is wrong for most economic series -- Matern is usually the better default
hyperparameters estimated by marginal likelihood can land in a local optimum that oversmooths dramatically
sources: Rasmussen & Williams 2006, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning

cards.method: Point-accuracy metric table across horizons and series
cards.when: the baseline of every forecast evaluation, and the input to every test of predictive ability
cards.when_not: the forecasts are densities rather than points (-> scoring rules); the series have no common scale and unscaled metrics would be meaningless

alternatives.criterion: one series, natural units
several series with different scales
the scale is ratio and there are no zeros

output_key_fields: metrics: the table by horizon, series and method
mase, rmsse: scaled metrics, comparable across series
theil_u: against a naive benchmark
bias: mean error, which the squared metrics hide
interpretation_traps: MAPE IS UNDEFINED AT ZERO AND ASYMMETRIC -- it penalises over-forecasts more than under-forecasts, which systematically favours forecasts biased low
averaging a scale-dependent metric across series lets the largest series dominate; that is what the scaled metrics exist to prevent
the mean error is the only metric that reveals bias, and reporting only squared or absolute metrics hides it entirely
sources: Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos 2020 (International Journal of Forecasting 36:54)

cards.method: Proper scoring rules: CRPS, log score, pinball and tail-weighted CRPS
cards.when: evaluating a density or quantile forecast, where a point metric throws away everything the forecast said about uncertainty
cards.when_not: the forecast is a point with no distribution; the evaluation sample is too small for score differences to be distinguishable

alternatives.criterion: the default for a full predictive distribution
strictly proper and local, but unbounded
the forecast is a set of quantiles

output_key_fields: scores: per observation and averaged
decomposition: reliability and resolution components where available
tail_weighted: scores emphasising a region of interest
skill: score against a reference forecast
interpretation_traps: THE LOG SCORE IS UNBOUNDED: a single observation in a region the forecast gave near-zero density produces an infinite score and destroys the average -- CRPS is bounded and usually preferred for that reason
a proper scoring rule cannot be gamed by hedging, but an improper one can -- and several popular ad hoc measures are improper
tail-weighted scores answer a different question from the unweighted version and rank forecasts differently
sources: Gneiting & Ranjan 2011 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 29:411)

cards.method: Clark-West and Giacomini-White conditional predictive ability
cards.when: comparing NESTED forecasting models, where Diebold-Mariano is invalid because the difference in expected loss is zero under the null
cards.when_not: the models are non-nested, where Diebold-Mariano applies directly

alternatives.criterion: non-nested models
nested models, adjusted for the estimation noise
conditional predictive ability, finite-sample based

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: the predictive-ability test
adjustment: the Clark-West correction term
conditional: whether ability varies with a state variable
loss_differential: the underlying series
interpretation_traps: DIEBOLD-MARIANO IS INVALID FOR NESTED MODELS -- the standard normal critical values are wrong and the test is badly undersized, which is exactly the case of adding one indicator to an autoregression
Clark-West tests equal predictive ability of the POPULATION models, not the estimated ones, which is a different and often less interesting null
Giacomini-White conditions on a state and can find ability that averages to zero unconditionally

cards.method: Superior predictive ability, reality check and StepM
cards.when: many forecasts are compared against a benchmark at once, and the best of many will beat it by chance alone
cards.when_not: there are two models, where a pairwise test suffices

alternatives.criterion: the original, conservative under poor models
less sensitive to poor models in the set
you want to identify WHICH models beat the benchmark

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: the joint test against the benchmark
superior_models: those surviving the stepwise procedure
n_models: how many were compared -- the source of the multiplicity
bootstrap: the resampling scheme used

cards.when: testing whether a forecast is unbiased and efficient, and whether one forecast contains everything another has to offer

whether one forecast subsumes another
efficiency with respect to specific information

cards.when: the forecast is an interval or a set of quantiles, and coverage alone can be bought by making the interval wide
cards.when_not: the forecast is a full density (-> scoring rules); the evaluation sample is too short for coverage to be estimated

alternatives.criterion: a first check, necessary but not sufficient
coverage and width in one number
several intervals summarised together

output_key_fields: coverage: realised against nominal, per level
winkler: interval score per observation
wis: the weighted interval score and its decomposition
width: mean interval width
interpretation_traps: COVERAGE AND WIDTH MUST BE READ TOGETHER: an interval from minus to plus infinity covers perfectly and is useless, which is why the Winkler score penalises width
the weighted interval score decomposes into spread, over-prediction and under-prediction, and that decomposition is where the diagnosis is
coverage estimated on a short sample has enormous sampling error; 19 of 20 is not evidence of 95% coverage

Pitfalls: COVERAGE AND WIDTH MUST BE READ TOGETHER: an interval from minus to plus infinity covers perfectly and is useless, which is why the Winkler score penalises width · the weighted interval score decomposes into spread, over-prediction and under-prediction, and that decomposition is where the diagnosis is · coverage estimated on a short sample has enormous sampling error; 19 of 20 is not evidence of 95% coverage

cards.method: Density comparison and calibration: Amisano-Giacomini and Berkowitz
cards.when: comparing density forecasts formally, and testing whether a predictive distribution is calibrated
cards.when_not: the forecasts are points; the sample is too short for the PIT distribution to be assessed

alternatives.criterion: comparing two density forecasts
calibration of one density, with a power advantage over raw PIT tests
a visual calibration check

output_key_fields: log_score_difference: with its test statistic
berkowitz: the calibration test
pit: probability-integral-transform values
autocorrelation: dependence in the PIT series, which independence requires
interpretation_traps: A UNIFORM PIT HISTOGRAM IS NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT: the PIT series must also be independent, and a calibrated-looking histogram with autocorrelated PITs is a failed forecast
the Berkowitz test transforms PITs to normality and gains power over a raw uniformity test, which is why it is preferred
weighted log-score comparisons emphasising a region are not proper unless constructed carefully
sources: Amisano & Giacomini 2007 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 25:177-190)
Berkowitz 2001 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 19:465)

cards.method: Regression diagnostic battery
cards.when: the standard checks a fitted regression must pass before its coefficients are reported
cards.when_not: the model is not a regression; the diagnostics are already run by the estimator

alternatives.criterion: White, Breusch-Pagan, Goldfeld-Quandt
RESET, Harvey-Collier, linktest
you would rather correct than test

output_key_fields: heteroskedasticity: test statistics and p-values
functional_form: RESET and related tests
normality: residual normality tests
influence: leverage, Cook's distance and DFBETAS
interpretation_traps: HETEROSKEDASTICITY DOES NOT BIAS THE COEFFICIENTS, only the standard errors; a rejected test calls for robust errors, not for a different estimator

cards.method: Non-nested model tests: Cox, Davidson-MacKinnon J and Vuong
cards.when: two models neither of which nests the other, where an information criterion gives a ranking but no test
cards.when_not: the models are nested (-> a likelihood-ratio or Clark-West test); they have different dependent variables

alternatives.criterion: regression models, simple to run
the classical non-nested likelihood test
likelihood models, including a test that they are equivalent

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: per direction of the test
conclusion: which model, if either, is rejected
vuong: the likelihood-ratio-based statistic with its variance correction
both_rejected: whether neither model survives
interpretation_traps: THESE TESTS CAN REJECT BOTH MODELS OR NEITHER, and both outcomes are informative -- a test that rejects model A against B is not evidence that B is correct
the J test is a regression-based approximation and has poor size in small samples
Vuong's test requires the models to be non-nested in a strict sense; applied to nested models its distribution is wrong
sources: Cox 1961 (Proceedings of the Fourth Berkeley Symposium 1:105)

cards.method: Meta-analysis and publication bias: meta-regression, PET-PEESE, Egger and funnel
cards.when: synthesising many estimates of the same parameter, and testing whether the literature is distorted by selective reporting
cards.when_not: the estimates are of different parameters and cannot be pooled; there are too few studies for bias tests to have power

alternatives.criterion: the studies estimate one common parameter
the true effect varies across studies
you suspect publication bias

output_key_fields: pooled: the synthesised estimate with its interval
heterogeneity: tau squared and I squared
egger: the small-study-effects test
pet_peese: bias-corrected estimate
interpretation_traps: A SIGNIFICANT EGGER TEST IS NOT PROOF OF PUBLICATION BIAS -- small-study effects also arise when smaller studies genuinely differ in design or population
PET-PEESE is known to over-correct when there is no bias and under-correct with strong heterogeneity; it is a diagnostic, not a definitive correction
fixed and random effects answer different questions, and with high heterogeneity the fixed-effect interval is far too narrow

cards.method: Ordered logit and probit
cards.when: the outcome has a natural order but no cardinal meaning -- survey scales, ratings, self-assessed categories
cards.when_not: the categories are unordered (-> multinomial); the proportional-odds assumption fails badly

alternatives.criterion: no natural order
ordered categories, proportional odds acceptable
proportional odds fails for some covariates

output_key_fields: params: coefficients, common across thresholds under proportional odds
thresholds: the estimated cut points
marginal_effects: per category, which is what is interpretable
brant_test: test of the proportional-odds assumption
interpretation_traps: THE PROPORTIONAL-ODDS ASSUMPTION forces one coefficient across every threshold, and it is frequently violated -- the Brant test is not optional
the coefficient sign tells you the direction for the highest and lowest categories only; middle-category marginal effects can go either way
thresholds are not parameters of interest and are not comparable across specifications

cards.method: Count models: Poisson, negative binomial, generalised Poisson, zero-inflated and hurdle
cards.when: the outcome is a non-negative count, where a linear model predicts impossible values and misstates the variance
cards.when_not: the counts are large enough to be treated as continuous; the outcome is a rate with a known exposure and no count structure

alternatives.criterion: mean equals variance
overdispersion
more zeros than the count distribution allows

output_key_fields: params: coefficients, interpretable as semi-elasticities
dispersion: the overdispersion parameter
zero_inflation: the inflation equation, where fitted
vuong: comparison of zero-inflated against the plain model
interpretation_traps: OVERDISPERSION DOES NOT BIAS POISSON COEFFICIENTS but makes its standard errors far too small; the choice between robust Poisson and negative binomial is about inference, not consistency
zero-inflated and hurdle models mean different things: hurdle treats all zeros as one process, zero-inflation mixes structural and sampling zeros
an exposure variable belongs in the model as an offset with coefficient one, not as a regressor
sources: Cameron & Trivedi 2013, Regression Analysis of Count Data, 2nd ed.

cards.method: Truncated and censored regression: Tobit and variants
cards.when: the outcome is observed only above or below a limit, or piles up at a corner -- hours worked, expenditure, bounded scores
cards.when_not: the limit is a genuine behavioural corner rather than a censoring of a latent variable; there is no censoring at all

alternatives.criterion: the latent variable is censored at a known limit
observations beyond the limit are absent entirely
participation and amount are separate decisions

output_key_fields: params: latent-variable coefficients
marginal_effects: on the latent variable, on the observed outcome and on the uncensored subpopulation -- three different things
sigma: the latent error standard deviation
censored_share: proportion at the limit
interpretation_traps: TOBIT COEFFICIENTS ARE FOR THE LATENT VARIABLE, not the observed outcome; reporting them as marginal effects overstates the effect on what is actually observed
Tobit forces the same parameters to govern participation and amount, which the two-part model relaxes -- and that restriction is testable and frequently rejected
Tobit is inconsistent under heteroskedasticity or non-normality, unlike ordinary least squares which is merely inefficient

cards.method: Heckman sample selection, two-step and full information
cards.when: the outcome is observed only for a selected subsample, and that selection is related to the outcome
cards.when_not: selection is on observables only, where weighting suffices; no exclusion restriction exists

alternatives.criterion: transparent, easy to diagnose
efficient if the joint normality holds
selection is on observables

output_key_fields: params: outcome and selection equation coefficients
lambda_: the inverse Mills ratio coefficient, which measures the selection
rho: correlation between the two errors
exclusion: whether an exclusion restriction was used
interpretation_traps: WITHOUT AN EXCLUSION RESTRICTION the model is identified only by the nonlinearity of the inverse Mills ratio, which is weak and makes the estimates extremely fragile -- this is the single most common failure
a significant lambda means selection matters; an insignificant one does not license using the selected subsample if the exclusion restriction is weak
the two-step estimator's standard errors must be corrected for the estimated first stage

cards.method: Fractional response and beta regression
cards.when: the outcome is a proportion or a share bounded in the unit interval, where a linear model predicts outside it
cards.when_not: the outcome is a count of successes out of a known total (use a binomial model); the bounds are not structural

alternatives.criterion: zeros and ones are present
the outcome is strictly inside the unit interval
there is a mass at the boundaries

output_key_fields: params: coefficients on the link scale
marginal_effects: on the proportion scale, which is what is interpretable
precision: the beta precision parameter, where fitted
boundary_share: proportion at exactly zero or one
interpretation_traps: BETA REGRESSION IS UNDEFINED AT EXACTLY ZERO OR ONE; the common fix of squeezing the data slightly is an arbitrary transformation that changes results, so a fractional or inflated model is usually better
the fractional response estimator is a quasi-likelihood and is consistent under correct mean specification alone, which is why it is robust
coefficients are on the link scale and must be converted to marginal effects before interpretation

cards.method: Multinomial and conditional logit for unordered outcomes
cards.when: the outcome is one of several unordered alternatives -- sector, tenure, mode
cards.when_not: the alternatives are ordered (-> ordered choice); IIA fails and substitution structure matters

alternatives.criterion: chooser-varying regressors
alternative-varying regressors
IIA must be relaxed without a nesting structure

output_key_fields: params: coefficients relative to a base alternative
marginal_effects: per alternative, which are what is interpretable
predicted_probabilities: fitted choice probabilities
iia_test: Hausman-McFadden test

the marginal effect of a covariate on one alternative can have the opposite sign to its coefficient, because the probabilities must sum to one
an alternative chosen by very few observations produces unstable, sometimes divergent, coefficients

cards.method: Classification evaluation: Brier decomposition, log score, reliability and PR curves
cards.when: a binary or categorical model produces probabilities, and both their ranking and their calibration must be assessed
cards.when_not: the model produces hard labels with no probabilities; the classes are so imbalanced that every metric is dominated by the majority

alternatives.criterion: ranking, insensitive to class balance
the positive class is rare
calibration of the probabilities

output_key_fields: auc, average_precision: ranking measures
brier: with its reliability, resolution and uncertainty decomposition
calibration_curve: predicted against realised frequency
confusion: at the chosen threshold

cards.when: several forecasts exist and combining them almost always beats selecting one
cards.when_not: one forecast dominates on every fold; the weight-estimation sample is too short and equal weights will do better

alternatives.criterion: the forecast combination puzzle: hard to beat
weight by past accuracy, no estimation of covariances
estimated weights, optionally constrained

improvement: accuracy against the best individual and against equal weights
method: which weighting produced them
interpretation_traps: THE FORECAST COMBINATION PUZZLE IS REAL: equal weights frequently beat estimated optimal weights out of sample, because estimating weights adds more variance than it removes bias
unconstrained regression weights can be negative or exceed one, which is legitimate but fragile; constraining them usually improves out-of-sample performance
weights estimated on the same data used to evaluate the combination overstate its benefit

cards.when: combining predictive DISTRIBUTIONS rather than points, where the pooling rule changes the shape of the answer

cards.method: Stacked generalisation of forecasters
cards.when: learning how to combine forecasts from their cross-validated errors, rather than from a fixed rule
cards.when_not: the cross-validation folds are too few for the meta-learner to be estimated; the components are near-identical

alternatives.criterion: few components, stable
you want learned weights with some structure
the best combination depends on the state

output_key_fields: meta_model: the fitted combination rule
weights: implied component weights, where the meta-learner is linear
cv_predictions: the out-of-fold predictions the meta-learner was trained on
improvement: against equal weights and the best component
interpretation_traps: THE META-LEARNER MUST BE TRAINED ON OUT-OF-FOLD PREDICTIONS; training it on in-sample fits leaks and produces weights that collapse onto the most overfitted component
the folds must respect time order for time-series data, or the combination learns from the future
a nonlinear meta-learner needs far more folds than a linear one and usually overfits with typical macro sample sizes

cards.method: Temporal-hierarchy combination: MAPA and THieF
cards.when: forecasts made at different frequencies for the same series disagree, and reconciling across the temporal hierarchy improves all of them
cards.when_not: there is a single frequency; the series cannot be aggregated to higher levels meaningfully

alternatives.criterion: one frequency only
aggregate, forecast and combine
full temporal-hierarchy reconciliation

output_key_fields: reconciled: forecasts coherent across every aggregation level
levels: the temporal aggregation levels used
weights: the reconciliation weights
improvement: accuracy per level against unreconciled forecasts
interpretation_traps: TEMPORAL AGGREGATION CHANGES THE APPARENT DYNAMICS: a series can look noisy monthly and strongly trending annually, which is exactly the information this method exploits
reconciliation guarantees coherence, not accuracy -- forecasts can be made coherent and worse if the covariance is badly estimated
the aggregation levels must divide the seasonal period evenly or the hierarchy is not well defined
sources: Athanasopoulos, Hyndman, Kourentzes & Petropoulos 2017 (European Journal of Operational Research 262:60-74)

fast, robust, the practitioner standard

the factors follow a time-series process

cards.method: Shadow short rate at the effective lower bound
cards.when: the policy rate is at its floor, and a curve model without the bound implies negative short rates the market cannot deliver

the widely used discrete-time construction
a continuous-time alternative with different properties

expected_lift_off: the expected time to leave the bound

bound: the effective lower bound imposed

cards.method: Bond excess-return predictability and the Cochrane-Piazzesi factor
cards.when: testing whether forward rates predict bond excess returns, which is the empirical case against the expectations hypothesis
cards.when_not: the sample is short relative to the overlapping horizon, where the inference is unreliable regardless of correction

alternatives.criterion: a simple, transparent test
a tent-shaped combination of forwards
you want a structural decomposition instead

output_key_fields: cp_factor: the fitted return-forecasting factor
r_squared: predictive fit per maturity
coefficients: forward-rate loadings, the tent shape
hac_inference: standard errors corrected for overlap

cards.method: Monthly Bry-Boschan dating with smoothing and cycle statistics
cards.when: the rule-based turning-point algorithm behind most published chronologies, with the censoring rules that make cycles meaningful
cards.when_not: the series is annual, where the censoring rules cannot apply; you want a probabilistic rather than deterministic chronology

alternatives.criterion: the standard deterministic rule
a probabilistic chronology
quarterly data with simplified rules

output_key_fields: peaks, troughs: the dated turning points
phases: expansion and contraction durations
amplitude, cumulation: depth and cumulative loss per phase
censoring: rules applied and turning points they removed
interpretation_traps: THE CENSORING RULES DO THE WORK: minimum phase and cycle durations are what stop the algorithm dating every wiggle, and changing them changes the chronology entirely
the algorithm cannot date turning points near the ends of the sample, so the most recent period is always provisional
smoothing before dating shifts turning points systematically, usually later
sources: Bry & Boschan 1971, Cyclical Analysis of Time Series (NBER)

cards.method: Online and sequential change detection
cards.when: detecting a regime change as soon as possible after it happens, rather than dating it retrospectively
cards.when_not: the analysis is retrospective, where offline segmentation is more accurate; false alarms are unacceptable and the delay budget is unlimited

alternatives.criterion: retrospective, most accurate
classical sequential detection
you want a run-length posterior

output_key_fields: detections: dated alarms
run_length_posterior: probability over time since the last change
delay: detection delay against known changes, where available
false_alarm_rate: at the chosen threshold
interpretation_traps: THERE IS ALWAYS A TRADE-OFF BETWEEN DETECTION DELAY AND FALSE ALARMS; a detector reported without both numbers cannot be assessed
online detectors are far less accurate than offline segmentation on the same data, which is the price of not seeing the future
the hazard rate in Bayesian detection is a prior on change frequency and drives the alarm rate directly
sources: Adams & MacKay 2007, Bayesian online changepoint detection (arXiv:0710.3742)

cards.method: Matrix-profile motif and discord detection
cards.when: finding repeated patterns and anomalies in a long series without specifying what to look for
cards.when_not: the series is short; the pattern length is unknown and results are very sensitive to it

alternatives.criterion: motif and discord discovery at a chosen window
you want regime boundaries, not patterns
you want periodicity, not motifs

output_key_fields: profile: the matrix profile and its index
motifs: the most repeated subsequences
discords: the most unusual subsequences
window: the subsequence length used
interpretation_traps: THE WINDOW LENGTH DETERMINES WHAT CAN BE FOUND: a motif shorter or longer than the window is invisible, and the results change completely with it
trivial matches -- a subsequence matching its own neighbour -- must be excluded or every point is its own motif
the matrix profile is scale sensitive unless the subsequences are normalised, which is the usual default and changes what counts as similar

cards.method: Adaptive lasso, square-root lasso and rigorous penalty selection
cards.when: variable selection where the penalty must be chosen by a rule that supports inference, not by cross-validation alone
cards.when_not: the design is low dimensional; you need exact zeros and the ridge alternative will not do

alternatives.criterion: prediction is the goal
you want the oracle selection property
you want a penalty independent of the unknown error variance

output_key_fields: coefficients: the penalised estimates
selected: the active set
lambda_: the penalty and the rule that chose it
penalty_loadings: heteroskedasticity-robust loadings, where used
interpretation_traps: CROSS-VALIDATED PENALTIES SELECT TOO MANY VARIABLES for inference purposes; the rigorous penalty exists precisely because the cross-validated one invalidates the post-selection theory
the square-root lasso's penalty does not depend on the unknown error variance, which is why it is pivotal and preferred in high dimensions
the adaptive lasso needs a consistent initial estimator, and with more variables than observations that is not free

the window length determines how fast the indicator moves and is a substantive choice

cards.when_not: the data are not a probability sample; the poverty line is not defined

a relative line at a share of median income

cards.method: Top incomes and Pareto tails
cards.when: the top of the income or wealth distribution is thin in surveys and heavy in reality, and a parametric tail is needed to say anything about it
cards.when_not: the top is well measured; there are too few top observations for a tail index to be estimated

alternatives.criterion: a single tail index
a semi-parametric index without fixing the threshold model
you want a full tail distribution, not one parameter

output_key_fields: alpha: the Pareto tail index; lower means heavier
threshold: where the tail begins
top_shares: shares of the top percentiles
goodness_of_fit: whether the Pareto assumption holds above the threshold
interpretation_traps: THE HILL ESTIMATOR IS ACUTELY SENSITIVE TO THE THRESHOLD, and the Hill plot is usually unstable enough that any index in a wide range can be justified
survey data systematically under-cover the top, so a tail fitted to survey data understates concentration regardless of the estimator
an index below 2 means infinite variance and below 1 an infinite mean, which invalidates many downstream statistics
sources: Blanchet, Fournier & Piketty 2022 (Review of Income and Wealth 68:357)

Output: alpha: the Pareto tail index; lower means heavier · threshold: where the tail begins · top_shares: shares of the top percentiles · goodness_of_fit: whether the Pareto assumption holds above the threshold
Pitfalls: THE HILL ESTIMATOR IS ACUTELY SENSITIVE TO THE THRESHOLD, and the Hill plot is usually unstable enough that any index in a wide range can be justified · survey data systematically under-cover the top, so a tail fitted to survey data understates concentration regardless of the estimator · an index below 2 means infinite variance and below 1 an infinite mean, which invalidates many downstream statistics
Sources: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009 (SIAM Review 51:661-703) · Blanchet, Fournier & Piketty 2022 (Review of Income and Wealth 68:357) · powerlaw

cards.method: Segregation and dissimilarity indices
cards.when: measuring how unevenly groups are distributed across areas, schools or firms
cards.when_not: there are only two areas, where the indices are degenerate; the group definition is not stable across units

alternatives.criterion: two groups, the standard measure
the experience of a group rather than evenness
more than two groups

output_key_fields: index: the requested segregation measure
decomposition: between and within larger areas
se: inference by simulation or bootstrap
n_units: the number of areas, which drives the bias
interpretation_traps: SEGREGATION INDICES ARE BIASED UPWARD WHEN UNITS ARE SMALL, because random allocation produces uneven counts -- the bias correction is not optional with small areas
the dissimilarity index measures evenness only; two cities with identical indices can differ completely in isolation and exposure
changing the areal unit changes the index, which is the modifiable areal unit problem in its purest form

cards.method: Spatial inequality decomposition
cards.when: splitting national inequality into what happens between regions and what happens within them
cards.when_not: there is no spatial dimension; the regional classification is unstable over the period

alternatives.criterion: exactly additive between and within
you want a Gini that accounts for neighbourhood
the Gini does not decompose cleanly and leaves a residual

output_key_fields: between, within: the two components
shares: each component's share of the total
by_region: within-region inequality per region
spatial_component: the neighbour-based part, where the spatial Gini is used
interpretation_traps: THE GINI DOES NOT DECOMPOSE ADDITIVELY when subgroup distributions overlap -- it leaves a residual overlap term, which is why the Theil index is used for decomposition
the between-share depends entirely on the regional classification; finer regions mechanically raise it
population-weighted and unweighted regional inequality answer different questions
sources: Rey & Smith 2013 (Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences 6:189)

cards.method: Intergenerational and income mobility
cards.when: measuring how much economic position persists between generations or over time, which inequality snapshots cannot show
cards.when_not: only one period or generation is observed; the linkage between generations is not reliable

alternatives.criterion: robust, scale free, the modern standard
the classic log-log measure, sensitive to lifecycle bias
you want the full mobility pattern

output_key_fields: rank_rank: the slope of child rank on parent rank
ige: the intergenerational elasticity
transition_matrix: quintile or decile mobility
upward_mobility: the expected rank of children from the bottom
interpretation_traps: THE INTERGENERATIONAL ELASTICITY IS SENSITIVE TO THE AGE AT WHICH INCOME IS MEASURED (lifecycle bias) and to changing inequality between generations; the rank-rank slope is robust to both, which is why it replaced it
single-year income is a noisy proxy for permanent income and attenuates every mobility measure
transition matrices with many cells and few observations produce zero probabilities that are artefacts of sample size
sources: Chetty, Hendren, Kline & Saez 2014 (Quarterly Journal of Economics 129:1553-1623)

cards.method: Polarisation indices
cards.when: inequality measures cannot distinguish a spread-out distribution from one splitting into clusters, and polarisation is about the clustering
cards.when_not: the distribution is plainly unimodal and no clustering is suspected

alternatives.criterion: bipolarisation around the median
general polarisation with an identification-alienation structure
the classic bipolarisation measure

output_key_fields: polarisation: the requested index
identification, alienation: the two components of the Esteban-Ray form
median_split: shares above and below the median
comparison: the Gini, for contrast
interpretation_traps: POLARISATION AND INEQUALITY CAN MOVE IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS: a transfer from a rich person to a middle-income person lowers the Gini and can raise bipolarisation
the Esteban-Ray index depends on a sensitivity parameter with no natural value; results must be reported across a range
polarisation measures require grouping or smoothing, and the grouping choice drives the identification component

cards.method: Equivalence scales and household-to-individual welfare aggregation
cards.when: household income must be adjusted for size and composition before it can be compared, and the scale chosen changes every distributional conclusion
cards.when_not: the unit of analysis is the household itself; the composition data needed for the scale are missing

alternatives.criterion: the European standard
simple, widely used in OECD comparisons
no economies of scale assumed

output_key_fields: equivalised: equivalised income per person
scale_values: the equivalence factor per household
sensitivity: how inequality and poverty move across scales
elasticity: the implied economies-of-scale elasticity
interpretation_traps: THE SCALE CHOICE MATERIALLY CHANGES MEASURED INEQUALITY AND POVERTY, and it changes them differently for households of different types -- reporting a sensitivity range is the honest practice
equivalised income is assigned to every household member, which assumes equal sharing within the household -- an assumption with no support in the data
comparisons across countries using different national scales are not comparable
sources: Buhmann, Rainwater, Schmaus & Smeeding 1988 (Review of Income and Wealth 34:115-142)
OECD 2013, Framework for Statistics on the Distribution of Household Income
