cards.method: Pseudo-real-time vintage construction from publication lags
cards.when: an honest out-of-sample exercise needs the data as they were, and a full vintage archive is rarely available
cards.when_not: a true vintage archive exists and should be used instead; the publication calendar is unknown

alternatives.criterion: the correct approach when available
approximate what was available
acceptable only for series that are never revised

output_key_fields: vintages: the constructed data as of each date
ragged_edge: the availability pattern at each vintage
publication_lags: the lags applied per series
coverage: how much of each vintage is real rather than assumed
interpretation_traps: PSEUDO-REAL-TIME CAPTURES THE RAGGED EDGE BUT NOT REVISIONS: it reproduces what was available, not what the values then were, and for heavily revised series that is the larger error
publication lags change over time and across statistical agencies; a constant lag is an approximation that biases early vintages
using final data in a forecast evaluation overstates accuracy, sometimes dramatically for real-activity series

cards.when: which vintage counts as the truth changes the measured accuracy, and the choice must be stated rather than defaulted
cards.when_not: the series is never revised, where the question does not arise

alternatives.criterion: forecasting what will be published
forecasting the true value
a compromise, released a stated number of periods later

cards.method: Revision-aware seasonal-adjustment diagnostics
cards.when: seasonal adjustment revises past values as new data arrive, and the size of those revisions is a property of the adjustment, not of the economy
cards.when_not: the series is not seasonally adjusted; the archive is too short for sliding spans

alternatives.criterion: stability of the adjustment across overlapping samples
how much the adjusted values move as data arrive
the practical size of the problem

output_key_fields: sliding_spans: maximum percentage difference across spans
revision_history: revisions to adjusted values by vintage
unstable_periods: periods failing the stability threshold
concurrent_vs_final: the systematic gap
interpretation_traps: A SERIES CAN PASS EVERY IN-SAMPLE ADJUSTMENT DIAGNOSTIC AND STILL REVISE HEAVILY; sliding spans and revision history are the only checks that see this
the conventional sliding-span thresholds are rules of thumb from the Census Bureau, not statistical tests
forecast extension at the end of the sample is what drives most of the revision, so the last observations are always the least reliable
sources: Findley, Monsell, Shulman & Pugh 1990 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 8:1-16)

cards.method: Homogeneous GMM panel vector autoregression
cards.when: short-T panels of countries or firms where the dynamics are assumed common and lags provide the instruments
cards.when_not: the time dimension is long enough for heterogeneous estimation; the slopes plainly differ across units

alternatives.criterion: slopes differ across units
short T, common dynamics
the series are persistent and difference GMM is weak

output_key_fields: params: the panel VAR coefficients
hansen_j: overidentification test
ar_tests: first- and second-order serial correlation in differences
irf, fevd: impulse responses and variance decompositions
interpretation_traps: INSTRUMENT PROLIFERATION IS THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: with many lags as instruments the Hansen test loses all power and reports a perfect p-value near 1, which is a warning sign rather than a pass
the AR(2) test in differences is the key diagnostic; a rejection means the lag structure is invalid
difference GMM is weak with persistent series, which is what system GMM exists to address -- at the cost of an extra assumption
sources: Roodman 2009 (Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics 71:135)

cards.when: testing causality across a panel where the relationship may hold in some units and not others
cards.when_not: the panel has strong cross-sectional dependence and no bootstrap is used; there is one unit

alternatives.criterion: homogeneity assumed
heterogeneous causality across units

cards.when: panel VAR inference assumes units are independent, and that assumption is almost always false for country panels
cards.when_not: the panel has one unit; the residuals are unavailable

alternatives.criterion: large N, small T
moderate dimensions
you want to remove the dependence rather than test it

output_key_fields: cd_statistic, p_value: the dependence test
average_correlation: mean absolute residual correlation
factor_structure: leading factors in the residuals
recommendation: whether robust inference or factor augmentation is needed

removing dependence by cross-sectional demeaning assumes a single common factor with equal loadings, which is restrictive

Output: foreign_variables: the constructed star variables per country · weights: the weight matrix used, row-normalised · weight_source: trade, financial or custom · concentration: how concentrated each country's weights are

Sources: Pesaran, Schuermann & Weiner 2004 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 22:129-162) · Dees, di Mauro, Pesaran & Smith 2007 (Journal of Applied Econometrics 22:1)

cards.method: Fitting continuous densities to probability bins
cards.when: surveys report probabilities over intervals, and almost every use of them needs a continuous density
cards.when_not: the respondent used one or two bins only, where a continuous fit is not identified

alternatives.criterion: the standard for bounded support
few bins, symmetric responses
many bins and no shape assumption wanted

output_key_fields: params: fitted distribution parameters per respondent
moments: mean, variance and skewness implied
fit_quality: how well the fitted density reproduces the reported bins
n_bins_used: respondents with too few bins to fit
interpretation_traps: RESPONDENTS USING ONE OR TWO BINS CANNOT SUPPORT A TWO-PARAMETER FIT; the convention of assigning a triangular or uniform density to them is an assumption that affects aggregate uncertainty measures
open-ended end bins require an assumption about their extent, and that assumption drives the variance
the aggregate density is the average of individual densities, which is not the density of the average
sources: Engelberg, Manski & Williams 2009 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 27:30-41)

cards.method: Disagreement and uncertainty from density forecasts
cards.when: survey densities contain two distinct things -- how uncertain each forecaster is, and how much they differ -- and conflating them is common
cards.when_not: only point forecasts are available, where uncertainty cannot be measured at all

alternatives.criterion: disagreement only, the common proxy
uncertainty only
both, plus their sum

output_key_fields: disagreement: variance of individual means
uncertainty: average individual variance
aggregate_variance: the sum, which is the variance of the aggregate density
correlation: between the two series over time
interpretation_traps: DISAGREEMENT IS NOT UNCERTAINTY: forecasters can agree precisely while all being very uncertain, and the dispersion of point forecasts measures only the first
the aggregate density's variance is the SUM of the two components, which is why using disagreement alone understates aggregate uncertainty
panel composition changes over time and moves disagreement without any change in beliefs

cards.method: Rational-expectations tests: Mincer-Zarnowitz and Coibion-Gorodnichenko
cards.when: testing whether survey expectations are unbiased and efficient, and whether forecasters update sluggishly
cards.when_not: the survey panel is too short; the forecast target is ambiguous

alternatives.criterion: unbiasedness and efficiency
information rigidity from forecast revisions
efficiency against a specific information set

output_key_fields: mz: unbiasedness and efficiency test
cg_coefficient: the error-on-revision coefficient measuring rigidity
implied_rigidity: the implied Kalman gain or attention parameter
individual_vs_consensus: rigidity at both levels, which differ
interpretation_traps: THE COIBION-GORODNICHENKO COEFFICIENT ON CONSENSUS DATA MEASURES INFORMATION RIGIDITY; the same regression on INDIVIDUAL data measures something different and is often negative -- the two must not be conflated
overlapping forecast horizons induce serial correlation, so HAC standard errors are required
rejecting rationality can reflect an asymmetric loss function rather than irrationality

cards.method: Survey weighting: raking, post-stratification and trimming
cards.when: the achieved sample does not match the population, and weights must be built and controlled before any estimate is produced
cards.when_not: the sample is a census; the population totals are unreliable

alternatives.criterion: few, well-populated cells
several marginal totals to match at once
extreme weights must be prevented

output_key_fields: weights: the final weights
design_effect: the variance inflation the weights cause
effective_sample_size: n over the design effect
trimmed: weights that hit the bounds
interpretation_traps: WEIGHTING TRADES BIAS FOR VARIANCE: a large design effect means the weights have cost you most of your sample, and the effective sample size is what should be reported
raking to inconsistent margins does not converge, and a truncated run silently returns weights matching nothing
trimming reduces variance and reintroduces the bias the weights were built to remove
sources: Valliant, Dever & Kreuter 2018, Practical Tools for Designing and Weighting Survey Samples

cards.method: Ordinal and rank agreement: Kendall W, kappa, Cronbach alpha and polychoric
cards.when: measuring how consistently respondents or raters order or score the same items
cards.when_not: there is one rater; the scale is continuous and ordinary correlation applies

alternatives.criterion: agreement on rankings across several raters
categorical agreement corrected for chance
internal consistency of an ordinal scale

output_key_fields: statistic: the requested agreement measure
conf_int: interval, usually by bootstrap
pairwise: agreement per rater pair
polychoric: the latent correlation matrix for ordinal items
interpretation_traps: CRONBACH'S ALPHA RISES MECHANICALLY WITH THE NUMBER OF ITEMS and is not a measure of unidimensionality; a high alpha on a multidimensional scale is routine and meaningless
kappa is sensitive to the marginal distribution, so it can be low despite high raw agreement when one category dominates
Pearson correlation between ordinal items is attenuated; the polychoric correlation is what a factor analysis of ordinal items needs
sources: Kendall & Babington Smith 1939 (Annals of Mathematical Statistics 10:275-287)

cards.method: Preprocessing and keyword extraction
cards.when: raw text must become a document-term matrix before anything else, and every choice in that pipeline changes downstream results
cards.when_not: the text is already tokenised and vectorised; the corpus is too small for frequency weighting to mean anything

alternatives.criterion: simple counts
downweights ubiquitous terms
phrases carry meaning single words lose

output_key_fields: dtm: the document-term matrix
vocabulary: the retained terms and the pruning applied
keywords: top terms per document by the chosen weighting
preprocessing: the exact steps applied, for reproducibility
interpretation_traps: THE STOP-WORD LIST AND THE PRUNING THRESHOLDS DETERMINE THE RESULT; a generic English stop-word list removes negations and modal verbs that carry the economic meaning in central-bank text
stemming conflates words with different economic meanings, and lemmatisation is usually the better choice for policy text
TF-IDF weights depend on the corpus, so a document's vector changes when other documents are added

cards.method: Topic models: LDA, correlated and dynamic
cards.when: discovering the themes in a large corpus and how they move over time, which no keyword list can do
cards.when_not: the corpus is small or the documents very short, where topics are unstable; you need supervised categories rather than discovered ones

alternatives.criterion: the standard, assumes topics are independent
topics co-occur systematically
topic content evolves over time

output_key_fields: topics: term distributions per topic
document_topics: topic shares per document
coherence: topic quality, which is how the topic count is chosen
n_topics: the number used and how it was selected
interpretation_traps: TOPIC LABELS ARE ASSIGNED BY THE ANALYST, not the model; the model returns term distributions, and naming them is interpretation that should be documented
topic solutions are not stable across random seeds, and reporting one run without checking stability is standard practice and standard error
the number of topics is chosen by coherence or perplexity, and these two criteria routinely disagree
sources: Blei, Ng & Jordan 2003 (Journal of Machine Learning Research 3:993-1022)
Hansen, McMahon & Prat 2018 (Quarterly Journal of Economics 133:801)

cards.method: Matrix-factorisation topics: NMF and latent semantic analysis
cards.when: a fast, deterministic alternative to probabilistic topic models, which is often more stable on short documents
cards.when_not: you need a generative model with document-level probabilities; the corpus is very large and sparse enough that a probabilistic model scales better

alternatives.criterion: non-negative, parts-based, deterministic given a seed
SVD-based, allows negative loadings
a probabilistic generative model

output_key_fields: components: term loadings per component
document_scores: component scores per document
explained_variance: for the SVD-based method
reconstruction_error: fit of the factorisation
interpretation_traps: LATENT SEMANTIC ANALYSIS PRODUCES NEGATIVE LOADINGS that have no interpretation as topic membership; NMF's non-negativity is what makes its components readable
these methods are deterministic given initialisation but sensitive to it; NMF with random initialisation still needs a seed
component count is chosen by reconstruction error, which decreases monotonically and therefore selects nothing on its own

cards.when: representing words or documents as vectors so semantic similarity becomes a computable distance
cards.when_not: the corpus is too small to train embeddings; you need interpretable features rather than dense vectors

alternatives.criterion: word-level semantics, trained on your corpus
document-level vectors
a simple document representation

similarity: nearest neighbours for queried terms

training_loss: convergence of the training

short informal text, handles intensity and negation
a domain-specific concept

alternatives.criterion: the classic readability indices
vocabulary richness
syntactic rather than lexical difficulty

lexical: type-token ratio and density
syntactic: sentence length and clause depth
n_words: document length, which several indices depend on

cards.method: Cross-spectral analysis: coherence, phase and gain
cards.when: how two series co-move frequency by frequency, and whether one leads the other at business-cycle frequencies
cards.when_not: the series are non-stationary and no transformation makes them so; the sample is too short for frequency resolution

alternatives.criterion: you want lead-lag in the time domain
co-movement by frequency band
the relationship changes over time

output_key_fields: coherence: squared coherence by frequency
phase: phase difference, convertible to a lead in periods
gain: the frequency-dependent amplitude ratio
conf_band: significance band for coherence
interpretation_traps: THE PHASE SPECTRUM IS ONLY INTERPRETABLE WHERE COHERENCE IS SIGNIFICANT; phase estimates at incoherent frequencies are uniformly distributed noise and reading a lead off them is meaningless
phase is identified modulo 2 pi, so a lead of k periods and one of k plus a full cycle are indistinguishable
smoothing the periodogram trades bias against variance and directly controls how much coherence you see
sources: Priestley 1981, Spectral Analysis and Time Series
Koopmans 1974, The Spectral Analysis of Time Series

cards.method: Multitaper and Welch spectral estimation with confidence intervals
cards.when: the raw periodogram is inconsistent, and a usable spectrum needs smoothing or tapering with honest uncertainty
cards.when_not: you need the exact periodogram ordinates; the series is too short for any segmentation

alternatives.criterion: simple, widely used
the best bias-variance trade-off, with proper degrees of freedom
you want a smooth spectrum from a fitted model

output_key_fields: spectrum: the estimated spectral density
frequencies: the frequency grid
conf_int: confidence band, from the chi-squared degrees of freedom
resolution: the frequency resolution actually achieved
interpretation_traps: THE RAW PERIODOGRAM IS NOT CONSISTENT: its variance does not fall as the sample grows, so an unsmoothed spectral plot is noise however long the series

the number of tapers sets the degrees of freedom and therefore the confidence band, and it must be reported

cards.method: Frequency-domain Granger causality
cards.when: causality can run at business-cycle frequencies and not at high frequencies, which a single time-domain statistic averages away
cards.when_not: the series are non-stationary; the VAR the decomposition rests on is misspecified

alternatives.criterion: one summary statistic
causality by frequency
linear feedback decomposed by frequency

output_key_fields: causality_spectrum: the measure by frequency
band_statistics: aggregated over named frequency bands
critical_values: which are frequency dependent
significant_bands: where causality is detected
interpretation_traps: THE FREQUENCY-DOMAIN MEASURE INTEGRATES TO THE TIME-DOMAIN STATISTIC, so a zero overall statistic is consistent with strong causality at some frequencies offset by none at others

critical values vary with frequency and using a single threshold across the spectrum is wrong

cards.when: decomposing a nonlinear, non-stationary series into oscillatory modes defined by the data rather than by a fixed basis
cards.when_not: the series is stationary and a Fourier or wavelet basis is appropriate and better understood

alternatives.criterion: a fixed basis with known properties
data-driven modes, handles non-stationarity
mode mixing is a problem

residual: the trend left after extraction
instantaneous_frequency: from the Hilbert transform
n_modes: how many were extracted

cards.method: Synchrosqueezing and reassigned time-frequency transforms
cards.when: a sharper time-frequency picture than a spectrogram, which smears energy across frequencies
cards.when_not: you only need a global spectrum; the series is too short for any time-frequency localisation

alternatives.criterion: the standard, smeared but simple
sharpened and invertible
sharpened but not invertible

ridges: extracted instantaneous-frequency curves
components: reconstructed modes from the ridges
invertible: whether the transform supports reconstruction
interpretation_traps: REASSIGNMENT SHARPENS BUT DESTROYS INVERTIBILITY; synchrosqueezing sharpens and remains invertible, which is the reason to prefer it when components must be reconstructed
sharpening does not create resolution that the data lack -- it redistributes energy, and closely spaced components remain unresolvable

cards.method: Lomb-Scargle periodogram and band-variance shares
cards.when: the series is irregularly sampled or has gaps, where the ordinary periodogram is not defined
cards.when_not: the sampling is regular, where standard spectral methods are better understood and faster

alternatives.criterion: irregular sampling

alternatives.alt: interpolate then use a standard periodogram
alternatives.criterion: gaps are few and short
you want variance shares rather than a spectrum

output_key_fields: power: the Lomb-Scargle periodogram
frequencies: the evaluated grid

Output: loadings: factor loadings after rotation · communalities, uniquenesses: variance explained and specific per variable · n_factors: chosen and the criterion that chose it · adequacy: KMO and Bartlett tests of whether factoring is appropriate
Pitfalls: FACTOR ANALYSIS AND PRINCIPAL COMPONENTS ARE DIFFERENT MODELS: PCA has no unique variances and its components are not latent factors, and the two are conflated constantly · the rotation is not identified by the data -- varimax, promax and oblimin give different loadings from the same fit, and the choice is interpretive · the KMO and Bartlett tests should be run first; factoring data that are nearly uncorrelated produces meaningless factors
Sources: Fabrigar, Wegener, MacCallum & Strahan 1999 (Psychological Methods 4:272-299) · Hyvarinen & Oja 2000 (Neural Networks 13:411) · factor-analyzer

cards.method: Time-series clustering: DTW k-means, k-Shape and kernel k-means
cards.when: series must be grouped by shape rather than by point-in-time level, which euclidean clustering cannot do
cards.when_not: the series are aligned and euclidean distance is adequate; the series are too long for the distance computation

alternatives.criterion: series are aligned and same length
shapes are similar but shifted or warped
shape-based with normalised cross-correlation

output_key_fields: labels: cluster assignment
centroids: cluster centroids, which are averaged series
inertia: within-cluster distance
distance: the distance measure used
interpretation_traps: AVERAGING SERIES UNDER DYNAMIC TIME WARPING IS NOT THE ARITHMETIC MEAN; naive averaging destroys the shape the warping was meant to preserve, which is why barycentre averaging exists
DTW without a warping-window constraint is both slow and prone to pathological alignments; the Sakoe-Chiba band is the usual fix
series must be normalised before shape clustering or the clusters reflect scale rather than shape

cards.method: Elastic distance measures at scale
cards.when: computing shape-aware distances between many series efficiently, which every shape-based method needs underneath
cards.when_not: euclidean distance is adequate; the number of pairs makes any elastic measure infeasible even with lower bounds

alternatives.criterion: aligned, equal-length series
warped alignment, the standard elastic measure
the series contain outliers or gaps DTW handles poorly

output_key_fields: distance_matrix: the pairwise distances
alignment: the warping path for a queried pair
measure: which distance was used
lower_bound_pruning: how many computations were avoided
interpretation_traps: DYNAMIC TIME WARPING IS NOT A METRIC -- it violates the triangle inequality, so methods requiring a metric space (some clustering and indexing schemes) are not valid on it
an unconstrained warping window allows pathological alignments that match a whole series to one point; constraining it is standard practice
the distance is not scale invariant unless the series are normalised first
sources: Sakoe & Chiba 1978 (IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing 26:43-49)

cards.method: Nonlinear embeddings: UMAP, t-SNE, Isomap and kernel PCA
cards.when: high-dimensional structure that linear projection cannot reveal, for visualisation or as features
cards.when_not: linear structure suffices (-> PCA); the embedding will be used for distances, which these methods do not preserve

alternatives.criterion: linear, preserves global structure, invertible
preserves more global structure than t-SNE, faster
excellent local structure, unreliable global structure

output_key_fields: embedding: the low-dimensional coordinates
trustworthiness: how well local neighbourhoods are preserved
parameters: the neighbourhood and distance parameters used
n_components: the embedding dimension
interpretation_traps: DISTANCES AND CLUSTER SIZES IN A t-SNE PLOT ARE NOT MEANINGFUL: the gap between two clusters says nothing about their dissimilarity, and this is the most misread output in applied machine learning
the perplexity or neighbour parameter changes the picture completely, and a structure visible at one setting can vanish at another
these embeddings are not stable across seeds and must not be used as reproducible features without fixing one
sources: van der Maaten & Hinton 2008 (Journal of Machine Learning Research 9:2579-2605)

cards.method: Biclustering and co-clustering
cards.when: rows and columns should be grouped together, because a subset of variables defines a subset of observations
cards.when_not: only rows or only columns need grouping; the matrix is too sparse for coherent blocks

alternatives.criterion: rows only
a checkerboard block structure
rows and columns cluster with different counts

output_key_fields: row_labels, column_labels: the two partitions
biclusters: the identified blocks
consensus_score: agreement against a reference where available
n_clusters: the counts used
interpretation_traps: BICLUSTERING ASSUMES A SPECIFIC BLOCK STRUCTURE -- checkerboard for co-clustering -- and data without that structure will still be partitioned into apparent blocks
the method is sensitive to row and column normalisation, and the normalisation choice determines what counts as a block
biclusters generally cannot overlap in these algorithms, which is restrictive for real data
